- the only place we need to update an issue file when the issue is partially complete is the "current behavior" section. We don't need to add append-logs to the end, it's better to update the main body to align with the current design, and the current behavior with the current status.

### feedback_cross_language_pitfalls.md

```markdown
---
name: Cross-language design pitfalls
description: Three approaches the user rejected when designing SoraMech's cross-language wire format
type: feedback
originSessionId: e9ed70c7-2b63-425c-987c-6431040bedfb
---
When designing anything that touches the cross-language data path, avoid these three shapes — the user pushed back on each and the rejections are load-bearing for the architecture.

**1. Don't propose runtime "handles" that route operations back to the originating spec.**

**Why:** Real library functions in the wild (qsort, libcurl, anything from libc) expect actual native values — a real `int (*)(int,int)` function pointer, a real `char *` — not a SoraMech-issued id string. They can't be modified to participate in our runtime's routing scheme. The wire must carry data the destination spec can fully reconstruct into a native value, not opaque tokens.

**How to apply:** When a value seems hard to serialize (function pointers, coroutines, opaque pointers), decompose to data primitives (address + signature, bytecode + upvalues, ptr + length). If the destination needs a callable, the destination spec synthesizes one at reconstruction time (libffi trampoline for C, `ffi.cast` for LuaJIT). The "phone home" callback that the trampoline performs internally is fine — it's an artifact of the destination spec's reconstruction, not exposed in the wire format. What's forbidden is a wire primitive that says "operations on this value cross back to the source."

**2. Don't propose pair-wise language conversion paths (lua→c, c→lua, etc.).**

**Why:** N languages means N² conversion paths, which means adding a new language breaks the existing ones. The wire must use a language-agnostic intermediate (JSON) and every spec must implement only the two pair-symmetric callbacks (`to_json`, `from_json`). New language = implement those two functions, nothing else touches.

**How to apply:** Never write code that names two specific languages in a conversion context. Specs only ever see JSON on the wire. If a JSON primitive needs an extension (like `$function_pointer`), it lives in the universal JSON contract, not as a lua-spec-specific or c-spec-specific concept.

**3. Don't propose per-function annotations for type ambiguities (lengths, discriminators, callback signatures).**

**Why:** The user pointed out that "discriminator" is a vocab word the system has no general way to ask about. We can't prompt "which param is the length?" because that pairing convention lives in the function's English documentation, not its types. Asking the user to write annotations means asking them to know specialized vocabulary they didn't sign up for.

**How to apply:** When a function signature has ambiguous types (`char *` with no length, `union` with no tag, `void *` with no signature), expose each parameter as a separate input slot on the box. The user wires the slots according to the function's documentation — `p` from one source, `n` from another. The system never infers pairings; the user expresses them by wiring. If the destination needs a length and no length wire is provided, the wire compile fails with a plain-English fix-it message ("destination needs length, source provides only a pointer — wire a length input here").

**Common thread:** all three rejections are the same principle in different clothes — **SoraMech bends to the language, not the other way around.** Users write idiomatic code in their language. Libraries are used as-is. Specs are self-contained and pair-symmetric. The system stays out of the user's vocabulary.

```

### project_cross_language_wire.md

```markdown
---
name: Cross-language wire format
description: Dual-ring slot per port (native ring + JSON ring + ordering ring). JSON only at language borders. Per-edge classification at graph load; per-cell precision at runtime.
type: project
originSessionId: 5670858b-274f-49c4-89b8-a4b83ce33d7c
---
Design corrected 2026-05-21 — replaces the older "JSON always" framing.

**Each input slot is a dual-ring buffer.** Per port: one `ring_native` (consumer-language native bytes), one `ring_json` (JSON bytes from cross-language producers), and one `ring_order` of `(which_ring, idx)` tuples in arrival order. Allocate `ring_json` and `ring_order` lazily — same-language-only ports pay nothing for them.

**Push selects ring by per-edge bit.** Producer's spec writes native bytes to `ring_native` if `output_edge_native[j]` is true; otherwise calls `native_to_json` and writes to `ring_json`. Either way, pushes a `(which_ring, idx)` tuple to `ring_order`.

**Pop reads ordering ring first.** Dispatch pops `ring_order`, gets `(which_ring, idx)`, then pops the indicated cell. The consumer's spec receives `(input_data[i], input_native[i])` per input port and dispatches per flag — decode native or decode JSON.

**Why dual-ring instead of per-port classification.** Per-port (slot is all-JSON if any fan-in is cross-lang) is the pessimistic approximation — same-language values eat JSON cost on mixed-fan-in ports. Dual-ring is precise per cell: a port fed by one Lua box and one C box keeps the Lua cells native and JSON-encodes only the C-sourced cells.

**Why JSON for the cross-language ring (not pair-wise paths, not type-annotated raw bytes).** JSON's structure is self-describing — every language has a natural mapping for object/array/number/string/bool/null. Adding language K means K's spec implements its own `native_to_json` and `json_to_native`. N spec-pairs, not N² language-pair paths. The native ring's format is each spec's private choice — Lua may pick msgpack or `cjson.encode` or a custom binary form; C uses `memcpy` of the wrapper struct; Bash uses strings.

**Sentinel primitives for non-JSON-mappable values.** `$ref` (pointer + length into the large-value heap), `$function_pointer`, `$lang_opaque` ("these bytes are language-X-internal"). Carried inside the JSON ring as object-shaped sentinels. Cross-language receivers that can't reconstruct fail at wire compile.

**`$function_pointer` reconstruction — wrapper binary + persistent subprocess (issue 318, amended 2026-05-22).** Earlier design had the consumer's spec FFI-cast the raw process-local address. Rejected: FFI is language-pair-specific, biases SoraMech toward the Lua↔C corner, breaks the N-not-N² rule. Replacement: at map-compile time the compiler asks the *producing* spec to compile the referenced function + its enumerable dependencies into a standalone wrapper binary on disk that speaks a small line protocol on stdio. The consumer spec spawns one persistent subprocess per `$function_pointer` it receives and talks to it over the same socket-like channel used for any out-of-process spec. Every language pays the same price; new languages only implement "compile a function to a wrapper binary" — no pair-wise FFI knowledge required.

**Spec `invoke` signature change.** Collapses `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` into one `invoke` with per-input/per-output flags: `int invoke(handle, ..., const int *input_native, int n_inputs, int output_native, void *out_buf, ...)`. The spec dispatches per input internally. This is the contract change that unblocks 306/307's typed marshalling.

**Two compile-time layers stack:**
- **Per-edge classification (issue 312, this design)** — graph loader computes `input_edge_native[]` and `output_edge_native[]` on each box; dispatch routes pushes accordingly. This issue is the wire-format design.
- **Same-language source merge (issue 313, research / blocked)** — concatenate every same-language box's source into one translation unit per language. Boxes still run as separate thread-pool tasks; what 313 thins is the spec invocation overhead inside the merged region (direct call into the worker's `lua_State` instead of dlsym + marshal + bridge). The dual-ring slot machinery does NOT collapse — tasks still need slots to wait for sibling inputs. 313 makes the ring cells cheaper to read/write; it doesn't remove them.

**Three rejected design shapes** (kept here so they don't get reinvented):
1. **Handles back-routing to the owning spec** — library functions in the wild can't be modified to use SoraMech-shaped handles. Rejected.
2. **Pair-wise language paths** — every new language would have to grow N-1 translation paths against existing languages. Rejected. The dual-ring's "two rings per slot" is the dimension-cap that prevents this.
3. **Per-function discriminator / length annotations on the wire** — the system has no universal vocabulary to ask "is param 2 the length?" Rejected; the user expresses these by wiring two separate input slots.

**How to apply:** When discussing wire format, slot store shape, dispatch routing, or spec callbacks: think dual-ring (native, JSON, ordering) per slot, per-edge classification at push time, per-cell tag at pop time, JSON-only-at-borders, language-private native bytes everywhere else.

```

### project_custom_translation_specs.md

```markdown
---
name: Custom translation specs per port
description: Users can override the default native/JSON wire path on any input port for any reason — a knob in the wire format vocabulary (issue 246)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**Per-port custom translation specs** let the user intervene at a specific input port and replace the default dual-ring decode path with user-written code. The override applies to that one port; the rest of the graph uses the default native-or-JSON path from issue 312.

**Motivating cases (any reason qualifies, not just cross-language):**
- Cross-language ambiguity the default specs can't infer: a C++ class with methods landing at a C box (drop methods? expose as fn pointers? restructure?), a `void *` carrying a libcurl handle, a union whose discriminator is on a separate wire.
- Same-language reshape: massaging a value into a different shape on its way in (rename fields, drop a layer, project a subset) without adding a transform box on the canvas.
- Validation / coercion: clamp a number, enforce a schema, fail loudly on unexpected shapes.

**How it composes with the dual-ring design:**
- The custom spec runs at *pop* time on the consumer side, after the ordering ring has been consulted and the cell has been read from the appropriate ring. The user's code receives the decoded value (native or JSON-decoded) and produces whatever the consumer's `invoke` will see.
- A port with a custom translation gets its own wire color in the editor (issue 245) — visible signal that this port doesn't use the default path.

**Why:** The default native/JSON contract covers the cases JSON's structure handles cleanly. Everything outside that needs a user escape hatch — *and* the same hatch is useful for purely-local "I want this input shaped differently" cases. One mechanism, many uses.

**How to apply:** When the design needs an override knob on the cross-language path, propose "custom translation spec on the destination port" rather than inventing per-function annotations, type discriminator metadata, or producer-side conversion hints (all three were rejected — see feedback_cross_language_pitfalls). The port is the unit of override; the spec is user code; the rest stays default.

```

### project_editor_visual_language.md

```markdown
---
name: Editor visual language for wires
description: Wire color in the canvas editor encodes language pairing across the edge, not just routing kind — a UI invariant future work should respect (issue 245)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**Wires are colored by language pairing across the edge**, with a separate color for wires whose destination port carries a user-written custom translation (issue 246). Pre-245 wires were colored purely by routing kind (default slate-blue, comparator branches orange/blue/green).

**The pairing-based palette:**
- **Same-language hop** — the wire carries native bytes; default neutral color.
- **Cross-language hop (forest green, ~`#228b22`)** — different producer/consumer languages; runtime translates via JSON at the wire. The color is a standing reminder that encode + decode is happening on that hop.
- **Custom-translation hop** — a third distinct color signaling the destination port has a user-written translation spec overriding the default path.
- Branch-routing colors (orange/blue/green from comparator boxes) compose on top — routing kind and language pairing are orthogonal axes the editor must show simultaneously.

**Why:** The runtime treats same-lang and cross-lang hops very differently (dual-ring slot design, issue 312), but pre-245 the editor gave the box author no visual signal that the JSON translation step existed. It was invisible until someone read the dispatch code. Translation cost should be legible from the canvas.

**How to apply:** Any future editor work that touches wire rendering must preserve "color encodes language pairing." Don't propose recoloring schemes that overload the cross-language signal onto another concept. New routing concepts get new axes (line style, glyphs, animation) rather than stealing color. When discussing wire visuals, name both axes — routing kind AND language pairing — even if only one is changing.

```

### project_encapsulated_map.md

```markdown
---
name: Encapsulated map as box
description: A sub-map opens as a single box on a parent canvas. Data boxes marked externally-supplied become input ports; write boxes marked externally-consumed become output ports. The documented exception to single-output-per-box (issue 248, amended 2026-05-23)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**A map directory has two ways to be opened:** as the top-level graph (existing map-select UI), or as an **encapsulated box** on the currently-edited parent map (issue 248). Opening through the file browser while a parent map is open instantiates the sub-map as a single box on the parent's canvas.

**The encapsulation contract — symmetric input and output toggles:**
- **Inputs:** any `data` box inside the sub-map can be toggled "externally-supplied" in its inspector. Each such box becomes a typed input port on the encapsulated box.
- **Outputs:** any `write` box inside the sub-map can be toggled "externally-consumed" in its inspector. Each such box surfaces as a **distinct output port** on the encapsulated box. A write box with the toggle on can still write to its `path` if one is set — the file destination and the parent-wire destination are independent.

**Encapsulated maps are the documented exception to issue 218's "single output per box" rule.** They have *N* output ports — one per externally-consumed write box, where *N* may be zero (pure side-effect map), one, or many. Every other box kind still has exactly one output.

**Rejected earlier design (2026-05-21):** packing all write-box outputs into a single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, single wire out. Rejected 2026-05-23 because it would have repurposed file-writing machinery to emit strings into wires — substituting one mechanism for another. The symmetric toggle design preserves the `write` box's "terminate a value" semantics and treats the destination kind as a mode toggle.

**Why:** Encapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph. The parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals — it sees declared input ports, declared output ports, and known semantics. Sub-maps can be edited independently, reused across parents, and packaged once for distribution. This is the closest SoraMech gets to "user-defined functions" while staying graph-native.

**How to apply:** When discussing map composition, reuse, or "how do users build libraries of behavior" — encapsulation is the answer. Don't propose alternative function-abstraction mechanisms (named subgraphs as text references, macro-style inlining, blob-packed outputs) without explicitly weighing them against the symmetric-toggle shape. Both toggles (`externally-supplied` on data boxes, `externally-consumed` on write boxes) are the user-facing port-declaration mechanism — don't invent a separate "ports manifest" file.

```

### project_soramech.md

```markdown
---
name: SoraMech project context
description: Core architecture decisions, file layout, and execution model for SoraMech, across phase 2 (current) and phase 3 (designed)
type: project
originSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a
---
SoraMech is a visual FSM/dataflow editor and execution engine at /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/.

**Why:** Primary use case is LLM orchestration on the SoraMind Alpine cluster. Strings flow between boxes like variables. History is explicit, loaded from disk only when a box needs it.

**Three independent programs sharing a map directory:**
- `src/006-server-main.lua` — thin HTTP file CRUD proxy. No runner management.
- Runner — phase 2: `src/007-runner-main.lua` (synchronous Lua). Phase 3: `soramech-pool` (C binary, designed in issues 301–311, not yet built).
- `assets/index.html` — vanilla JS canvas editor. Editor only — no run button. Compile button (issue 222) is a phase 2 placeholder; it triggers the phase 3 build pipeline (issue 219).

**Key architecture decisions (current truth):**
- Each box is its own JSON file in `boxes/<id>.json`. Connections written to BOTH endpoint files; loader validates both ends agree — hard error if not.
- **Single output wire per box** (issue 218 complete). No `outputs` array. The function returns one value; routing is by `from_branch` on the connection.
- **Comparator-based branching** (issue 210) — replaces the earlier `branch` box kind with named ports. A box may carry a `comparand`; the dispatch layer fires `lt`/`eq`/`gt` connections. No spec is invoked for comparators.
- **Iterator boxes** (issue 221) — pure routing primitives, no `ref`/`fn`. Dispatch layer cycles through `iterator_outputs` based on a per-task counter.
- **Phase 2 drivers** are shell scripts under `drivers/` (one process per call, stdout as channel). **Phase 3 language specs** are `.so` libraries under `langs/<name>/spec.so` loaded via `dlopen` (issue 303). Lua and C are in-process; Bash is out-of-process via Unix domain socket.
- Data files: per-map JSON in `data/`. Section-level `constant` flag. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua`.
- State/ephemeral: `tmp/` is a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Phase 2 writes `last-run.json` (single doc). Phase 3 writes `last-run.jsonl` (JSON Lines, issue 311) — decoupled from the editor, consumed by LLMs / CLI viewers / test harness.
- **Phase 3 runtime model**: C pool runner owns a 3d-rts task pool; per-task slots in process heap (issue 302) with refcounting and a separate large-value heap; dispatch layer (304) is the worker action; graph loader is C (305), no embedded Lua at the runner level. Phase 2's synchronous executor retires when phase 3 lands.

**How to apply:** When working on any component, respect the three-way separation. Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server. Map directory format is the only shared contract. The phase 2 driver model and the phase 3 spec model coexist conceptually (phase 2 is current, phase 3 is fully designed) but the runtime mechanism differs entirely; box JSON and the editor are unchanged across the cutover.

```

### project_threading.md

```markdown
---
name: threading_model
description: SoraMech's threading model — phase 2 synchronous, phase 3 SoraMech-owned C thread pool with per-port slots and language specs
type: project
originSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a
---
**Phase 2 (current)**: synchronous executor in `src/004-executor.lua`. Single-threaded, sequential box execution. One driver shell-out per box call. The phase 2 path goes away when phase 3 lands — no fallback, no coroutine intermediate.

**Phase 3 (designed, not yet built)**: C pool runner with a SoraMech-owned thread pool. The 3d-rts pool at `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` is the **design reference**, not vendored — SoraMech owns its pool implementation so the spawn primitive, worker context, init barrier, and iterator-pinning extensions are all under our control. The architecture is fully specified across issues 301–313.

Key phase 3 concepts:
- **Per-input-port slots** (not per-task), allocated at graph load and durable for the run. Each slot is a ring buffer (`n_cells` cells of `cell_capacity` bytes). 1-cell slots use peek-not-drain (literals, single-push wires); N-cell slots use pop-and-drain (queued / multi-push wires). No per-slot refcounting — slot lifetime is the whole run.
- **Tasks are ephemeral**: spawned dynamically by the dispatch layer when a box's input set is ready. Tasks carry just `box_id` and a counter snapshot. Box state (counter, input slots, language handle) is durable.
- **Language specs** under `langs/<name>/spec.so`, loaded via `dlopen` at startup. Uniform `lang_spec_t`. No language is privileged.
- **Same-language fast path** (issue 312): wire format defaults to JSON, but two adjacent same-language boxes use the language's native serialization (Lua `lua_dump`, C struct memcpy). Compile-time wire classification picks the path.
- **In-process specs** (Lua, C) via `lua_pcall` / `dlsym`. **Out-of-process specs** (Bash) via Unix domain sockets to a persistent per-worker subprocess.
- **Dispatch layer** (304) is the worker-side action: pop inputs → branch on box mode → invoke spec → push to downstream input slots → end. No blocking, no wait lists; tasks spawn on input arrival and run to completion.
- **Iterator and comparator routing** in the dispatch layer. Comparator runs the function and routes by output value. Iterator skips the function and routes by per-box counter (atomic spawn-time increment). Iterator tasks parallelize across workers; ordering preserved via per-push counter tags on consumer slots.
- **No-null rule** (issue 230): every input port must be wired, given a literal, or marked optional. Compile fails on missing inputs.
- **Init barrier**: pool startup waits until every worker has run every spec's `init(worker_idx)` before submitting tasks. Avoids tasks landing on uninitialized handles.
- **Hard-crash error policy**: nonzero return from any spec aborts the program.
- **Blocking semantics**: long-running operations tie up a worker. Pool size is the budget. Cooperative split (kickoff + check-done iterator) avoids holding a worker. See `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.

**Effil is explicitly NOT used.** Coroutines are not used. The C pool is the chosen mechanism. 3d-rts is referenced as design inspiration, not vendored.

**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC: phase 2 is synchronous shell-out drivers; phase 3 is the SoraMech-owned C pool runner with `lang_spec_t`, per-port slot stores, and dispatch-layer routing. Never suggest effil. 3d-rts is a reference, not a dependency. Issues 301–313 carry the design.

```

I meant the C preprocessor — the standalone tool that handles #include, #define, macro expansion. It's a C\n  utility, ships with gcc, and we're already shelling out to gcc for the compile step. To remove the ambiguity entirely we just invoke gcc -E\n   (preprocess-only mode) which is what compilers actually call. No C++ in the pool runner.\n\n  Library types vs spec rules — yes, separate\n\n  Important distinction you drew, and it changes the design. Two different scopes:\n\n  Library functions are immutable. Some 1990s C library function takes a void (*callback)(int) parameter and returns a struct rusage*. We\n  don't get to refuse it. The parser walks the signature, identifies the un-serializable pieces, and the resulting \"signature\" carries flags\n  like \"param 2 is a callback hole\" and \"return value is a pointer to an opaque struct.\"\n\n  The spec config is where the user resolves the holes. When the editor renders the box for this library function, the un-serializable\n  parameters become editor slots that demand a resolution rule. Concretely, for each hole the user picks one of:\n\n  - Wire from another box (the default for serializable params)\n  - Pass a constant (the user types a literal value into a slot)\n  - Pass NULL / a default zero (for optional params)\n  - Callback into the graph (the parameter is a function pointer; the user picks a Lua/C/bash box that should run when the C library invokes\n  the callback; SoraMech generates a C trampoline)\n  - Ignore the return value (for ptr-to-opaque returns the user doesn't care about)\n\n  The schema captures these choices per parameter and the wrapper generator emits the appropriate glue. Box JSON for a library box becomes\n  something like:\n\n  { \"id\": \"qsort_box\", \"kind\": \"call\", \"lang\": \"c\",\n    \"ref\": \"<stdlib.h>\", \"fn\": \"qsort\", \"link_libs\": [],\n    \"param_rules\": {\n      \"base\":    \"wire_in:items\",\n      \"nmemb\":   \"wire_in:count\",\n      \"size\":    \"constant:4\",\n      \"compar\":  \"callback:Lua:compare_box\"\n    } }\n\n  (Editor writes this; user doesn't type it.)\n\n  This isolates the rule \"errors loudly on un-serializable types\" to only the user-written code case (where the user does control the API and\n   can fix it). For library functions the parser produces a signature with holes, and the holes get filled in the spec config.\n\n  \"C is just built-ins and structs, right?\"\n\n  Almost. The full set of type forms in C is:\n\n  - Primitives — int / long / char / double / etc, plus the signed/unsigned and width variants\n  - Pointers — T* for any T\n  - Arrays — T[N] (or T[] decayed at function-call sites)\n  - Structs — collection of named fields\n  - Unions — alternative interpretations of the same memory\n  - Enums — named integer constants, but always backed by an int\n  - Function pointers — a special-case pointer\n  - typedefs — aliases for any of the above\n\n  For JSON round-tripping:\n\n  - Primitives → JSON number/boolean/string. Always works.\n  - Pointer-to-primitive + length → \"bytes\" or \"array of T.\" Works.\n  - Pointer-to-struct + length → JSON array of objects. Works.\n  - Structs → JSON objects. Works.\n  - Arrays → JSON arrays. Works.\n  - Enums → JSON number (or JSON string by name, our choice). Works.\n  - Unions → ambiguous without a discriminator; user resolves in the spec config (which variant is active).\n  - Function pointers → callback holes per above.\n  - Pointers without a length → ambiguous (how many elements?); user resolves in the spec config (either \"one element\" / \"null-terminated\" /\n  \"size from param N\").\n\n  So the parser walks any C type tree down to primitives and produces a serialization plan. The plan can have unresolved nodes (callback\n  holes, union discriminator unknowns, length-unknown pointers) that the spec config fills in.\n\n  C struct → Lua table round-trip\n\n  Yes, this works cleanly. C → JSON → Lua:\n\n  struct point { int x; int y; }  →  { \"x\": 1, \"y\": 2 }  →  { x=1, y=2 }  (Lua table)\n\n Lua → JSON → C requires the destination C type to be known (which it\n   always is, because the receiving C box declared its input). The Lua\n   spec's native_to_json walks the table and emits JSON; the receiving\n   C box's wrapper parses the JSON into the typed struct it expects.\n  Mismatches (Lua table missing a field, wrong type, extra fields) get\n   rejected at unpack time with a precise error.\n\n  Lua-specific values landing in C\n\n  The hard cases you pointed at:\n\n  - Lua function in a Lua table that crosses to C. Only meaningful if\n  the receiving C field is a function pointer. SoraMech handles this\n  via the callback rule: the user declares in the spec that this C\n  field is a callback to a Lua function; the wrapper generator emits a\n   C trampoline that captures a reference to the Lua function\n  (registered in LUA_REGISTRYINDEX) and invokes it when called.\n  - Lua-only types (coroutine, userdata, metatables): can't cross to\n  C. The Lua spec's native_to_json refuses them with a clear error.\n  The user moves them or restructures.\n\n  So the rule is: Lua → C only succeeds if every Lua value has a C\n  type that can receive it. Most do (numbers, strings,\n  tables-as-structs, functions-as-callbacks). The exotic ones\n  (coroutines, raw userdata) don't.\n\n  Is infer_signature part of the spec?\n\n  Yes — and you've pushed me to make it part of the spec contract\n  uniformly. Every spec exposes:\n\n  typedef struct {\n      /* ... */\n  } sm_signature_t;\n\n  /* List the function names declared in `path` that this spec can\n   * recognise. Editor uses this to populate the function-name\n   * dropdown after the user picks a source file. */\n  char **(*list_functions)(void *handle, const char *path, int\n  *out_count);\n\n  /* Return the inferred signature for `path::fn` plus any holes\n   * the user needs to resolve. The editor uses this to render\n   * input/output slots and to render the \"param rules\" form when\n   * holes are present. */\n  sm_signature_t *(*infer_signature)(void *handle,\n                                     const char *path, const char\n  *fn);\n\n  Two more lang_spec_t callbacks. The C spec's implementation does the\n   gcc--E-then-parse dance. The Lua spec inspects the file via the\n  per-worker lua_State (find a returned function, check its\n  debug.getinfo for parameter names, infer types from the\n  user-declared annotations or sentinel-default heuristics). The Bash\n  spec probably returns a trivial signature (every input is a string,\n  return is a string) because bash functions don't carry types.\n\n  This means the editor speaks one API to every language, and 307's\n  parser becomes the C-side implementation of a contract that 317\n  already shares.       "content":"---\nname: SoraMech project context\ndescription: Core architecture decisions, file layout, and execution model for SoraMech, across phase 2 (current) and phase 3 (designed)\ntype: project\noriginSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a\n---\nSoraMech is a visual FSM/dataflow editor and execution engine at /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/.\n\n**Why:** Primary use case is LLM orchestration on the SoraMind Alpine cluster. Strings flow between boxes like variables. History is explicit, loaded from disk only when a box needs it.\n\n**Three independent programs sharing a map directory:**\n- `src/006-server-main.lua` — thin HTTP file CRUD proxy. No runner management.\n- Runner — phase 2: `src/007-runner-main.lua` (synchronous Lua). Phase 3: `soramech-pool` (C binary, designed in issues 301–311, not yet built).\n- `assets/index.html` — vanilla JS canvas editor. Editor only — no run button. Compile button (issue 222) is a phase 2 placeholder; it triggers the phase 3 build pipeline (issue 219).\n\n**Key architecture decisions (current truth):**\n- Each box is its own JSON file in `boxes/<id>.json`. Connections written to BOTH endpoint files; loader validates both ends agree — hard error if not.\n- **Single output wire per box** (issue 218 complete). No `outputs` array. The function returns one value; routing is by `from_branch` on the connection.\n- **Comparator-based branching** (issue 210) — replaces the earlier `branch` box kind with named ports. A box may carry a `comparand`; the dispatch layer fires `lt`/`eq`/`gt` connections. No spec is invoked for comparators.\n- **Iterator boxes** (issue 221) — pure routing primitives, no `ref`/`fn`. Dispatch layer cycles through `iterator_outputs` based on a per-task counter.\n- **Phase 2 drivers** are shell scripts under `drivers/` (one process per call, stdout as channel). **Phase 3 language specs** are `.so` libraries under `langs/<name>/spec.so` loaded via `dlopen` (issue 303). Lua and C are in-process; Bash is out-of-process via Unix domain socket.\n- Data files: per-map JSON in `data/`. Section-level `constant` flag. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua`.\n- State/ephemeral: `tmp/` is a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Phase 2 writes `last-run.json` (single doc). Phase 3 writes `last-run.jsonl` (JSON Lines, issue 311) — decoupled from the editor, consumed by LLMs / CLI viewers / test harness.\n- **Phase 3 runtime model**: C pool runner owns a 3d-rts task pool; per-task slots in process heap (issue 302) with refcounting and a separate large-value heap; dispatch layer (304) is the worker action; graph loader is C (305), no embedded Lua at the runner level. Phase 2's synchronous executor retires when phase 3 lands.\n\n**How to apply:** When working on any component, respect the three-way separation. Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server. Map directory format is the only shared contract. No blocking, no wait lists; tasks spawn on input arrival and run to completion.\n- **Iterator and comparator routing** in the dispatch layer. Comparator runs the function and routes by output value. Iterator skips the function and routes by per-box counter (atomic spawn-time increment). Iterator tasks parallelize across workers; ordering preserved via per-push counter tags on consumer slots.\n- **No-null rule** (issue 230): every input port must be wired, given a literal, or marked optional. Avoids tasks landing on uninitialized handles.\n- **Hard-crash error policy**: nonzero return from any spec aborts the program.\n- **Blocking semantics**: long-running operations tie up a worker. Pool size is the budget. Cooperative split (kickoff + check-done iterator) avoids holding a worker. See `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.\n\n**Effil is explicitly NOT used.** Coroutines are not used. {

  "parentUuid":"05a5d6a4-69d8-4289-a08b-1e95b1bb3c65",

  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Reading the memory now. Good — I'm aligned on the project shape. Here's where I land after re-reading your message.\n\n## Unions — not a tuple\n\nA tuple is a *product type*: all fields exist at once, each at its own offset. A C `struct point { int x; int y; }` is a tuple — `x` and `y` both live, both readable.\n\nA union is a *sum type*: all fields share the same bytes. Only one is \"live\" at a time. The classic shape:\n\n```c\nunion value { int i; float f; char *s; };  /* 8 bytes, one of three meanings */\n```\n\nYou write `v.i = 42`, then read `v.f`, and you get the float interpretation of `0x0000002a` — garbage, because you reinterpreted the bytes. Unions are almost always paired with a discriminator field that says \"which variant is currently live\":\n\n```c\nstruct tagged {\n    enum { INT, FLOAT, STR } tag;\n    union { int i; float f; char *s; } v;\n};\n```\n\nThe reason this matters for serialization: a bare union has no way to tell you which variant to serialize. Three different fields lay claim to the same bytes. Without a discriminator we'd have to pick arbitrarily. With a discriminator we're fine — read the tag, serialize that variant.\n\nSo at the spec layer, bare unions become another \"user provides a rule\" case — same shape as length-unknown pointers. The rule says either \"field X is the discriminator\" or \"this union is always variant Y in this context.\" The system never guesses.\n\n## The core design — handles as the universal fallback\n\nYour push to make this language-agnostic with no special cases reframes the whole thing. Let me state what I think you're actually proposing, because it's a cleaner design than what I had:\n\n**Every value in every language factors into exactly one of two cases:**\n\n1. **Decomposable.** The spec can break it down into a tree of primitives (numbers, strings, bytes, bools, plus ordered lists and named records and tagged variants). Round-trips natively to any other spec.\n\n2. **Handle.** The spec can't (or won't) decompose it. Instead it emits a *handle* — a tiny primitive token (an id string plus a list of operations it supports). The handle crosses the wire. The underlying state stays in the originating language. When some other language wants to act on the handle, the runtime routes the operation back to the owning spec.\n\nThat's the whole serialization rule. No third case. **Nothing is unserializable, because the worst case is \"this becomes a handle.\"**\n\nA Lua coroutine? Handle. The Lua spec owns the coroutine; the handle says `ops: [\"resume\",\"status\",\"close\"]`. C never sees the call stack — it just calls `invoke_handle(id, \"resume\", args)` and the runtime dispatches back to Lua.\n\nA C function pointer to unknown code? Handle. The C spec owns the pointer; the handle says `ops: [\"call\"]` plus the signature (if known). Lua never dereferences — it asks the runtime to invoke, and the C spec does the actual call.\n\nA C pointer-to-opaque-struct? Handle. The struct stays on the C heap. C-side accessors are the `ops`.\n\nThis works because *no language ever has to understand another language's exotic types*. Every spec only ever sees primitives, composites of primitives, or handles. Handles are also primitives (just a string id with op metadata). The spec interface is uniform.\n\n## Teaching the system to decompose\n\nThe handle is the safe default. But sometimes you *want* a type to be transparent — you want a Lua userdata to flow into C as a real struct, not as an opaque token. That's where user-written rules come in:\n\nEach spec exposes a **rule registry**. The user writes rules in the spec's own native form (Lua rules for Lua types, C rules for C types) and registers them. A rule says \"for values of type T, here's how to decompose to a tree, and here's how to rebuild from a tree.\" Once the rule exists, the spec's `to_tree` uses it instead of falling back to a handle.\n\nThis means:\n- The Lua spec ships with built-in rules for the easy types (number, string, table-as-record, table-as-list).\n- The user writes rules for their own exotic types (a custom userdata class, a coroutine they want decomposed into call-stack metadata).\n- The C spec ships with rules for primitives, structs, arrays, length-tracked pointers.\n- The user writes rules for the awkward C cases (length-unknown pointers via a length hint, unions via a discriminator hint, opaque pointers via accessor functions).\n\nThe Lua spec doesn't know what C does. The C spec doesn't know what Lua does. Both produce the same tree format, both consume the same tree format. The runtime is dumb glue.\n\n## Compatibility mode — the C parallel allocation tracker\n\nRight — when a C library returns a pointer without length info, we shim around it. The C spec owns an **allocation table**: pointer → (length, owning-fn-or-rule, freed-flag). Every pointer that flows out of a C box gets an entry. Length comes from one of:\n\n- The function's documented behavior (rule says \"return value's length is param 3\")\n- A heuristic the user opted into (rule says \"null-terminated\")\n- A wrapper around the C call that captured the length at allocation time (rule says \"wrap malloc/strdup/etc. and record the size\")\n\nIf none of those apply and the user hasn't written a rule — the pointer becomes a handle. The user gets a UI prompt: \"this output has a length-unknown pointer; add a rule to make it transparent.\" Two clicks, type a rule, done.\n\nYou called this \"doing things twice\" — yes, exactly. The C library doesn't tell us the length; we have to track it separately. The cost is paid once, in the wrapper layer, and only for libraries that don't carry length info themselves.\n\n## What I'd like to go over with you\n\nA few things genuinely puzzle me about this design, and I want your call before I commit to anything:\n\n1. **Handle lifetime.** A Lua coroutine becomes a handle that flows to C. C stores it in some structure for an hour. When does Lua garbage-collect the underlying coroutine? Options I see:\n\n   - **Refcount in the runtime.** Every box that holds a handle increments; when the box's slot is overwritten or the run ends, decrement; at zero, runtime calls `release_handle` on the owning spec. Simple, but it means *every* handle-touch on every wire is a refcount op.\n   - **Pin until end of run.** Handles live until the run is over; spec releases everything then. Wasteful for long runs but trivially correct.\n   - **Generation tags.** Each run has a generation; handles carry the generation; the runtime sweeps releasable handles between runs. Cheap during the run, complex at boundaries.\n\n   Do you have a preference, or want me to try option 2 first as a baseline and only complicate if it bites us?\n\n2. **Handle equality.** If two boxes both produce a handle to the same underlying Lua coroutine, should the handles compare equal? (Same id.) That requires the spec's `to_tree` to maintain a \"object → id\" map so it returns the same id for the same object. Cheap on the spec side (a pointer-keyed table), but it's a design choice — do we want this invariant? I'd argue yes, because otherwise you can't tell whether two outputs are the same coroutine or two different ones.\n\n3. **The recursion question.** A Lua table contains 9 known fields and 1 unknown userdata. Do we (a) emit a handle for the whole table, or (b) emit a record where 9 fields are decomposed and the 10th is a nested handle? I'd push for (b) — decompose maximally, leave handles only where the spec genuinely can't proceed. That makes user-rule-writing incremental: each rule eliminates one handle, the rest of the structure was already useful. Agree?\n\n4. **Where rules live.** Per-spec, in a file under `langs/<name>/rules/`, written in the spec's native syntax? Or per-map, so each map can have its own type vocabulary? Or both — global default rules plus per-map overrides? My instinct says per-spec global with per-map overrides, but I haven't thought hard about it.\n\n5. **The tagged-variant primitive.** The tree format needs four leaf-and-shape kinds: primitive (number/string/bytes/bool/null), ordered list, named record, *and* a tagged variant (for sum types — `{\"tag\": \"INT\", \"value\": 42}`). That fourth one is what we need to round-trip C unions and Rust enums and Lua \"table-as-variant\" patterns. Sound right? I want to make sure we have product *and* sum types in the tree, because without sum types we'd be unable to represent any tagged union losslessly.\n\n6. **Does a handle have a \"type name\"?** I'm thinking yes — the handle carries `{id, owner_lang, type_name, ops}`. The type_name is what the user references when writing a rule (\"for handles of type Lua.coroutine, decompose like this\"). Without a type_name there's no way for the user to target a rule at a category of handles.\n\nWhere would you like to start? I'd suggest 1 and 5 first — they're the load-bearing decisions. The others can follow once those are nailed."

        "text":"You're right. Let me re-articulate, because I was tangled.\n\n## Conceding handles\n\nThe argument that broke it for me: a real library function (`qsort`, `pthread_create`, anything from libc) expects a real native value. It can't accept a SoraMech-id-string and route operations back via the runtime — it has no notion of SoraMech and never will. If our system can't hand a real `int (*)(const void*, const void*)` to qsort, the whole story falls apart for library integration. So handles as a wire format are out.\n\n## What the design actually is\n\nEvery value, no matter how exotic, decomposes to a tree of primitives. That tree is the wire format. The destination spec reconstructs the value as a real native value of whatever type its declared input signature says — *including* synthesizing native executables (trampolines, FFI bridges) when the destination expects something callable.\n\nThe wire only ever carries data. The \"handle\"-shaped thing — a callable pointer whose body routes calls back to the originating worker — is reconstructed *at receive time* by the destination spec, transparently. From the library function's perspective: it sees a normal function pointer. From the wire's perspective: it carried `{address_in_source_worker, signature, owner_worker_id}` as primitives. The destination C spec's reconstruction step, given that tree and the declared C type \"function pointer with signature (int,int)->int\", emits a libffi-generated trampoline that, when called by qsort, marshals args back across to the originating worker. The trampoline IS the reconstructed value.\n\nSame trick for Lua coroutines into C: the source Lua spec decomposes the coroutine into its parts (bytecode of frames, locals, upvalues, status, pc) — pure data. If the C box's input signature is `struct lua_frame[]`, the C spec walks the tree and fills the struct. If the C box's input signature is \"callable that returns next value\" — C spec emits a trampoline that ships resume calls back to the source Lua worker.\n\nWhat this means: **every concrete value the user wires up is a real, callable, dereferenceable, native value in the destination language.** The wire is just bytes; the destination spec does whatever it needs to make those bytes into the native form its signature demands.\n\n## \"The user won't know the edge cases\"\n\nRight — and the answer is: **the user doesn't have to.** The spec author handles every type form the language has. The Lua spec ships knowing how to decompose: number, string, bool, nil, table, function, userdata, thread/coroutine, lightuserdata. *Every* Lua type form. The C spec ships knowing how to handle primitives, structs, unions (when they have a discriminator), arrays (when they have a length), function pointers (when they have a signature), enums, typedefs. *Every* C type form.\n\nWhat the user might have to fill in is **per-library-function** ambiguities — things the C type system can't express but the library's documentation does. Three of them:\n\n- Union with no discriminator field declared in the same struct → user marks which other param carries the tag.\n- Pointer with no length field declared in the same struct → user marks which other param carries the length (or marks the pointer as null-terminated, or as \"single element\").\n- Function pointer parameter typed as bare `void *` → user provides the signature.\n\nThese three are not \"edge cases the user has to discover.\" They're **prompts surfaced by the editor** the first time the user wires up a library function whose signature parser couldn't fully resolve. The editor renders the box with a red \"type hole\" slot. The user clicks, fills in the answer (\"discriminator is in param 2\"), saves. The answer stores as an annotation on that library function name + header path, lives in `langs/c/library-annotations/`, ships back across runs and machines. Next user who wires up the same function: no prompt, annotation already there. First-party libc functions ship with annotations pre-filled.\n\nSo the user is never expected to *think about* what an ambiguous case might be. The editor tells them, in context, when one occurs. Three categories total, finite and learnable.\n\n## The per-call vs. per-function vs. per-type question\n\nYou asked: \"How else would we mark a certain argument to the function as the discriminator?\" My answer is per-function, not per-call-site, not per-type:\n\n- **Per-type** doesn't work — same union appears in many functions, each with a different discriminator convention.\n- **Per-call-site** is overkill — the same function called twice in a graph has the same discriminator semantics.\n- **Per-function** is the right granularity. The annotation attaches to \"function `foo` declared in header `<bar.h>`.\" Once written, it applies everywhere `foo` is used.\n\nThe annotations live in the C spec's library-annotations directory. They are part of the spec, not the map. A compiled map artifact carries no spec knowledge — it just carries the graph, and depends on the destination machine having the relevant specs and annotations.\n\n## Where there's still tension\n\nTwo cases I want you to weigh in on before I treat them as settled:\n\n1. **Cross-process function pointers.** Lua-and-C are in-process (`dlsym`, `lua_pcall`). Bash is out-of-process (UDS to a per-worker subprocess). If a C box outputs a function pointer wired into a Bash box's input, what should happen? My instinct: this is incoherent — a Bash subprocess can't call into another process's address space, full stop. The compile step should detect \"callable being wired into an out-of-process language\" and error. Sound right, or do you see a way to make it work that I'm missing?\n\n2. **A Lua coroutine fully decomposed → received by C.** We can decompose the coroutine to its data parts (frames, locals, upvalues, pc, status). The C box that receives it... can do what with it? If the C box's signature is `struct lua_coroutine_snapshot { ... }`, the C spec fills the struct from the tree and C reads it as data. Fine — that's introspection. But if the C box wants to *resume* the coroutine, the only way is to ship resume calls back to the Lua side. The destination spec's reconstruction would have to synthesize a \"resumeable handle\" — which is basically the handle pattern I was conceding, just localized to the destination spec. Does that count as a violation of \"no handles\"? I think the distinction is: the wire carried only data, and the destination spec chose to wrap that data in a callable bridge to make it useful. It's a destination-side artifact, not a wire concern. Agree?\n\n3. **One thing I want to confirm about your \"no handles\" position.** A Lua function being passed as a callback into C is the same shape as #2 above. The function decomposes to `{bytecode, upvalues, ...}` — data. The C spec receives that tree and synthesizes a real C function pointer (libffi trampoline) that, when called, marshals args back to the originating Lua worker, executes the function there, marshals the return back. From qsort's perspective: real function pointer. From the wire's perspective: just data crossed. From the C spec's perspective: a trampoline was synthesized, and it owns a back-reference to the source worker. Is this fine, or are you also pushing back on the \"back-reference\" part? Because without some back-reference, there's no way for the trampoline to know where to send the call when it gets invoked.\n\nWhere I think we are: the wire is pure data, the destination spec reconstructs into real native values, and any \"phone home\" mechanism for callbacks is private to the destination spec's reconstruction artifact. The wire stays agnostic; the bridges live in the specs. Does that match what you're driving at?"

The JSON carries the reference. Receiving spec sees `$ref`, decides what to do with it: C reads at the pointer directly; Lua does `lua_pushlstring(L, ptr, len)` (which copies, because Lua owns its string memory); Bash subprocess can't dereference a pointer from another address space, so the marshaller at the UDS boundary inlines the bytes into the JSON before sending. The decision lives in each spec's `from_json`, not in the wire format. The wire is JSON, end of story; the `$ref` primitive is just one of the things JSON can carry.\n\nThis means specs stay completely decoupled. Done.\n\n## The length-pairing question dissolves\n\nYou're right that we can't know which int is \"the length.\" A signature `void foo(char *p, int n)` is two independent parameters as far as the type system is concerned. The convention \"n is length of p\" lives in the function's documentation, not its types. We have no way to infer.\n\nSo we don't. The C box for `foo` has two inputs: a `char *` slot and an `int` slot. They're separate wires. The user reads the function's docs and wires accordingly — `p` from one source, `n` from another (or from a `strlen`-style box, or as a literal). The system never asks \"is this the length?\" — it just exposes both as inputs and lets the user wire them.\n\nSame shape for unions: if the C signature has a variant and a tag, those are two inputs. The editor surfaces the slots; the user fills them with wires.\n\n## No back-routing — confirmed\n\nSpecs are self-contained. If a destination spec's `from_json` can't interpret the JSON it receives, the call errors and the run aborts (hard-crash policy). If no wire consumes a value, the slot just expires — the source-language GC reclaims whatever was there. ## [51]

```json
{
  "userType":"external",
  "parentUuid":"4d2c43bf-ecb7-467a-9c2b-d98e72387c51",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-20T00:25:38.466Z",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "toolUseResult":{
    "type":"text",
    "file":{
      "content":"# 317 — Language spec JSON bridge for data boxes\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA data box (`kind: data` in box JSON) emits a value the rest of\nthe graph routes downstream. Today the runner reads the box's\n`ref` file as raw bytes and emits them — there's no concept of\n\"authoring this datum in a particular language using that\nlanguage's natural structures.\" If you want to declare a Lua\ntable as a data box's value, you either:\n\n- Hand-translate the table to JSON, save it as a `.json` file,\n  and lose the Lua syntax niceties; or\n- Make it a call box that returns the table, paying for a full\n  spec invocation just to read a constant; or\n- Hard-code the bytes inline in the box's `data` field, with no\n  syntactic help from any host language.\n\nThis is the wrong shape. **A box author writes idiomatic code in\nthe language of their choice.** That's the rule 307 establishes\nfor call boxes: a C-box author writes a plain C function, no\nSoraMech-specific glue. The data-box equivalent should hold —\na Lua-data-box author should write a Lua file that returns\nwhatever they want returned (a table, a string, a number), and\nSoraMech should know how to lift that into the graph as a JSON\nwire value without the author writing a single SoraMech-specific\ncharacter.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEvery language spec gains two callbacks, declared in\n`lang_spec_t` (issue 303):\n\n```c\n/* Serialize a native-language value into JSON text.\n *\n *   ctx       — per-worker handle from spec.init.\n *   src       — caller-meaningful pointer to the native value.\n *               Format is spec-specific (see \"Native handle\n *               representation\" below).\n *   src_size  — size hint, or 0 if the spec interprets `src`\n *               without a length.\n *   out_buf   — destination buffer for JSON text (caller-owned).\n *   out_cap   — capacity of out_buf.\n *   out_size  — set to the bytes written.\n *\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error. Writes an error message\n * via the spec's existing error-reporting plumbing. */\nint (*native_to_json)(void *ctx,\n                      const void *src, uint32_t src_size,\n                      char *out_buf, uint32_t out_cap, uint32_t *out_size);\n\n/* Inverse: parse JSON text into a native-language value. The\n * native value is stored wherever the spec considers natural\n * (Lua: pushed to the worker's lua_State stack; C: written into\n * a typed struct supplied by `dst`; Bash: written as a textual\n * representation back into dst).\n *\n *   ctx       — per-worker handle.\n *   src       — JSON text.\n *   src_size  — JSON text length in bytes.\n *   dst       — caller-supplied target; semantics per spec.\n *   dst_cap   — capacity, where meaningful.\n *   dst_size  — set to the bytes / native units consumed.\n *\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error. */\nint (*json_to_native)(void *ctx,\n                      const char *src, uint32_t src_size,\n                      void *dst, uint32_t dst_cap, uint32_t *dst_size);\n```\n\nThese are the same fields 312's same-language fast path\nreserves; this issue is the one that requires every spec to\n**actually implement them**, driven by the data-box use case.\n(312 needs them too, but its driver is performance; 317 needs\nthem for correctness — a data box can't function without them.)\n\n### The rule, restated\n\nThe author of a data box writes a `.lua` / `.c` / `.sh` /\n`.<whatever>` file that returns or produces a value using\n*their language's native idioms*. No SoraMech macros. No\nSoraMech includes. No SoraMech-specific JSON shape constraints\nbeyond \"what your spec's native_to_json can convert.\"\n\nIf the author returns a Lua table, the Lua spec's\n`native_to_json` converts it. If they return a C struct, the C\nspec's `native_to_json` walks it according to the type declared\nin the box. If they print JSON-ish text from a bash script, the\nbash spec's `native_to_json` is a no-op identity (the script\nalready produced JSON).\n\nThe contract belongs to the spec author, not the box author.\nThat's the inversion: **SoraMech bends to the language, not the\nother way around.**\n\n## Native handle representation\n\nThe shape of `src` / `dst` in the callbacks is per-spec. Each\nspec documents what it accepts:\n\n- **Lua spec**: `src` is the index of a value already pushed\n  onto the worker's `lua_State`. `src_size` is unused. The\n  spec's `native_to_json` reads the value at that stack index\n  and writes JSON. `json_to_native` pushes the parsed JSON value\n  onto the stack, and `dst_size` reports the number of stack\n  slots used (always 1 for SoraMech's flat-value model).\n- **C spec**: `src` is a typed pointer + the box's declared\n  output type drives the walk. `src_size` is the type's\n  storage footprint. Mirror image for `json_to_native`. (This\n  ties into 307's typed-wrapper-generation work — the same\n  type system describes both the wrapper signature and the\n  JSON shape.)\n- **Bash spec**: `src` is text the script produced.\n  `native_to_json` validates and reshapes to JSON if needed (a\n  bash script that prints `42` becomes JSON `42`; a script that\n  prints `{\"a\":1}` passes through unchanged). `json_to_native`\n  is similarly a near-identity. The spec author is encouraged\n  to require scripts produce well-formed JSON in the first\n  place rather than write a bash-syntax parser.\n\nThe dispatch layer doesn't know or care which representation a\nspec uses. It only ever passes `src` and `src_size` to the\nspec's callback. The spec is opaque to the runtime; that's the\nwhole point.\n\n## Data box semantics\n\nA data box's `data` field becomes optional. The box gains\noptional `lang` and `ref` fields:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"config\",\n  \"kind\": \"data\",\n  \"lang\": \"lua\",\n  \"ref\": \"config.lua\"\n}\n```\n\nAt graph load, the runner:\n\n1. Resolves the spec for `lang`.\n2. Calls the spec's `init` (already done at worker startup).\n3. At box-fire time, asks the spec to execute the `ref` file\n   and produce a native value (this is essentially the same\n   \"load this file, run it, get its return value\" path the\n   spec already implements for call boxes — call boxes call a\n   named function; data boxes take the file's return value).\n4. Calls the spec's `native_to_json` to convert the native\n   value to JSON text.\n5. Pushes that JSON text down the wire as the box's output —\n   same as today's data path, just with the value sourced\n   from a language-native file.\n\nIf the box has no `lang` and a literal `data` field, the legacy\ninline-data path applies unchanged.\n\n## Why every spec must implement these\n\nThe same JSON the data box emits is consumed by some downstream\nbox (call, comparator, file_write, whatever). That downstream\nbox, if it's in a different language, will eventually need\n*its* spec's `json_to_native` to convert the JSON back. So the\ntwo callbacks are paired — every spec that participates in the\ngraph needs both. A spec that implements `native_to_json` but\nnot `json_to_native` can only be data-box sources; a spec with\nonly `json_to_native` can only be call-box sinks. We require\nboth so any language can play any role.\n\nSpecs that haven't been updated yet should set both callbacks\nto a stub that returns -1 with a clear error message (\"spec\n`<name>`: native_to_json not implemented; this box's value\ncan't be routed cross-language\"). The hard-fail makes the gap\nloud rather than producing wrong output.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. ```json
{
  "userType":"external",
  "parentUuid":"09aecabc-d59d-4c71-abf7-30287446f767",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-20T00:25:38.944Z",

  "toolUseResult":{

    "file":{
      "content":"# 307 — C language spec implementation\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nC boxes today run via `drivers/c.sh`, which compiles the source on\ndemand (mtime-based recompile to a binary), then spawns the binary as\na subprocess and reads stdout. Process spawn cost dominates; each call\nis its own freshly-launched executable. The phase 2 driver compiles\nto a standalone binary, not a `.so`.\n\n## Concept\nThe C language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for C. It is\nthe second reference implementation, and the first one that exercises\nthe `compile` callback. After compile, invocation is in-process via\n`dlopen` / `dlsym` — the user's compiled function is called directly\nthrough a function pointer, with no subprocess and no IPC.\n\nThis is the \"Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI\" model from\n`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`, applied to C: same-process call,\nnanosecond-overhead invocation, native-typed access. The only thing\nthe C spec adds over the Lua spec is the compile step.\n\n## Per-worker state\n\n`init` returns a small struct holding the dlopen-handle cache:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void  *so_handles[MAX_BOXES];   // per-file .so handle, indexed by file id\n    void  *fn_ptrs   [MAX_BOXES];   // per-(file, fn) cached function pointer\n    int    n_cached;\n    // (a hash table could replace these arrays if MAX_BOXES grows large)\n} c_handle_t;\n\nvoid *c_init(int worker_idx);\nvoid  c_teardown(void *handle);    // dlclose every cached handle\n```\n\nEach worker thread has its own cache. The same `.so` will end up\nloaded once per worker, since `dlopen` with the same path on the same\nprocess returns a refcounted handle (the underlying code segment is\nshared across all callers — the per-worker `dlopen` is just a\nrefcount bump after the first).\n\n## Compile callback\n\nThe C spec's `compile` callback receives the box's metadata in\naddition to the source and output paths, so it knows the function's\nsignature and can generate the wrapper:\n\n```c\nint c_compile(const char *src_path, const char *out_path, const box_t *box);\n```\n\n(This is a small extension to `lang_spec_t` in issue 303 — `compile`\ngains a `box_t` pointer. Lua's compile is NULL, so unaffected.)\n\nThe callback:\n1. Reads `box->inputs`, `box->returns`, `box->headers`, `box->link_libs`,\n   `box->cflags` from the box metadata.\n2. Generates a wrapper `.c` file (see \"Wrapper generation\" below) in\n   the map's `compiled/bin/` directory next to where the `.so` will\n   land.\n3. Forks and execs the system `cc` with:\n   - `-shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall` (defaults)\n   - The user's `cflags`, if any\n   - The wrapper `.c` and the user's `src_path` (if `ref` is set)\n   - `-o out_path`\n   - `-l<lib>` for each entry in `box->link_libs`\n4. Waits for the compiler, returns 0 on success, 1 on failure.\n\nIf the resulting `.so` is newer than the user's source and the\nwrapper, compile is skipped (mtime check, same as phase 2).\n\nThe compiler is `cc` — the system default. `gcc` on most Linux,\n`clang` on macOS. No SoraMech-specific compiler dependency.\n\n### cflags in box JSON\nThe `cflags` field on the box JSON is a string of additional compiler\nflags (`-O0 -g`, `-mavx2`, etc.). It is set by the user in the\ninspector — a \"Compile flags\" text input shown when a C-language box\nis selected. The editor saves it as part of the box's JSON; reads\npreserve the field; saves write it back. Nothing overwrites it.\n\n## Box file convention: any C function, no boilerplate\n\n**The rule, stated as a rule:** a box author writes code as if\nSoraMech does not exist. The function they write must be a\nfunction their non-SoraMech compiler can compile, their\nnon-SoraMech editor can lint, their non-SoraMech test harness\ncan call. No SoraMech-prefixed macros. No SoraMech-shaped\nreturn types. No `#include \"soramech.h\"`. Nothing in the\nauthor's source betrays that the function will ever cross\nSoraMech's wire.\n\nSoraMech bends to the language. The language never bends to\nSoraMech. This is non-negotiable across every spec; it's the\nreason for the spec interface in the first place.\n\nUsers do not write a SoraMech-specific C signature. They reference\nany C function — whether one they wrote themselves, or one from a\nlibrary (zlib, OpenCV, libcurl, anything they have headers for) —\nand the C spec generates a thin wrapper that bridges SoraMech's\nbytes-in / bytes-out ABI to the function's natural typed C\nsignature.\n\n### What the user provides\nEither:\n- A `.c` file containing the function, referenced by `ref` in the\n  box JSON; or\n- A library function from a header, no `.c` file of their own — the\n  `ref` field is omitted, the function name and headers are\n  declared in the box JSON, and the library is named in\n  `link_libs`.\n\n### Box JSON for a user-written function\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"classify\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"c\",\n  \"ref\": \"classify.c\",\n  \"fn\": \"classify\",\n  \"inputs\": [\n    {\"name\": \"text\",   \"type\": \"string\"},\n    {\"name\": \"weight\", \"type\": \"int\"}\n  ],\n  \"returns\": \"int\"\n}\n```\n\nThe user's `.c` file is naturally written:\n\n```c\n// maps/<name>/src/classify.c\nint classify(const char *text, int weight) {\n    if (text[0] >= '0' && text[0] <= '9') return weight * 1;\n    return weight * 2;\n}\n```\n\nNo header to include, no macro, no `int classify(SM_BOX_ARGS)`.\nJust a function with a typed signature.\n\n### Box JSON for a library function (no user source)\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"compress\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"c\",\n  \"fn\": \"compress2\",\n  \"headers\": [\"<zlib.h>\"],\n  \"link_libs\": [\"z\"],\n  \"inputs\": [\n    {\"name\": \"src\",   \"type\": \"bytes\"},\n    {\"name\": \"level\", \"type\": \"int\"}\n  ],\n  \"returns\": \"bytes\"\n}\n```\n\nThe wrapper includes `<zlib.h>`, calls `compress2`, and the linker\npulls in `libz` via `-lz`. No user-written `.c` file.\n\n### Wrapper generation\n\nThe compile callback emits a wrapper `.c` for each C box. The\nwrapper has a fixed entry-point name (`sm_box_entry`) that the spec\nalways `dlsym`s. It declares the user's function (extern), unpacks\nSoraMech's input bytes into typed C arguments per the box's `inputs`\ndeclaration, calls the user's function, and writes the return value\ninto `sm_out_buf` per the box's `returns` declaration.\n\nFor `classify` above, the generated wrapper is roughly:\n\n```c\n// generated: classify_wrap.c\nextern int classify(const char *, int);\n\nint sm_box_entry(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n                 void *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size) {\n    const char *text   = (const char *)inputs[0];\n    int         weight = atoi((const char *)inputs[1]);\n    int         result = classify(text, weight);\n    *out_size = snprintf(out_buf, out_cap, \"%d\", result);\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\nThe wrapper is mechanical — same template for every box, varying\nonly in the input-marshalling lines and the return-encoding line.\nThe compile step writes it to `compiled/bin/<box-id>_wrap.c` and\ncompiles `<box-id>_wrap.c` plus the user's source (if any) into a\nsingle `.so`.\n\nThis means the C spec implements typed function calls without\nlibffi (which would do the marshalling at runtime via the C ABI\nmetadata). The same effect is achieved at compile time with\nstraightforward generated code, no runtime dependency.\n\n## Input marshalling (in the generated wrapper)\n\nThe wrapper converts SoraMech's `(bytes, size)` input pairs into the\ntyped C arguments the user's function expects, based on the\ndeclared input types in the box JSON:\n\n| Declared type | Wrapper action                                                  |\n|---------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `string`      | `(const char *)inputs[i]`                                       |\n| `int`         | `atoi((const char *)inputs[i])`                                 |\n| `long`        | `strtoll(...)`                                                  |\n| `double`      | `strtod(...)`                                                   |\n| `bool`        | `strcmp(\"true\", inputs[i]) == 0`                                |\n| `bytes`       | `(const void *)inputs[i]`, paired with `sizes[i]` for the size  |\n| `json`        | `cJSON_ParseWithLength(inputs[i], sizes[i])` → `cJSON *`        |\n\nThe `json` case uses the same vendored cJSON the graph loader uses\n(issue 305) — one JSON library shared across the runner. When a box\ninput is declared `\"type\": \"json\"`, the wrapper passes a `cJSON *`\nto the user's function. The user navigates the tree with cJSON's\nAPI (`cJSON_GetObjectItem`, `cJSON_GetArrayItem`, etc.) and the\nwrapper frees the parsed tree after the function returns.\n\nIf a parse fails (a `json` input that is not valid JSON, an `int`\ninput that does not parse as an integer), the wrapper aborts the\nprogram with the box id and the input position (per issue 303).\n\n## Output encoding (in the generated wrapper)\n\nThe wrapper takes the user function's return value and serializes\nit into `sm_out_buf`, based on the declared `returns` type:\n\n| Declared `returns` | Wrapper action                                              |\n|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `string`           | the user returns `const char *`; `strcpy` + set `out_size` |\n| `int`              | `snprintf(\"%d\", ret)`                                       |\n| `long`             | `snprintf(\"%lld\", ret)`                                     |\n| `double`           | `snprintf(\"%.17g\", ret)`                                    |\n| `bool`             | write `\"true\"` or `\"false\"`                                 |\n| `bytes`            | the user returns `(void *, int)` via an out-parameter pair (see below) |\n| `json`             | the user returns `cJSON *`; `cJSON_PrintUnformatted` → bytes |\n| `void`             | `*out_size = 0` (zero-byte output)                          |\n\nFor `bytes` returns, the user function's signature has the form\n`int my_fn(... const char *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size)` —\nextra parameters that the wrapper passes through from\n`sm_out_buf` / `sm_out_capacity` / `sm_out_size`. This handles\nlibrary functions like `compress` that write their output via an\nout-pointer rather than a return value. The box JSON declares\n`\"returns\": \"bytes\"` and the wrapper threads the buffer through.\n\nIf the encoded value exceeds `sm_out_capacity`, the wrapper aborts\n(per issue 303). For boxes whose output capacity is not known at\ncompile time, see \"Variable-size outputs\" below — the wrapper\nroutes through the large-value heap.\n\n## Variable-size outputs\n\nFor boxes whose output capacity is not known at compile time (issue\n302's large-value heap): the box JSON declares `output_capacity = 0`\nand the wrapper allocates from the large-value heap on each call.\nFor `bytes` and `json` returns, the wrapper transparently picks the\nheap path when the box is variable-size — the user's function is\nunchanged either way. The handle (pointer + size into the\nlarge-value heap) is what ends up in `sm_out_buf`.\n\nFor string returns, similarly: if the returned string exceeds the\ndeclared fixed `output_capacity`, the wrapper falls back to the\nlarge-value heap. This decision is made at compile time based on the\nbox JSON, not at runtime.\n\n## Thread safety of user code\n\nThe same `.so` is loaded by every worker thread that may call into\nit. **Static variables and globals declared in the user's C source\nare shared mutable state across all workers** unless explicitly\nmade `const`.\n\nA note on `static` in C: it does not mean immutable. `static` at\nfile scope means \"this symbol has internal linkage, only visible\ninside this `.c` file.\" `static` inside a function means \"this\nvariable persists across calls.\" Either way, the variable itself is\nmutable — `static int counter = 0; counter++;` is perfectly legal\nand does what it says, just with internal linkage. Immutable in C\nis `const`.\n\nSo:\n- `static int counter = 0;` at file scope — racy, shared across workers.\n- `static int x = 0;` inside a function body — racy, shared across workers calling that function.\n- `const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n- `static const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n\nBox functions must be reentrant — no mutable shared state without\nexplicit locking. The C spec does not enforce this; the rule lives\nin `docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written) for box authors to\nread.\n\n### Library functions that need global init\n\nMany real C libraries require a one-time setup call before any of\ntheir functions work — `curl_global_init` for libcurl,\n`OPENSSL_init_crypto` for OpenSSL, etc. A SoraMech box that calls\ninto such a library cannot just be wired in cold; the library's\nstate has to exist before the call.\n\nTwo patterns handle this without changing the spec interface:\n\n1. **Init box wired as an entry point.** The user creates a small C\n   box whose function is the library's init call (e.g.\n   `curl_global_init`). They mark it as an entry box and wire it\n   such that any box using libcurl is downstream of it. The init\n   runs once at startup before any consumer fires. Process-global\n   library state — which is what most C libraries actually use — is\n   set up by the time anyone needs it. Pairs with a teardown box\n   wired as a terminal node if needed.\n\n2. **Per-worker init via spec extension** (future). For libraries\n   that need per-worker setup (each thread gets its own handle),\n   the C spec gains an optional per-box `worker_init_fn` field in\n   the box JSON. The spec calls that function once per worker\n   thread during pool startup, before any box invoke. Not in scope\n   yet — pattern (1) covers the common case.\n\nThe init-box approach is the recommended starting point. The\nspec-extension path is the escape hatch when (1) does not fit.\n\nA future fallback exists: `dlmopen`, a Linux variant of `dlopen`\nthat loads each library into its own isolated \"namespace,\" giving\neach worker its own copy of the library's symbols (statics\nincluded). Two threads using two different namespaces would not\nshare static state. Less portable than `dlopen` (Linux-only), so\nnot the default — flagged here as the escape hatch if static-\nvariable races become a real problem.\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/c/\n    spec.c              ← lang_spec_t implementation\n    soramech-c.h        ← user-facing header (shipped to maps via compile step)\n    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so             ← built artifact (gitignored)\n```\n\nSpec Makefile target:\n```make\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall -o $@ $< -ldl\n```\n\nLinking against `libdl` for `dlopen` / `dlsym` is the only\ndependency. No interpreter, no helper library beyond libc.\n\n### What `dlopen` and `dlsym` do\n- `dlopen(\"path/to/file.so\", flags)` loads a shared library at\n  runtime. The OS loader maps the library's code into the process's\n  memory and returns a handle. Same idea as Windows'\n  `LoadLibrary`.\n- `dlsym(handle, \"name\")` looks up a symbol — a function or a\n  variable — by name inside an already-loaded library, and returns\n  a pointer to it. Same idea as Windows' `GetProcAddress`.\n\nTogether they are how a program loads and calls code that wasn't\nlinked at compile time. Plugin systems are the classic use case.\nHere, every C box compiles to its own `.so`; the spec `dlopen`s the\n`.so` once per worker, `dlsym`s `sm_box_entry` once per file, and\ncalls the resulting function pointer per invocation.\n\nThe user's C box files are compiled by the `compile` callback at map\nload time, not by this Makefile. The Makefile here builds only the\nspec itself.\n\n## Error handling\n\n- `dlopen` failure (missing `.so`, link errors): print path + `dlerror()`\n  to stderr, return 1, dispatch layer aborts.\n- `dlsym` failure (missing function): print file/fn + `dlerror()`,\n  return 1, abort.\n- Compile failure: `cc` exit nonzero, print compiler stderr (already\n  routed there by `cc`), return 1, abort.\n- User function returns nonzero: propagate that as the spec's return,\n  abort.\n\nNo retry, no fallback. Per issue 303.\n\n## Open questions\n\n(none currently — earlier questions resolved as follows:)\n\n- Per-box `cflags`: yes, add the field to the box JSON. The\n  inspector shows a \"Compile flags\" text input when a C-language\n  box is selected (phase 2 inspector work).\n- Typed signatures: handled via compile-time wrapper generation\n  (see \"Box file convention\" above). No libffi runtime dependency.\n- Static-variable isolation via `dlmopen`: deferred. Current rule\n  is \"C box authors write reentrant code\"; if that breaks down in\n  practice, fall back to per-worker `dlmopen` namespaces (Linux-only).\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Set up `langs/c/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n2. Implement `init` and `teardown` with the dlopen-handle cache.\n3. Implement `compile` — fork/exec `cc` with the standard flags.\n   Smoke test: compile a single hello-world `.c` file.\n4. Implement `invoke` — dlsym, direct call, propagate return.\n5. Write `soramech-c.h` with the `SM_BOX_ARGS` macro and the basic\n   input/output helpers.\n6. Smoke test: a C box that takes one string input, writes a string\n   output, runs end-to-end through the pool.\n7. Add the typed input helpers (`sm_in_int`, `sm_in_double`, etc.).\n8. Add the typed output helpers.\n9. Test against `maps/driver-test` (C portions).\n10. Add variable-size output support (`sm_out_alloc`, `sm_out_handle`).\n11. Document in `docs/005-language-specs.md` once it exists, with a\n    note on thread safety.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/c.sh` — phase 2 C driver, retired by this spec\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n  `invoke`\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap\n- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — where compiled\n  `.so`s live (`compiled/bin/`)\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — sister spec; same shape, no\n  compile step\n- `maps/driver-test` — multi-language test map including C boxes\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### Compile + invoke — 2026-05-12\n\n`langs/c/spec.c`:\n- `compile(src, out)` forks gcc with `-shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall`.\n- `init` allocates a 32-entry dlopen cache; `teardown` walks it.\n- `invoke` looks up the .so in the cache or dlopens it, dlsyms\n  the named function, and calls it through a fixed signature:\n  `int fn(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n  void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)`.\n\nConvention: C box functions all match that signature. The\noptional typed-wrapper mode (per-box signature parsing +\ngenerated marshaller) is deferred until a box wants types that\ndiverge from the byte-array shape.\n\n`tests/maps/hello/src/echo.c` ships two fixture functions; five\ntests in `tests/307-c-spec-test.c` compile and invoke them, plus\nthe missing-symbol and bad-source failure modes.\n",
