Process spawn cost dominates; each call\n10\tis its own freshly-launched executable. The phase 2 driver compiles\n11\tto a standalone binary, not a `.so`.\n12\t\n13\t## Concept\n14\tThe C language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for C. It is\n15\tthe second reference implementation, and the first one that exercises\n16\tthe `compile` callback. After compile, invocation is in-process via\n17\t`dlopen` / `dlsym` — the user's compiled function is called directly\n18\tthrough a function pointer, with no subprocess and no IPC.\n19\t\n20\tThis is the \"Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI\" model from\n21\t`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`, applied to C: same-process call,\n22\tnanosecond-overhead invocation, native-typed access. The only thing\n23\tthe C spec adds over the Lua spec is the compile step.\n24\t\n25\t## Per-worker state\n26\t\n27\t`init` returns a small struct holding the dlopen-handle cache:\n28\t\n29\t```c\n30\ttypedef struct {\n31\t    void  *so_handles[MAX_BOXES];   // per-file .so handle, indexed by file id\n32\t    void  *fn_ptrs   [MAX_BOXES];   // per-(file, fn) cached function pointer\n33\t    int    n_cached;\n34\t    // (a hash table could replace these arrays if MAX_BOXES grows large)\n35\t} c_handle_t;\n36\t\n37\tvoid *c_init(int worker_idx);\n38\tvoid  c_teardown(void *handle);    // dlclose every cached handle\n39\t```\n40\t\n41\tEach worker thread has its own cache. The same `.so` will end up\n42\tloaded once per worker, since `dlopen` with the same path on the same\n43\tprocess returns a refcounted handle (the underlying code segment is\n44\tshared across all callers — the per-worker `dlopen` is just a\n45\trefcount bump after the first).\n46\t\n47\t## Compile callback\n48\t\n49\tThe C spec's `compile` callback receives the box's metadata in\n50\taddition to the source and output paths, so it knows the function's\n51\tsignature and can generate the wrapper:\n52\t\n53\t```c\n54\tint c_compile(const char *src_path, const char *out_path, const box_t *box);\n55\t```\n56\t\n57\t(This is a small extension to `lang_spec_t` in issue 303 — `compile`\n58\tgains a `box_t` pointer. The user navigates the tree with cJSON's\n225\tAPI (`cJSON_GetObjectItem`, `cJSON_GetArrayItem`, etc.) and the\n226\twrapper frees the parsed tree after the function returns.\n227\t\n228\tIf a parse fails (a `json` input that is not valid JSON, an `int`\n229\tinput that does not parse as an integer), the wrapper aborts the\n230\tprogram with the box id and the input position (per issue 303).\n231\t\n232\t## Output encoding (in the generated wrapper)\n233\t\n234\tThe wrapper takes the user function's return value and serializes\n235\tit into `sm_out_buf`, based on the declared `returns` type:\n236\t\n237\t| Declared `returns` | Wrapper action                                              |\n238\t|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|\n239\t| `string`           | the user returns `const char *`; `strcpy` + set `out_size` |\n240\t| `int`              | `snprintf(\"%d\", ret)`                                       |\n241\t| `long`             | `snprintf(\"%lld\", ret)`                                     |\n242\t| `double`           | `snprintf(\"%.17g\", ret)`                                    |\n243\t| `bool`             | write `\"true\"` or `\"false\"`                                 |\n244\t| `bytes`            | the user returns `(void *, int)` via an out-parameter pair (see below) |\n245\t| `json`             | the user returns `cJSON *`; `cJSON_PrintUnformatted` → bytes |\n246\t| `void`             | `*out_size = 0` (zero-byte output)                          |\n247\t\n248\tFor `bytes` returns, the user function's signature has the form\n249\t`int my_fn(... const char *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size)` —\n250\textra parameters that the wrapper passes through from\n251\t`sm_out_buf` / `sm_out_capacity` / `sm_out_size`. This handles\n252\tlibrary functions like `compress` that write their output via an\n253\tout-pointer rather than a return value. The box JSON declares\n254\t`\"returns\": \"bytes\"` and the wrapper threads the buffer through.\n255\t\n256\tIf the encoded value exceeds `sm_out_capacity`, the wrapper aborts\n257\t(per issue 303). For boxes whose output capacity is not known at\n258\tcompile time, see \"Variable-size outputs\" below — the wrapper\n259\troutes through the large-value heap.\n260\t\n261\t## Variable-size outputs\n262\t\n263\tFor boxes whose output capacity is not known at compile time (issue\n264\t302's large-value heap): the box JSON declares `output_capacity = 0`\n265\tand the wrapper allocates from the large-value heap on each call.\n266\tFor `bytes` and `json` returns, the wrapper transparently picks the\n267\theap path when the box is variable-size — the user's function is\n268\tunchanged either way. The handle (pointer + size into the\n269\tlarge-value heap) is what ends up in `sm_out_buf`.\n270\t\n271\tFor string returns, similarly: if the returned string exceeds the\n272\tdeclared fixed `output_capacity`, the wrapper falls back to the\n273\tlarge-value heap. This decision is made at compile time based on the\n274\tbox JSON, not at runtime.\n275\t\n276\t## Thread safety of user code\n277\t\n278\tThe same `.so` is loaded by every worker thread that may call into\n279\tit. **Static variables and globals declared in the user's C source\n280\tare shared mutable state across all workers** unless explicitly\n281\tmade `const`.\n282\t\n283\tA note on `static` in C: it does not mean immutable. `static` at\n284\tfile scope means \"this symbol has internal linkage, only visible\n285\tinside this `.c` file.\" `static` inside a function means \"this\n286\tvariable persists across calls.\" Either way, the variable itself is\n287\tmutable — `static int counter = 0; counter++;` is perfectly legal\n288\tand does what it says, just with internal linkage. Immutable in C\n289\tis `const`.\n290\t\n291\tSo:\n292\t- `static int counter = 0;` at file scope — racy, shared across workers.\n293\t- `static int x = 0;` inside a function body — racy, shared across workers calling that function.\n294\t- `const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n295\t- `static const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n296\t\n297\tBox functions must be reentrant — no mutable shared state without\n298\texplicit locking. The C spec does not enforce this; the rule lives\n299\tin `docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written) for box authors to\n300\tread.\n301\t\n302\t### Library functions that need global init\n303\t\n304\tMany real C libraries require a one-time setup call before any of\n305\ttheir functions work — `curl_global_init` for libcurl,\n306\t`OPENSSL_init_crypto` for OpenSSL, etc. A SoraMech box that calls\n307\tinto such a library cannot just be wired in cold; the library's\n308\tstate has to exist before the call.\n309\t\n310\tTwo patterns handle this without changing the spec interface:\n311\t\n312\t1. **Init box wired as an entry point.** The user creates a small C\n313\t   box whose function is the library's init call (e.g.\n314\t   `curl_global_init`). They mark it as an entry box and wire it\n315\t   such that any box using libcurl is downstream of it. The init\n316\t   runs once at startup before any consumer fires. Process-global\n317\t   library state — which is what most C libraries actually use — is\n318\t   set up by the time anyone needs it. Pairs with a teardown box\n319\t   wired as a terminal node if needed.\n320\t\n321\t2. **Per-worker init via spec extension** (future). For libraries\n322\t   that need per-worker setup (each thread gets its own handle),\n323\t   the C spec gains an optional per-box `worker_init_fn` field in\n324\t   the box JSON. The spec calls that function once per worker\n325\t   thread during pool startup, before any box invoke. Not in scope\n326\t   yet — pattern (1) covers the common case.\n327\t\n328\tThe init-box approach is the recommended starting point. The\n329\tspec-extension path is the escape hatch when (1) does not fit.\n330\t\n331\tA future fallback exists: `dlmopen`, a Linux variant of `dlopen`\n332\tthat loads each library into its own isolated \"namespace,\" giving\n333\teach worker its own copy of the library's symbols (statics\n334\tincluded). Two threads using two different namespaces would not\n335\tshare static state. Less portable than `dlopen` (Linux-only), so\n336\tnot the default — flagged here as the escape hatch if static-\n337\tvariable races become a real problem.\n338\t\n339\t## Build\n340\t\n341\t```\n342\tlangs/c/\n343\t    spec.c              ← lang_spec_t implementation\n344\t    soramech-c.h        ← user-facing header (shipped to maps via compile step)\n345\t    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n346\t    spec.so             ← built artifact (gitignored)\n347\t```\n348\t\n349\tSpec Makefile target:\n350\t```make\n351\tspec.so: spec.c\n352\t\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall -o $@ $< -ldl\n353\t```\n354\t\n355\tLinking against `libdl` for `dlopen` / `dlsym` is the only\n356\tdependency. No interpreter, no helper library beyond libc.\n357\t\n358\t### What `dlopen` and `dlsym` do\n359\t- `dlopen(\"path/to/file.so\", flags)` loads a shared library at\n360\t  runtime. The OS loader maps the library's code into the process's\n361\t  memory and returns a handle. Same idea as Windows'\n362\t  `LoadLibrary`.\n363\t- `dlsym(handle, \"name\")` looks up a symbol — a function or a\n364\t  variable — by name inside an already-loaded library, and returns\n365\t  a pointer to it. Same idea as Windows' `GetProcAddress`.\n366\t\n367\tTogether they are how a program loads and calls code that wasn't\n368\tlinked at compile time. Plugin systems are the classic use case.\n369\tHere, every C box compiles to its own `.so`; the spec `dlopen`s the\n370\t`.so` once per worker, `dlsym`s `sm_box_entry` once per file, and\n371\tcalls the resulting function pointer per invocation.\n372\t\n373\tThe user's C box files are compiled by the `compile` callback at map\n374\tload time, not by this Makefile. The Makefile here builds only the\n375\tspec itself.\n376\t\n377\t## Error handling\n378\t\n379\t- `dlopen` failure (missing `.so`, link errors): print path + `dlerror()`\n380\t  to stderr, return 1, dispatch layer aborts.\n381\t- `dlsym` failure (missing function): print file/fn + `dlerror()`,\n382\t  return 1, abort.\n383\t- Compile failure: `cc` exit nonzero, print compiler stderr (already\n384\t  routed there by `cc`), return 1, abort.\n385\t- User function returns nonzero: propagate that as the spec's return,\n386\t  abort.\n387\t\n388\tNo retry, no fallback. Per issue 303.\n389\t\n390\t## Open questions\n391\t\n392\t(none currently — earlier questions resolved as follows:)\n393\t\n394\t- Per-box `cflags`: yes, add the field to the box JSON. The\n395\t  inspector shows a \"Compile flags\" text input when a C-language\n396\t  box is selected (phase 2 inspector work).\n397\t- Typed signatures: handled via compile-time wrapper generation\n398\t  (see \"Box file convention\" above). No libffi runtime dependency.\n399\t- Static-variable isolation via `dlmopen`: deferred. Current rule\n400\t  is \"C box authors write reentrant code\"; if that breaks down in\n401\t  practice, fall back to per-worker `dlmopen` namespaces (Linux-only).\n402\t\n403\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n404\t\n405\t1. Set up `langs/c/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n406\t   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n407\t2. Implement `init` and `teardown` with the dlopen-handle cache.\n408\t3. Implement `compile` — fork/exec `cc` with the standard flags.\n409\t   Smoke test: compile a single hello-world `.c` file.\n410\t4. Implement `invoke` — dlsym, direct call, propagate return.\n411\t5. Write `soramech-c.h` with the `SM_BOX_ARGS` macro and the basic\n412\t   input/output helpers.\n413\t6. Smoke test: a C box that takes one string input, writes a string\n414\t   output, runs end-to-end through the pool.\n415\t7. Add the typed input helpers (`sm_in_int`, `sm_in_double`, etc.).\n416\t8. Add the typed output helpers.\n417\t9. Test against `maps/driver-test` (C portions).\n418\t10. Add variable-size output support (`sm_out_alloc`, `sm_out_handle`).\n419\t11. Document in `docs/005-language-specs.md` once it exists, with a\n420\t    note on thread safety.\n421\t\n422\t## Relevant files\n423\t\n424\t- `drivers/c.sh` — phase 2 C driver, retired by this spec\n425\t- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n426\t- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n427\t- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n428\t  `invoke`\n429\t- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap\n430\t- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — where compiled\n431\t  `.so`s live (`compiled/bin/`)\n432\t- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — sister spec; same shape, no\n433\t  compile step\n434\t- `maps/driver-test` — multi-language test map including C boxes\n435\t\n436\t## Implementation log\n437\t\n438\t### Compile + invoke — 2026-05-12\n439\t\n440\t`langs/c/spec.c`:\n441\t- `compile(src, out)` forks gcc with `-shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall`.\n442\t- `init` allocates a 32-entry dlopen cache; `teardown` walks it.\n443\t- `invoke` looks up the .so in the cache or dlopens it, dlsyms\n444\t  the named function, and calls it through a fixed signature:\n445\t  `int fn(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n446\t  void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)`.\n447\t\n448\tConvention: C box functions all match that signature. The\n449\toptional typed-wrapper mode (per-box signature parsing +\n450\tgenerated marshaller) is deferred until a box wants types that\n451\tdiverge from the byte-array shape.\n452\t\n453\t`tests/maps/hello/src/echo.c` ships two fixture functions; five\n454\ttests in `tests/307-c-spec-test.c` compile and invoke them, plus\n455\tthe missing-symbol and bad-source failure modes.\n456\t"

          "content":"---\nname: Cross-language wire format\ndescription: How values cross language boundaries in SoraMech — JSON-always with shared-memory $ref primitives, no handles, no back-routing\ntype: project\n---\n\nThe cross-language data passing design, validated 2026-05-19.\n\n**Wire format is JSON always.** Every spec exposes only `to_json(native_value, output_signature)` and `from_json(json, input_signature)`. Specs never know about other languages — adding a new language means implementing those two functions. No pair-wise paths (no \"lua → c\" code path); the language-agnostic JSON intermediate is non-negotiable.\n\n**JSON can carry shared-memory references.** A primitive like `{\"$ref\": {\"ptr\": 140234..., \"len\": 1048576, \"type\": \"bytes\"}}` references bytes living in shared heap. In-process specs (Lua, C) deref directly or copy per their language's needs (`lua_pushlstring` copies into Lua's heap; C reads at the pointer). Cross-process boundaries (anything ↔ Bash) inline the bytes at the UDS marshaller. The wire format itself is always JSON; `$ref` is just one primitive form.\n\n**No handles, no back-routing.** A \"handle that routes operations back to the owning spec\" was rejected — real library functions (qsort, libcurl, etc.) can't interpret SoraMech ids. Destination spec either has the means to interpret what arrived (e.g. Lua's spec uses LuaJIT FFI to wrap a `$function_pointer` primitive into a callable) or the wire compile fails. Specs are self-contained.\n\n**Type ambiguities resolved by wiring, not annotation.** The system never asks vocab questions like \"is param 2 the discriminator?\" or \"is this int the length?\" — it can't, because that vocabulary isn't universal. A C function `void foo(char *p, int n)` exposes two independent input slots; the user wires them according to the function's documentation. Same for unions (one slot for the variant bytes, one slot for the tag). The system never infers pairings; the user expresses them by wiring.\n\n**Spec interface (final shape):**\n- `to_json(native_value, output_signature) → json` — emits JSON with embedded `$ref` / `$function_pointer` / `$lang_opaque` primitives as needed.\n- `from_json(json, input_signature) → native_value` — reconstructs the value as the destination language's native form. May synthesize callables (libffi trampolines for C, `ffi.cast` for LuaJIT) when the destination's signature is a function-pointer type.\n- `list_functions(path)` and `infer_signature(path, fn)` — editor introspection. All function parameters exposed as separate slots; no inference about pairings.\n- plus existing `init`, `call`, `shutdown`.\n\n**Wire primitives in the JSON contract:**\n- `$ref` — pointer + length + type tag for shared-memory bytes. In-process only; marshaller inlines bytes at cross-process boundary.\n- `$function_pointer` — address + signature for callables. In-process only; wire compile fails into Bash.\n- `$lang_opaque` — tag saying \"these bytes are language-X-internal.\" Destination spec either knows what to do or wire compile fails. Used for things like Lua coroutines into C where C has no general way to interpret the bytes.\n\n**Why:** Three corrections drove the design:\n1. Handles were rejected because library functions in the wild can't be modified to use them.\n2. Pair-wise paths were rejected because every new language would break the system.\n3. Per-function discriminator/length annotations were rejected because the system has no vocabulary to ask about them universally.\n\n**How to apply:** When discussing cross-language data passing, spec design, the wire format, or the JSON bridge: every wire carries JSON, period. Big values use `$ref` primitives that reference shared heap. Specs implement only the two pair-symmetric callbacks. Type ambiguities are user wiring decisions, not system prompts. The natural home for this design in the issue tree is issue 317; the C-side parser/wrapper work is issue 307.\n",

The wire format itself is always JSON; `$ref` is just one primitive form.\n\n**No handles, no back-routing.** A \"handle that routes operations back to the owning spec\" was rejected — real library functions (qsort, libcurl, etc.) can't interpret SoraMech ids. Destination spec either has the means to interpret what arrived (e.g. Lua's spec uses LuaJIT FFI to wrap a `$function_pointer` primitive into a callable) or the wire compile fails. Specs are self-contained.\n\n**Type ambiguities resolved by wiring, not annotation.** The system never asks vocab questions like \"is param 2 the discriminator?\" or \"is this int the length?\" — it can't, because that vocabulary isn't universal. A C function `void foo(char *p, int n)` exposes two independent input slots; the user wires them according to the function's documentation. Same for unions (one slot for the variant bytes, one slot for the tag). The system never infers pairings; the user expresses them by wiring.\n\n**Spec interface (final shape):**\n- `to_json(native_value, output_signature) → json` — emits JSON with embedded `$ref` / `$function_pointer` / `$lang_opaque` primitives as needed.\n- `from_json(json, input_signature) → native_value` — reconstructs the value as the destination language's native form. May synthesize callables (libffi trampolines for C, `ffi.cast` for LuaJIT) when the destination's signature is a function-pointer type.\n- `list_functions(path)` and `infer_signature(path, fn)` — editor introspection. All function parameters exposed as separate slots; no inference about pairings.\n- plus existing `init`, `call`, `shutdown`.\n\n**Wire primitives in the JSON contract:**\n- `$ref` — pointer + length + type tag for shared-memory bytes. In-process only; marshaller inlines bytes at cross-process boundary.\n- `$function_pointer` — address + signature for callables. In-process only; wire compile fails into Bash.\n- `$lang_opaque` — tag saying \"these bytes are language-X-internal.\" Destination spec either knows what to do or wire compile fails. Used for things like Lua coroutines into C where C has no general way to interpret the bytes.\n\n**Why:** Three corrections drove the design:\n1. Handles were rejected because library functions in the wild can't be modified to use them.\n2. Pair-wise paths were rejected because every new language would break the system.\n3. Per-function discriminator/length annotations were rejected because the system has no vocabulary to ask about them universally.\n\n**How to apply:** When discussing cross-language data passing, spec design, the wire format, or the JSON bridge: every wire carries JSON, period. Big values use `$ref` primitives that reference shared heap. Specs implement only the two pair-symmetric callbacks. Type ambiguities are user wiring decisions, not system prompts. The natural home for this design in the issue tree is issue 317; the C-side parser/wrapper work is issue 307.\n",

          "content":"---\nname: Cross-language design pitfalls\ndescription: Three approaches the user rejected when designing SoraMech's cross-language wire format\ntype: feedback\n---\n\nWhen designing anything that touches the cross-language data path, avoid these three shapes — the user pushed back on each and the rejections are load-bearing for the architecture.\n\n**1. Don't propose runtime \"handles\" that route operations back to the originating spec.**\n\n**Why:** Real library functions in the wild (qsort, libcurl, anything from libc) expect actual native values — a real `int (*)(int,int)` function pointer, a real `char *` — not a SoraMech-issued id string. They can't be modified to participate in our runtime's routing scheme. The wire must carry data the destination spec can fully reconstruct into a native value, not opaque tokens.\n\n**How to apply:** When a value seems hard to serialize (function pointers, coroutines, opaque pointers), decompose to data primitives (address + signature, bytecode + upvalues, ptr + length). If the destination needs a callable, the destination spec synthesizes one at reconstruction time (libffi trampoline for C, `ffi.cast` for LuaJIT). The \"phone home\" callback that the trampoline performs internally is fine — it's an artifact of the destination spec's reconstruction, not exposed in the wire format. What's forbidden is a wire primitive that says \"operations on this value cross back to the source.\"\n\n**2. Don't propose pair-wise language conversion paths (lua→c, c→lua, etc.).**\n\n**Why:** N languages means N² conversion paths, which means adding a new language breaks the existing ones. The wire must use a language-agnostic intermediate (JSON) and every spec must implement only the two pair-symmetric callbacks (`to_json`, `from_json`). New language = implement those two functions, nothing else touches.\n\n**How to apply:** Never write code that names two specific languages in a conversion context. Specs only ever see JSON on the wire. If a JSON primitive needs an extension (like `$function_pointer`), it lives in the universal JSON contract, not as a lua-spec-specific or c-spec-specific concept.\n\n**3. Don't propose per-function annotations for type ambiguities (lengths, discriminators, callback signatures).**\n\n**Why:** The user pointed out that \"discriminator\" is a vocab word the system has no general way to ask about. We can't prompt \"which param is the length?\" because that pairing convention lives in the function's English documentation, not its types. Asking the user to write annotations means asking them to know specialized vocabulary they didn't sign up for.\n\n**How to apply:** When a function signature has ambiguous types (`char *` with no length, `union` with no tag, `void *` with no signature), expose each parameter as a separate input slot on the box. The user wires the slots according to the function's documentation — `p` from one source, `n` from another. The system never infers pairings; the user expresses them by wiring. If the destination needs a length and no length wire is provided, the wire compile fails with a plain-English fix-it message (\"destination needs length, source provides only a pointer — wire a length input here\").\n\n**Common thread:** all three rejections are the same principle in different clothes — **SoraMech bends to the language, not the other way around.** Users write idiomatic code in their language. Libraries are used as-is. Specs are self-contained and pair-symmetric. The system stays out of the user's vocabulary.\n",

    "stdout":"/* langs/lang-spec.h — public interface for SoraMech language specs.\n *\n * What it is, in a sentence: the C contract that every language\n * spec (Lua, C, Bash, anything user-added) implements. The pool\n * runner discovers specs by dlopen()ing langs/<name>/spec.so at\n * startup and reading the exported soramech_lang_spec symbol.\n *\n * Designed in issue 303. The init barrier (issue 301) calls init()\n * for every spec on every worker before unblocking task dispatch;\n * the dispatch action (issue 304) calls invoke() per task; the\n * compile-button pipeline (issue 309) calls compile() per source\n * file for languages whose compile pointer is non-NULL.\n *\n * Errors: a nonzero return from any callback is fatal. The dispatch\n * layer prints the error context and aborts. There is no recovery,\n * no retry, no per-task failed state. This is intentional.\n *\n * Issue 312 extends this contract with optional fast-path\n * callbacks: `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` are specialised\n * variants the dispatch layer prefers when wire classification\n * says they apply; `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` are\n * bridges used at language boundaries. Specs that don't set them\n * fall back to `invoke` for every call.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_LANG_SPEC_H\n#define SORAMECH_LANG_SPEC_H\n\n#include <stddef.h>\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ Shared signatures */\n/* Invoke signature — shared by `invoke`, `invoke_native`, and\n * `invoke_json`. The dispatch layer picks which one to call based\n * on the wire-format classification in issue 312. */\ntypedef int (*lang_invoke_fn)(void *handle,\n                              const char *file_path,\n                              const char *fn_name,\n                              const void **input_data,\n                              const int   *input_sizes,\n                              int          n_inputs,\n                              void        *out_buf,\n                              int          out_buf_capacity,\n                              int         *out_size);\n\n/* Wire-format bridge: convert one direction of native ↔ JSON.\n * Used when a value crosses a language boundary. Spec sets one\n * or both; if NULL, the dispatch layer treats native and JSON as\n * identical byte streams (the current uniform-byte default). */\ntypedef int (*lang_bridge_fn)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                              void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ lang_spec_t */\ntypedef struct lang_spec {\n    const char *name;       /* \"lua\", \"bash\", \"c\", \"python\", ... */\n    const char *file_ext;   /* \".lua\", \".sh\", \".c\", \".py\"        */\n\n    /* init: once per worker thread at pool startup. Returns an\n     * opaque handle stored in the worker context; the dispatch\n     * layer passes this handle back to invoke() for every call. */\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n\n    /* teardown: once per worker at pool shutdown. Frees the handle\n     * and any per-worker resources (e.g. lua_State, dlopen caches,\n     * persistent socket connections). */\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n\n    /* compile: optional. Called once per source file at map-load\n     * (or at editor compile-button time). For languages that don't\n     * compile (Lua, Bash), leave this NULL. For C, it runs\n     * gcc -shared -fPIC -o out_path src_path. Returns 0 on\n     * success, nonzero on failure. */\n    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path);\n\n    /* invoke: per box call. Inputs are arrays of (bytes, size) pairs,\n     * already read from slots by the dispatch layer. Returns the\n     * function's output by writing to out_buf and setting *out_size.\n     * Returns 0 on success, nonzero (fatal) on error.\n     *\n     * This is the canonical entry point; every spec implements it.\n     * The dispatch layer falls back to it when the specialised\n     * paths below are not set. */\n    lang_invoke_fn invoke;\n\n    /* invoke_native — optional fast path used when every wire\n     * adjacent to this box (input and output) stays inside this\n     * spec's language. Bytes on the wire are this language's\n     * native serialisation (Lua tables via msgpack, C struct\n     * memcpy, etc.) and the encode/decode round trip is skipped.\n     * NULL means the spec hasn't specialised; dispatch falls\n     * back to `invoke`. Issue 312. */\n    lang_invoke_fn invoke_native;\n\n    /* invoke_json — optional universal-interop path. Bytes on the\n     * wire are JSON. NULL means the spec hasn't specialised;\n     * dispatch falls back to `invoke`. Issue 312. */"
  },

      "content":"/* langs/lua/spec.c — Lua language spec for SoraMech.\n *\n * Per-worker handle is a `lua_State` with the standard libraries\n * opened. Invocation convention: the box's source file is expected\n * to return a Lua table (`return M` at the bottom), and the\n * fn_name is a key into that table. Inputs arrive as byte arrays;\n * each one is pushed as a Lua string. The function's single return\n * value is converted to a string (via tostring semantics) and\n * memcpy'd into the caller's output buffer.\n *\n * Designed in issue 306. Implementation choices that matter:\n *\n *  - One lua_State per worker thread. lua_State is not\n *    thread-safe, but per-thread requires no locking.\n *  - The state's stack is rewound to its baseline depth at every\n *    invoke entry/exit so cross-call leaks don't accumulate.\n *  - File caching (luaL_loadfile once, replayed via lua_call) is\n *    deferred — this iteration loads the chunk on every invoke.\n *    Lands as a follow-on once profiling justifies it.\n *  - The chunk's side effects run on every invoke too (since\n *    we re-load and re-execute).       "content":"#!/bin/bash\n# scripts/run-tests.sh — phase 3 integration tests.\n#\n# Runs every fixture map under tests/maps/ through `soramech-pool`\n# and asserts that the captured outputs match a hardcoded\n# expectation per map. The point is to catch regressions\n# end-to-end — past the spec interface, past the dispatch action,\n# past JSONL writing — rather than via the in-process unit tests.\n#\n# Per the project convention: scripts run from any directory via a\n# hard-coded ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths are\n# relative to ${DIR}.\n\nset -u\n\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nif [[ $# -ge 1 ]]; then\n    DIR=\"$1\"\nfi\n\ncd \"$DIR\"\n\npass=0\nfail=0\nfailures=()\n\n# {{{ check_map() — run one fixture, verify expected substrings\ncheck_map() {\n    local map=\"$1\"\n    shift\n    local expected=(\"$@\")\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"$map\"\n\n    local output\n    output=$(\"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map\" 2>&1)\n    local rc=$?\n\n    local missing=\"\"\n    if [[ $rc -ne 0 ]]; then\n        missing=\"exit=$rc\"\n    fi\n    for e in \"${expected[@]}\"; do\n        if [[ \"$output\" != *\"$e\"* ]]; then\n            missing+=\"${missing:+; }missing '$e'\"\n        fi\n    done\n\n    if [[ -z \"$missing\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — %s\\n\" \"$missing\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"$map: $missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ pipeline_output_check() — additional: the pipeline writes to disk\npipeline_output_check() {\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\" > /dev/null 2>&1\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"pipeline file_write output\"\n    if [[ -f \"$file\" ]]; then\n        local content\n        content=$(cat \"$file\")\n        if [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL — expected '11!', got '%s'\\n\" \"$content\"\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"pipeline file: $content\")\n        fi\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output file missing\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"pipeline: $file missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ compile_pipeline_check() — soramech-compile produces a portable artifact\n# Verifies issue 309's compile pipeline: bundles all spec.so + sources\n# into compiled/, then runs the artifact from /tmp (i.e. with no\n# dependency on the project's cwd) and verifies it produces the same\n# output as the source map.\ncompile_pipeline_check() {\n    local map=\"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\"\n    local compiled=\"$map/compiled\"\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"compile pipeline (portable run)\"\n\n    rm -rf \"$compiled\"\n    if ! \"$DIR/scripts/soramech-compile.sh\" \"$map\" --dir \"$DIR\" >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"FAIL — soramech-compile failed\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: script returned non-zero\")\n        return\n    fi\n    if [[ ! -x \"$compiled/pool-runner\" ]]; then\n        printf \"FAIL — compiled/pool-runner missing or not executable\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: pool-runner missing\")\n        return\n    fi\n\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    local output\n    output=$(cd /tmp && \"$compiled/pool-runner\" \"$compiled\" 2>&1)\n\n    local content=\"\"\n    [[ -f \"$file\" ]] && content=$(cat \"$file\")\n\n    if [[ \"$output\" == *\"addone → 11\"* ]] && [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output='%s' file='%s'\\n\" \"$output\" \"$content\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: bad output\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ run all fixtures\necho \"integration tests (fixture maps):\"\n\ncheck_map \"calc\" \\\n    \"add → 42\"\n\ncheck_map \"hello\" \\\n    \"who → World\" \\\n    \"greet → Hello, World!\"\n\ncheck_map \"comparator\" \\\n    \"classify → 8\" \\\n    \"high → HIGH:8\" \\\n    \"low → (no output)\" \\\n    \"mid → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"iter-route\" \\\n    \"iter → hi\" \\\n    \"a → A:hi\" \\\n    \"b → (no output)\" \\\n    \"c → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"pipeline\" \\\n    \"input → 5\" \\\n    \"double → 10\" \\\n    \"addone → 11\" \\\n    \"shout → 11!\"\n\npipeline_output_check\ncompile_pipeline_check\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ parser_tests() — issue 232: unit tests for langs/<lang>/parser.js\n# Run Node's built-in test runner over each per-language parser test\n# file and fold the result into the surrounding pass/fail counters.\n# Each .mjs file is one logical \"test\" from this script's perspective;\n# Node prints its own subtest breakdown on failure for the diagnostic.\nparser_tests() {\n    if ! command -v node >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"  %-44s SKIP — node not installed\\n\" \"parser tests (lua, bash)\"\n        return\n    fi\n    for tf in \"$DIR/tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs\"; do\n        local label\n        label=$(basename \"$tf\")\n        printf \"  %-44s \" \"$label\"\n        local out\n        out=$(SORAMECH_DIR=\"$DIR\" node --test \"$tf\" 2>&1)\n        local rc=$?\n        if [[ $rc -eq 0 ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL\\n\"\n            echo \"$out\" | sed 's/^/      /'\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"$label: node --test exit=$rc\")\n        fi\n    done\n}\nparser_tests\n# }}}\n\necho\necho \"  $pass passed, $fail failed\"\n\nif [[ $fail -gt 0 ]]; then\n    echo\n    echo \"  failures:\"\n    for f in \"${failures[@]}\"; do\n        echo \"    - $f\"\n    done\nfi\n\nexit $fail\n",

      "content":"/* libs/json/json.h — small DOM JSON parser + streaming writer.\n *\n * Written for SoraMech, not vendored. Designed in issue 314. Two\n * halves: a DOM parser with arena-allocated nodes (used by the\n * phase 3 graph loader, issue 305), and a streaming writer with a\n * fixed buffer (used by the JSONL run-log writer, issue 311).\n *\n * The parser is hand-rolled recursive descent. The DOM is read-only\n * once parsed; constructing JSON goes through the writer, not the\n * DOM. Numbers are doubles; integer-shaped fields read via\n * (int)json_number_value(...). UTF-8 strict, BMP \\uXXXX with\n * surrogate-pair handling. No comments, no trailing commas.\n *\n * Errors: json_parse returns NULL on failure, with *err_offset\n * and *err_msg filled. The graph loader maps the offset to a\n * filename:line:column diagnostic before surfacing it.\n *\n * Memory: every parse tree lives in one json_arena_t. Destroying\n * the arena frees every node and every string in one call. There\n * is no per-node free.\n *\n * Threading: single-threaded — the parser is meant to run on the\n * graph-load thread before the pool spins up. Concurrency comes in\n * at the writer side, where each writer call is independent and the\n * caller owns the buffer.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_JSON_H\n#define SORAMECH_JSON_H\n\n#include <stddef.h>\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ Types */\ntypedef enum {\n    JSON_NULL,\n    JSON_BOOL,\n    JSON_NUMBER,\n    JSON_STRING,\n    JSON_ARRAY,\n    JSON_OBJECT,\n} json_kind_t;\n\ntypedef struct json_arena json_arena_t;\ntypedef struct json_node  json_node_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Arena lifecycle */\n/* Construct an empty arena. Returns NULL on allocation failure. */\njson_arena_t *json_arena_create(void);\n\n/* Free every chunk in the arena. Safe on NULL. */\nvoid          json_arena_destroy(json_arena_t *a);\n\n/* Bytes currently allocated across all chunks (for diagnostics). */\nsize_t        json_arena_bytes(const json_arena_t *a);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Parser */\n/* Parse a NUL-terminated UTF-8 source into a tree owned by the\n * arena. Returns NULL on syntax error; *err_offset (if non-NULL)\n * receives the byte offset where parsing failed, and *err_msg\n * (if non-NULL) receives a static-string description. */\njson_node_t *json_parse(json_arena_t *a,\n                        const char  *src,\n                        int         *err_offset,\n                        const char **err_msg);\n\n/* Read a file end-to-end and parse it. *err_line (if non-NULL) is\n * the 1-based line number where parsing failed, computed from the\n * byte offset against the file contents. */\njson_node_t *json_parse_file(json_arena_t *a,\n                             const char  *path,\n                             int         *err_line,\n                             const char **err_msg);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Accessors */\njson_kind_t   json_kind        (const json_node_t *n);\nint           json_is_null     (const json_node_t *n);\nint           json_bool_value  (const json_node_t *n);\ndouble        json_number_value(const json_node_t *n);\n\n/* NUL-terminated; lives in the arena. */\nconst char   *json_string_value(const json_node_t *n);\n\nint           json_array_size  (const json_node_t *n);\njson_node_t  *json_array_at    (const json_node_t *n, int i);\n\nint           json_object_size (const json_node_t *n);\nconst char   *json_object_key  (const json_node_t *n, int i);\njson_node_t  *json_object_value(const json_node_t *n, int i);\n\n/* Linear scan; returns NULL if key not present. */\njson_node_t  *json_object_get  (const json_node_t *n, const char *key);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Writer (declared; implementation deferred) */\ntypedef struct {\n    char *buf;\n    int   cap;\n    int   used;\n    int   err;        /* 0 ok; nonzero = truncation or bad call */\n    /* Internal: depth stack (commas + bracket pairing). */\n    unsigned char depth;\n    unsigned char first[16];\n} json_writer_t;\n\nvoid json_writer_init   (json_writer_t *w, char *buf, int cap);\nvoid json_writer_object (json_writer_t *w);\nvoid json_writer_array  (json_writer_t *w);\nvoid json_writer_end    (json_writer_t *w);\nvoid json_writer_key    (json_writer_t *w, const char *key);\nvoid json_writer_string (json_writer_t *w, const char *s);\nvoid json_writer_int    (json_writer_t *w, long long v);\nvoid json_writer_number (json_writer_t *w, double v);\nvoid json_writer_bool   (json_writer_t *w, int v);\nvoid json_writer_null   (json_writer_t *w);\n/* Returns used bytes (excluding NUL), or -1 if w->err. */\nint  json_writer_finish (json_writer_t *w);\n/* }}} */\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\n}\n#endif\n\n#endif /* SORAMECH_JSON_H */\n",

{
  "userType":"external",
  "parentUuid":"9028cb43-02ef-4052-b34c-637437dc5252",

    "noOutputExpected":false,
    "stdout":"# SoraMech — top-level build orchestration.\n#\n# What it does, in a sentence: builds the phase 3 pool runner binary\n# plus one shared library per language spec. Release by default;\n# DEBUG=1 keeps symbols and disables optimization, STRICT=1 promotes\n# warnings to errors. `make clean` removes everything that was built.\n#\n# Invokable from any directory: `make -C /path/to/soramech` works,\n# and the DIR variable can be overridden if needed (e.g. for an\n# out-of-tree checkout). All paths in this Makefile are relative to\n# $(DIR) per the project convention.\n#\n# Designed in issue 309. Implementation of the runner's runtime is\n# split across issues 301–308; this Makefile builds whatever sources\n# exist under src/, libs/task-pool/, and libs/json/, so it scales as\n# those issues land.\n\n# {{{ Resolve project root\nDIR ?= $(abspath $(dir $(lastword $(MAKEFILE_LIST))))\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Toolchain & flags\nCC      ?= gcc\n\n# Shared header search path: every C source can find langs/lang-spec.h\n# and any future libs/<name>/ headers via -I flags below.\nCPPFLAGS = -I$(DIR)/langs -I$(DIR)/libs/task-pool -I$(DIR)/libs/json -I$(DIR)/src\n\n# Default to release; DEBUG and STRICT toggle alternates.\nifeq ($(DEBUG),1)\n  CFLAGS = -O0 -g -DDEBUG -Wall -pthread -fPIC\nelse ifeq ($(STRICT),1)\n  CFLAGS = -O2 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -pthread -fPIC\nelse\n  CFLAGS = -O2 -Wall -pthread -fPIC\nendif\n\nLDFLAGS = -ldl -pthread\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Paths and source discovery\nBUILD_DIR = $(DIR)/build\nPOOL_BIN  = $(DIR)/soramech-pool\n\n# Wildcards: empty subdirs return empty lists, which is fine. As\n# issues 301/302/303/304/305 land their C sources here, they get\n# compiled automatically — no Makefile edit required.\nPOOL_SOURCES = \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/src/*.c) \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/libs/task-pool/*.c) \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/libs/json/*.c)\n\nPOOL_OBJECTS = $(POOL_SOURCES:$(DIR)/%.c=$(BUILD_DIR)/%.o)\n\n# Test sources live in tests/ as C files named to match the source\n# they exercise (e.g. tests/009-slot-store-test.c exercises\n# src/009-slot-store.c). Each builds to a separate executable that\n# `make test` runs in turn.\nTEST_SOURCES = $(wildcard $(DIR)/tests/*.c)\nTEST_BINS    = $(TEST_SOURCES:$(DIR)/tests/%.c=$(BUILD_DIR)/tests/%)\n\nLANGS = lua c bash\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Public targets\n.PHONY: all runner specs clean test help\n\nall: runner specs\n\nrunner: $(POOL_BIN)\n\nspecs:\n\t@for lang in $(LANGS); do \\\n\t  echo \"  → langs/$$lang\"; \\\n\t  $(MAKE) -s -C $(DIR)/langs/$$lang DIR=$(DIR) || exit 1; \\\n\tdone\n\nclean:\n\trm -f $(POOL_BIN)\n\trm -rf $(BUILD_DIR)"
  },

        "type":"tool_result",
        "tool_use_id":"toolu_011CUDvXYw7PKdtxRPegoCca",
        "is_error":false,
        "content":"# SoraMech — top-level build orchestration.\n#\n# What it does, in a sentence: builds the phase 3 pool runner binary\n# plus one shared library per language spec. Release by default;\n# DEBUG=1 keeps symbols and disables optimization, STRICT=1 promotes\n# warnings to errors. `make clean` removes everything that was built.\n#\n# Invokable from any directory: `make -C /path/to/soramech` works,\n# and the DIR variable can be overridden if needed (e.g. for an\n# out-of-tree checkout). All paths in this Makefile are relative to\n# $(DIR) per the project convention.\n#\n# Designed in issue 309. Implementation of the runner's runtime is\n# split across issues 301–308; this Makefile builds whatever sources\n# exist under src/, libs/task-pool/, and libs/json/, so it scales as\n# those issues land.\n\n# {{{ Resolve project root\nDIR ?= $(abspath $(dir $(lastword $(MAKEFILE_LIST))))\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Toolchain & flags\nCC      ?= gcc\n\n# Shared header search path: every C source can find langs/lang-spec.h\n# and any future libs/<name>/ headers via -I flags below.\nCPPFLAGS = -I$(DIR)/langs -I$(DIR)/libs/task-pool -I$(DIR)/libs/json -I$(DIR)/src\n\n# Default to release; DEBUG and STRICT toggle alternates.\nifeq ($(DEBUG),1)\n  CFLAGS = -O0 -g -DDEBUG -Wall -pthread -fPIC\nelse ifeq ($(STRICT),1)\n  CFLAGS = -O2 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -pthread -fPIC\nelse\n  CFLAGS = -O2 -Wall -pthread -fPIC\nendif\n\nLDFLAGS = -ldl -pthread\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Paths and source discovery\nBUILD_DIR = $(DIR)/build\nPOOL_BIN  = $(DIR)/soramech-pool\n\n# Wildcards: empty subdirs return empty lists, which is fine. As\n# issues 301/302/303/304/305 land their C sources here, they get\n# compiled automatically — no Makefile edit required.\nPOOL_SOURCES = \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/src/*.c) \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/libs/task-pool/*.c) \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/libs/json/*.c)\n\nPOOL_OBJECTS = $(POOL_SOURCES:$(DIR)/%.c=$(BUILD_DIR)/%.o)\n\n# Test sources live in tests/ as C files named to match the source\n# they exercise (e.g. tests/009-slot-store-test.c exercises\n# src/009-slot-store.c). Each builds to a separate executable that\n# `make test` runs in turn.\nTEST_SOURCES = $(wildcard $(DIR)/tests/*.c)\nTEST_BINS    = $(TEST_SOURCES:$(DIR)/tests/%.c=$(BUILD_DIR)/tests/%)\n\nLANGS = lua c bash\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Public targets\n.PHONY: all runner specs clean test help\n\nall: runner specs\n\nrunner: $(POOL_BIN)\n\nspecs:\n\t@for lang in $(LANGS); do \\\n\t  echo \"  → langs/$$lang\"; \\\n\t  $(MAKE) -s -C $(DIR)/langs/$$lang DIR=$(DIR) || exit 1; \\\n\tdone\n\nclean:\n\trm -f $(POOL_BIN)\n\trm -rf $(BUILD_DIR)"
      }],
    "role":"user"
  }
}

        "content":"/* libs/json/json.h — small DOM JSON parser + streaming writer.\n *\n * Written for SoraMech, not vendored. Designed in issue 314. Two\n * halves: a DOM parser with arena-allocated nodes (used by the\n * phase 3 graph loader, issue 305), and a streaming writer with a\n * fixed buffer (used by the JSONL run-log writer, issue 311).\n *\n * The parser is hand-rolled recursive descent. The DOM is read-only\n * once parsed; constructing JSON goes through the writer, not the\n * DOM. Numbers are doubles; integer-shaped fields read via\n * (int)json_number_value(...). UTF-8 strict, BMP \\uXXXX with\n * surrogate-pair handling. No comments, no trailing commas.\n *\n * Errors: json_parse returns NULL on failure, with *err_offset\n * and *err_msg filled. The graph loader maps the offset to a\n * filename:line:column diagnostic before surfacing it.\n *\n * Memory: every parse tree lives in one json_arena_t. Destroying\n * the arena frees every node and every string in one call. There\n * is no per-node free.\n *\n * Threading: single-threaded — the parser is meant to run on the\n * graph-load thread before the pool spins up. Concurrency comes in\n * at the writer side, where each writer call is independent and the\n * caller owns the buffer.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_JSON_H\n#define SORAMECH_JSON_H\n\n#include <stddef.h>\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ Types */\ntypedef enum {\n    JSON_NULL,\n    JSON_BOOL,\n    JSON_NUMBER,\n    JSON_STRING,\n    JSON_ARRAY,\n    JSON_OBJECT,\n} json_kind_t;\n\ntypedef struct json_arena json_arena_t;\ntypedef struct json_node  json_node_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Arena lifecycle */\n/* Construct an empty arena. Returns NULL on allocation failure. */\njson_arena_t *json_arena_create(void);\n\n/* Free every chunk in the arena. Safe on NULL. */\nvoid          json_arena_destroy(json_arena_t *a);\n\n/* Bytes currently allocated across all chunks (for diagnostics). */\nsize_t        json_arena_bytes(const json_arena_t *a);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Parser */\n/* Parse a NUL-terminated UTF-8 source into a tree owned by the\n * arena. Returns NULL on syntax error; *err_offset (if non-NULL)\n * receives the byte offset where parsing failed, and *err_msg\n * (if non-NULL) receives a static-string description. */\njson_node_t *json_parse(json_arena_t *a,\n                        const char  *src,\n                        int         *err_offset,\n                        const char **err_msg);\n\n/* Read a file end-to-end and parse it. *err_line (if non-NULL) is\n * the 1-based line number where parsing failed, computed from the\n * byte offset against the file contents. */\njson_node_t *json_parse_file(json_arena_t *a,\n                             const char  *path,\n                             int         *err_line,\n                             const char **err_msg);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Accessors */\njson_kind_t   json_kind        (const json_node_t *n);\nint           json_is_null     (const json_node_t *n);\nint           json_bool_value  (const json_node_t *n);\ndouble        json_number_value(const json_node_t *n);\n\n/* NUL-terminated; lives in the arena. */\nconst char   *json_string_value(const json_node_t *n);\n\nint           json_array_size  (const json_node_t *n);\njson_node_t  *json_array_at    (const json_node_t *n, int i);\n\nint           json_object_size (const json_node_t *n);\nconst char   *json_object_key  (const json_node_t *n, int i);\njson_node_t  *json_object_value(const json_node_t *n, int i);\n\n/* Linear scan; returns NULL if key not present. */\njson_node_t  *json_object_get  (const json_node_t *n, const char *key);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Writer (declared; implementation deferred) */\ntypedef struct {\n    char *buf;\n    int   cap;\n    int   used;\n    int   err;        /* 0 ok; nonzero = truncation or bad call */\n    /* Internal: depth stack (commas + bracket pairing). */\n    unsigned char depth;\n    unsigned char first[16];\n} json_writer_t;\n\nvoid json_writer_init   (json_writer_t *w, char *buf, int cap);\nvoid json_writer_object (json_writer_t *w);\nvoid json_writer_array  (json_writer_t *w);\nvoid json_writer_end    (json_writer_t *w);\nvoid json_writer_key    (json_writer_t *w, const char *key);\nvoid json_writer_string (json_writer_t *w, const char *s);\nvoid json_writer_int    (json_writer_t *w, long long v);\nvoid json_writer_number (json_writer_t *w, double v);\nvoid json_writer_bool   (json_writer_t *w, int v);\nvoid json_writer_null   (json_writer_t *w);\n/* Returns used bytes (excluding NUL), or -1 if w->err. */\nint  json_writer_finish (json_writer_t *w);\n/* }}} */\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\n}\n#endif\n\n#endif /* SORAMECH_JSON_H */\n",

        "content":"#!/bin/bash\n# scripts/run-tests.sh — phase 3 integration tests.\n#\n# Runs every fixture map under tests/maps/ through `soramech-pool`\n# and asserts that the captured outputs match a hardcoded\n# expectation per map. The point is to catch regressions\n# end-to-end — past the spec interface, past the dispatch action,\n# past JSONL writing — rather than via the in-process unit tests.\n#\n# Per the project convention: scripts run from any directory via a\n# hard-coded ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths are\n# relative to ${DIR}.\n\nset -u\n\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nif [[ $# -ge 1 ]]; then\n    DIR=\"$1\"\nfi\n\ncd \"$DIR\"\n\npass=0\nfail=0\nfailures=()\n\n# {{{ check_map() — run one fixture, verify expected substrings\ncheck_map() {\n    local map=\"$1\"\n    shift\n    local expected=(\"$@\")\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"$map\"\n\n    local output\n    output=$(\"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map\" 2>&1)\n    local rc=$?\n\n    local missing=\"\"\n    if [[ $rc -ne 0 ]]; then\n        missing=\"exit=$rc\"\n    fi\n    for e in \"${expected[@]}\"; do\n        if [[ \"$output\" != *\"$e\"* ]]; then\n            missing+=\"${missing:+; }missing '$e'\"\n        fi\n    done\n\n    if [[ -z \"$missing\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — %s\\n\" \"$missing\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"$map: $missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ pipeline_output_check() — additional: the pipeline writes to disk\npipeline_output_check() {\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\" > /dev/null 2>&1\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"pipeline file_write output\"\n    if [[ -f \"$file\" ]]; then\n        local content\n        content=$(cat \"$file\")\n        if [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL — expected '11!', got '%s'\\n\" \"$content\"\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"pipeline file: $content\")\n        fi\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output file missing\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"pipeline: $file missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ compile_pipeline_check() — soramech-compile produces a portable artifact\n# Verifies issue 309's compile pipeline: bundles all spec.so + sources\n# into compiled/, then runs the artifact from /tmp (i.e. with no\n# dependency on the project's cwd) and verifies it produces the same\n# output as the source map.\ncompile_pipeline_check() {\n    local map=\"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\"\n    local compiled=\"$map/compiled\"\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"compile pipeline (portable run)\"\n\n    rm -rf \"$compiled\"\n    if ! \"$DIR/scripts/soramech-compile.sh\" \"$map\" --dir \"$DIR\" >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"FAIL — soramech-compile failed\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: script returned non-zero\")\n        return\n    fi\n    if [[ ! -x \"$compiled/pool-runner\" ]]; then\n        printf \"FAIL — compiled/pool-runner missing or not executable\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: pool-runner missing\")\n        return\n    fi\n\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    local output\n    output=$(cd /tmp && \"$compiled/pool-runner\" \"$compiled\" 2>&1)\n\n    local content=\"\"\n    [[ -f \"$file\" ]] && content=$(cat \"$file\")\n\n    if [[ \"$output\" == *\"addone → 11\"* ]] && [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output='%s' file='%s'\\n\" \"$output\" \"$content\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: bad output\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ run all fixtures\necho \"integration tests (fixture maps):\"\n\ncheck_map \"calc\" \\\n    \"add → 42\"\n\ncheck_map \"hello\" \\\n    \"who → World\" \\\n    \"greet → Hello, World!\"\n\ncheck_map \"comparator\" \\\n    \"classify → 8\" \\\n    \"high → HIGH:8\" \\\n    \"low → (no output)\" \\\n    \"mid → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"iter-route\" \\\n    \"iter → hi\" \\\n    \"a → A:hi\" \\\n    \"b → (no output)\" \\\n    \"c → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"pipeline\" \\\n    \"input → 5\" \\\n    \"double → 10\" \\\n    \"addone → 11\" \\\n    \"shout → 11!\"\n\npipeline_output_check\ncompile_pipeline_check\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ parser_tests() — issue 232: unit tests for langs/<lang>/parser.js\n# Run Node's built-in test runner over each per-language parser test\n# file and fold the result into the surrounding pass/fail counters.\n# Each .mjs file is one logical \"test\" from this script's perspective;\n# Node prints its own subtest breakdown on failure for the diagnostic.\nparser_tests() {\n    if ! command -v node >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"  %-44s SKIP — node not installed\\n\" \"parser tests (lua, bash)\"\n        return\n    fi\n    for tf in \"$DIR/tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs\" \\\n              \"$DIR/tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs\"; do\n        local label\n        label=$(basename \"$tf\")\n        printf \"  %-44s \" \"$label\"\n        local out\n        out=$(SORAMECH_DIR=\"$DIR\" node --test \"$tf\" 2>&1)\n        local rc=$?\n        if [[ $rc -eq 0 ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL\\n\"\n            echo \"$out\" | sed 's/^/      /'\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"$label: node --test exit=$rc\")\n        fi\n    done\n}\nparser_tests\n# }}}\n\necho\necho \"  $pass passed, $fail failed\"\n\nif [[ $fail -gt 0 ]]; then\n    echo\n    echo \"  failures:\"\n    for f in \"${failures[@]}\"; do\n        echo \"    - $f\"\n    done\nfi\n\nexit $fail\n",

    "content":{
      "type":"text",
      "file":{
        "content":"/* langs/lua/spec.c — Lua language spec for SoraMech.\n *\n * Per-worker handle is a `lua_State` with the standard libraries\n * opened. Invocation convention: the box's source file is expected\n * to return a Lua table (`return M` at the bottom), and the\n * fn_name is a key into that table. Inputs arrive as byte arrays;\n * each one is pushed as a Lua string. The function's single return\n * value is converted to a string (via tostring semantics) and\n * memcpy'd into the caller's output buffer.\n *\n * Designed in issue 306. Implementation choices that matter:\n *\n *  - One lua_State per worker thread. lua_State is not\n *    thread-safe, but per-thread requires no locking.\n *  - The state's stack is rewound to its baseline depth at every\n *    invoke entry/exit so cross-call leaks don't accumulate.\n *  - File caching (luaL_loadfile once, replayed via lua_call) is\n *    deferred — this iteration loads the chunk on every invoke.\n *    Lands as a follow-on once profiling justifies it.\n *  - The chunk's side effects run on every invoke too (since\n *    we re-load and re-execute). Box source files should be pure\n *    \"return M\" modules for now.\n */\n\n#include \"lang-spec.h\"\n\n#include <lua.h>\n#include <lauxlib.h>\n#include <lualib.h>\n\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <string.h>\n\n/* Registry key for the per-worker file → module-table cache. The\n * key is a string in the Lua registry; the value is a Lua table\n * keyed by file path. Each entry's value is the module table the\n * file's chunk returned.\n *\n * Caching is per-`lua_State` (i.e. per-worker), which matches the\n * thread model: each worker has its own state, never shared. No\n * locking needed because only the worker that owns the state ever\n * touches the cache. */\n#define LUA_CACHE_KEY \"soramech.module_cache\"\n\n/* {{{ lua_init() — create a state, open standard libs, seed cache */\nstatic void *lua_init(int worker_idx)\n{\n    (void)worker_idx;\n    lua_State *L = luaL_newstate();\n    if (!L) return NULL;\n    luaL_openlibs(L);\n    /* Seed the empty cache table. */\n    lua_newtable(L);\n    lua_setfield(L, LUA_REGISTRYINDEX, LUA_CACHE_KEY);\n    return L;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ lua_teardown() */\nstatic void lua_teardown(void *handle)\n{\n    if (handle) lua_close((lua_State *)handle);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ lua_invoke() */\nstatic int lua_invoke(void *handle,\n                      const char  *file_path,\n                      const char  *fn_name,\n                      const void **input_data,\n                      const int   *input_sizes,\n                      int          n_inputs,\n                      void        *out_buf,\n                      int          out_buf_capacity,\n                      int         *out_size)\n{\n    lua_State *L = (lua_State *)handle;\n    if (!L || !file_path || !fn_name) return -1;\n\n    int baseline = lua_gettop(L);\n\n    /* Module cache lookup. The cache table lives in the registry\n     * under LUA_CACHE_KEY; each key is a file path, each value is\n     * the module table the file's chunk returned. Stack after this\n     * block: ..., cache, module. */\n    lua_getfield(L, LUA_REGISTRYINDEX, LUA_CACHE_KEY);\n    lua_getfield(L, -1, file_path);\n    if (lua_isnil(L, -1)) {\n        lua_pop(L, 1);   /* discard nil */\n        /* Stack: ..., cache */\n\n        if (luaL_loadfile(L, file_path) != 0) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: loadfile('%s'): %s\\n\",\n                    file_path, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        if (lua_pcall(L, 0, 1, 0) != 0) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: chunk exec '%s': %s\\n\",\n                    file_path, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        if (!lua_istable(L, -1)) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: '%s' did not return a table\\n\", file_path);\n            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        /* Stack: ..., cache, module. Cache the module under\n         * file_path. */\n        lua_pushvalue(L, -1);\n        lua_setfield(L, -3, file_path);\n    }\n    /* Stack at this point: ..., cache, module. */\n\n    /* Pull the function out of the module table. */\n    lua_getfield(L, -1, fn_name);\n    if (!lua_isfunction(L, -1)) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: '%s' is not a function in %s\\n\",\n                fn_name, file_path);\n        lua_settop(L, baseline);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    /* Stack: ..., cache, module, function. Drop module + cache. */\n    lua_remove(L, -2);   /* drop module */\n    lua_remove(L, -2);   /* drop cache  */\n\n    /* Push each input as a Lua string. */\n    for (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n        if (input_data[i] == NULL && input_sizes[i] > 0) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: input %d is NULL with size %d\\n\",\n                    i, input_sizes[i]);\n            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        lua_pushlstring(L, (const char *)input_data[i], (size_t)input_sizes[i]);\n    }\n\n    /* Call. One return value expected. */\n    if (lua_pcall(L, n_inputs, 1, 0) != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: %s.%s: %s\\n\",\n                file_path, fn_name, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n        lua_settop(L, baseline);\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    /* Convert the return to a string. tostring handles numbers /\n     * booleans / nil; if the spec needs richer marshaling later\n     * (tables, structs), that's an issue-312-shaped change. */\n    size_t len = 0;\n    const char *result = lua_tolstring(L, -1, &len);\n    if (!result) {\n        /* Non-coercible value. For now, surface as zero-length\n         * output rather than an error — the box returned something\n         * we can't serialize, but the call itself succeeded. */\n        if (out_size) *out_size = 0;\n        lua_settop(L, baseline);\n        return 0;\n    }\n    if ((int)len > out_buf_capacity) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: %s.%s returned %zu bytes; \"\n                        \"buffer is %d\\n\",\n                file_path, fn_name, len, out_buf_capacity);\n        lua_settop(L, baseline);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    if (out_buf && len > 0) memcpy(out_buf, result, len);\n    if (out_size) *out_size = (int)len;\n\n    lua_settop(L, baseline);\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ soramech_lang_spec */\nlang_spec_t soramech_lang_spec = {\n    .name     = \"lua\",\n    .file_ext = \".lua\",\n    .init     = lua_init,\n    .teardown = lua_teardown,\n    .compile  = 0,\n    .invoke   = lua_invoke,\n};\n/* }}} */\n",
        "numLines":185,
        "startLine":1,
        "totalLines":185,
        "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/langs/lua/spec.c"
      }
    },
    "filename":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/langs/lua/spec.c",
    "displayPath":"langs/lua/spec.c"
  }
}

    "content":{
      "type":"text",
      "file":{
        "content":"/* langs/lang-spec.h — public interface for SoraMech language specs.\n *\n * What it is, in a sentence: the C contract that every language\n * spec (Lua, C, Bash, anything user-added) implements. The pool\n * runner discovers specs by dlopen()ing langs/<name>/spec.so at\n * startup and reading the exported soramech_lang_spec symbol.\n *\n * Designed in issue 303. The init barrier (issue 301) calls init()\n * for every spec on every worker before unblocking task dispatch;\n * the dispatch action (issue 304) calls invoke() per task; the\n * compile-button pipeline (issue 309) calls compile() per source\n * file for languages whose compile pointer is non-NULL.\n *\n * Errors: a nonzero return from any callback is fatal. The dispatch\n * layer prints the error context and aborts. There is no recovery,\n * no retry, no per-task failed state. This is intentional.\n *\n * Issue 312 extends this contract with optional fast-path\n * callbacks: `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` are specialised\n * variants the dispatch layer prefers when wire classification\n * says they apply; `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` are\n * bridges used at language boundaries. Specs that don't set them\n * fall back to `invoke` for every call.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_LANG_SPEC_H\n#define SORAMECH_LANG_SPEC_H\n\n#include <stddef.h>\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ Shared signatures */\n/* Invoke signature — shared by `invoke`, `invoke_native`, and\n * `invoke_json`. The dispatch layer picks which one to call based\n * on the wire-format classification in issue 312. */\ntypedef int (*lang_invoke_fn)(void *handle,\n                              const char *file_path,\n                              const char *fn_name,\n                              const void **input_data,\n                              const int   *input_sizes,\n                              int          n_inputs,\n                              void        *out_buf,\n                              int          out_buf_capacity,\n                              int         *out_size);\n\n/* Wire-format bridge: convert one direction of native ↔ JSON.\n * Used when a value crosses a language boundary. Spec sets one\n * or both; if NULL, the dispatch layer treats native and JSON as\n * identical byte streams (the current uniform-byte default). */\ntypedef int (*lang_bridge_fn)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                              void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ lang_spec_t */\ntypedef struct lang_spec {\n    const char *name;       /* \"lua\", \"bash\", \"c\", \"python\", ... */\n    const char *file_ext;   /* \".lua\", \".sh\", \".c\", \".py\"        */\n\n    /* init: once per worker thread at pool startup. Returns an\n     * opaque handle stored in the worker context; the dispatch\n     * layer passes this handle back to invoke() for every call. */\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n\n    /* teardown: once per worker at pool shutdown. Frees the handle\n     * and any per-worker resources (e.g. lua_State, dlopen caches,\n     * persistent socket connections). */\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n\n    /* compile: optional. Called once per source file at map-load\n     * (or at editor compile-button time). For languages that don't\n     * compile (Lua, Bash), leave this NULL. For C, it runs\n     * gcc -shared -fPIC -o out_path src_path. Returns 0 on\n     * success, nonzero on failure. */\n    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path);\n\n    /* invoke: per box call. Inputs are arrays of (bytes, size) pairs,\n     * already read from slots by the dispatch layer. Returns the\n     * function's output by writing to out_buf and setting *out_size.\n     * Returns 0 on success, nonzero (fatal) on error.\n     *\n     * This is the canonical entry point; every spec implements it.\n     * The dispatch layer falls back to it when the specialised\n     * paths below are not set. */\n    lang_invoke_fn invoke;\n\n    /* invoke_native — optional fast path used when every wire\n     * adjacent to this box (input and output) stays inside this\n     * spec's language. Bytes on the wire are this language's\n     * native serialisation (Lua tables via msgpack, C struct\n     * memcpy, etc.) and the encode/decode round trip is skipped.\n     * NULL means the spec hasn't specialised; dispatch falls\n     * back to `invoke`. Issue 312. */\n    lang_invoke_fn invoke_native;\n\n    /* invoke_json — optional universal-interop path. Bytes on the\n     * wire are JSON. NULL means the spec hasn't specialised;\n     * dispatch falls back to `invoke`. Issue 312. */\n    lang_invoke_fn invoke_json;\n\n    /* Bridges between native and JSON wire forms. Used when a\n     * value crosses a language boundary — the producer writes\n     * native, the dispatch layer converts via the producer's\n     * native_to_json, hands the JSON bytes to the consumer's\n     * json_to_native. NULL means the spec hasn't specialised;\n     * dispatch treats native and JSON as identical bytes. Issue\n     * 312. */\n    lang_bridge_fn native_to_json;\n    lang_bridge_fn json_to_native;\n} lang_spec_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\n}\n#endif\n\n#endif /* SORAMECH_LANG_SPEC_H */\n",

        "startLine":1,

{
  "userType":"external",
  "parentUuid":"d41f58f7-ae2d-4840-a6b4-6f6a518dcd73",
  "entrypoint":"cli",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "sessionId":"e9ed70c7-2b63-425c-987c-6431040bedfb",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "uuid":"56fb77d0-17f2-4acd-87c5-c1f7477263bd",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "type":"attachment",
  "slug":"ancient-bouncing-wall",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-20T02:16:49.638Z",
  "attachment":{
    "type":"file",
    "content":{
      "type":"text",
      "file":{
        "content":"---\nname: Cross-language design pitfalls\ndescription: Three approaches the user rejected when designing SoraMech's cross-language wire format\ntype: feedback\noriginSessionId: e9ed70c7-2b63-425c-987c-6431040bedfb\n---\nWhen designing anything that touches the cross-language data path, avoid these three shapes — the user pushed back on each and the rejections are load-bearing for the architecture.\n\n**1. Don't propose runtime \"handles\" that route operations back to the originating spec.**\n\n**Why:** Real library functions in the wild (qsort, libcurl, anything from libc) expect actual native values — a real `int (*)(int,int)` function pointer, a real `char *` — not a SoraMech-issued id string. They can't be modified to participate in our runtime's routing scheme. The wire must carry data the destination spec can fully reconstruct into a native value, not opaque tokens.\n\n**How to apply:** When a value seems hard to serialize (function pointers, coroutines, opaque pointers), decompose to data primitives (address + signature, bytecode + upvalues, ptr + length). If the destination needs a callable, the destination spec synthesizes one at reconstruction time (libffi trampoline for C, `ffi.cast` for LuaJIT). The \"phone home\" callback that the trampoline performs internally is fine — it's an artifact of the destination spec's reconstruction, not exposed in the wire format. What's forbidden is a wire primitive that says \"operations on this value cross back to the source.\"\n\n**2. Don't propose pair-wise language conversion paths (lua→c, c→lua, etc.).**\n\n**Why:** N languages means N² conversion paths, which means adding a new language breaks the existing ones. The wire must use a language-agnostic intermediate (JSON) and every spec must implement only the two pair-symmetric callbacks (`to_json`, `from_json`). New language = implement those two functions, nothing else touches.\n\n**How to apply:** Never write code that names two specific languages in a conversion context. Specs only ever see JSON on the wire. If a JSON primitive needs an extension (like `$function_pointer`), it lives in the universal JSON contract, not as a lua-spec-specific or c-spec-specific concept.\n\n**3. Don't propose per-function annotations for type ambiguities (lengths, discriminators, callback signatures).**\n\n**Why:** The user pointed out that \"discriminator\" is a vocab word the system has no general way to ask about. We can't prompt \"which param is the length?\" because that pairing convention lives in the function's English documentation, not its types. Asking the user to write annotations means asking them to know specialized vocabulary they didn't sign up for.\n\n**How to apply:** When a function signature has ambiguous types (`char *` with no length, `union` with no tag, `void *` with no signature), expose each parameter as a separate input slot on the box. The user wires the slots according to the function's documentation — `p` from one source, `n` from another. The system never infers pairings; the user expresses them by wiring. If the destination needs a length and no length wire is provided, the wire compile fails with a plain-English fix-it message (\"destination needs length, source provides only a pointer — wire a length input here\").\n\n**Common thread:** all three rejections are the same principle in different clothes — **SoraMech bends to the language, not the other way around.** Users write idiomatic code in their language. Libraries are used as-is. Specs are self-contained and pair-symmetric. The system stays out of the user's vocabulary.\n",
        "numLines":28,
        "startLine":1,
        "totalLines":28,
        "filePath":"/home/ritz/.claude/projects/-mnt-mtwo-programs-sora-soramech/memory/feedback_cross_language_pitfalls.md"
      }
    },

    "originalFile":"/* langs/lang-spec.h — public interface for SoraMech language specs.\n *\n * What it is, in a sentence: the C contract that every language\n * spec (Lua, C, Bash, anything user-added) implements. The pool\n * runner discovers specs by dlopen()ing langs/<name>/spec.so at\n * startup and reading the exported soramech_lang_spec symbol.\n *\n * Designed in issue 303. The init barrier (issue 301) calls init()\n * for every spec on every worker before unblocking task dispatch;\n * the dispatch action (issue 304) calls invoke() per task; the\n * compile-button pipeline (issue 309) calls compile() per source\n * file for languages whose compile pointer is non-NULL.\n *\n * Errors: a nonzero return from any callback is fatal. The dispatch\n * layer prints the error context and aborts. There is no recovery,\n * no retry, no per-task failed state. This is intentional.\n *\n * Issue 312 extends this contract with optional fast-path\n * callbacks: `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` are specialised\n * variants the dispatch layer prefers when wire classification\n * says they apply; `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` are\n * bridges used at language boundaries. Specs that don't set them\n * fall back to `invoke` for every call.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_LANG_SPEC_H\n#define SORAMECH_LANG_SPEC_H\n\n#include <stddef.h>\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ Shared signatures */\n/* Invoke signature — shared by `invoke`, `invoke_native`, and\n * `invoke_json`. The dispatch layer picks which one to call based\n * on the wire-format classification in issue 312. */\ntypedef int (*lang_invoke_fn)(void *handle,\n                              const char *file_path,\n                              const char *fn_name,\n                              const void **input_data,\n                              const int   *input_sizes,\n                              int          n_inputs,\n                              void        *out_buf,\n                              int          out_buf_capacity,\n                              int         *out_size);\n\n/* Wire-format bridge: convert one direction of native ↔ JSON.\n * Used when a value crosses a language boundary. Spec sets one\n * or both; if NULL, the dispatch layer treats native and JSON as\n * identical byte streams (the current uniform-byte default). */\ntypedef int (*lang_bridge_fn)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                              void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ lang_spec_t */\ntypedef struct lang_spec {\n    const char *name;       /* \"lua\", \"bash\", \"c\", \"python\", ... */\n    const char *file_ext;   /* \".lua\", \".sh\", \".c\", \".py\"        */\n\n    /* init: once per worker thread at pool startup. Returns an\n     * opaque handle stored in the worker context; the dispatch\n     * layer passes this handle back to invoke() for every call. */\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n\n    /* teardown: once per worker at pool shutdown. Frees the handle\n     * and any per-worker resources (e.g. lua_State, dlopen caches,\n     * persistent socket connections). */\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n\n    /* compile: optional. Called once per source file at map-load\n     * (or at editor compile-button time). For languages that don't\n     * compile (Lua, Bash), leave this NULL. For C, it runs\n     * gcc -shared -fPIC -o out_path src_path. Returns 0 on\n     * success, nonzero on failure. */\n    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path);\n\n    /* invoke: per box call. Inputs are arrays of (bytes, size) pairs,\n     * already read from slots by the dispatch layer. Returns the\n     * function's output by writing to out_buf and setting *out_size.\n     * Returns 0 on success, nonzero (fatal) on error.\n     *\n     * This is the canonical entry point; every spec implements it.\n     * The dispatch layer falls back to it when the specialised\n     * paths below are not set. */\n    lang_invoke_fn invoke;\n\n    /* invoke_native — optional fast path used when every wire\n     * adjacent to this box (input and output) stays inside this\n     * spec's language. Bytes on the wire are this language's\n     * native serialisation (Lua tables via msgpack, C struct\n     * memcpy, etc.) and the encode/decode round trip is skipped.\n     * NULL means the spec hasn't specialised; dispatch falls\n     * back to `invoke`. Issue 312. */\n    lang_invoke_fn invoke_native;\n\n    /* invoke_json — optional universal-interop path. Bytes on the\n     * wire are JSON. NULL means the spec hasn't specialised;\n     * dispatch falls back to `invoke`. Issue 312. */\n    lang_invoke_fn invoke_json;\n\n    /* Bridges between native and JSON wire forms. Used when a\n     * value crosses a language boundary — the producer writes\n     * native, the dispatch layer converts via the producer's\n     * native_to_json, hands the JSON bytes to the consumer's\n     * json_to_native. NULL means the spec hasn't specialised;\n     * dispatch treats native and JSON as identical bytes. Issue\n     * 312. */\n    lang_bridge_fn native_to_json;\n    lang_bridge_fn json_to_native;\n} lang_spec_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\n}\n#endif\n\n#endif /* SORAMECH_LANG_SPEC_H */\n",
