Release by default;\n# DEBUG=1 keeps symbols and disables optimization, STRICT=1 promotes\n# warnings to errors. `make clean` removes everything that was built.\n#\n# Invokable from any directory: `make -C /path/to/soramech` works,\n# and the DIR variable can be overridden if needed (e.g. for an\n# out-of-tree checkout). All paths in this Makefile are relative to\n# $(DIR) per the project convention.\n#\n# Designed in issue 309. Implementation of the runner's runtime is\n# split across issues 301–308; this Makefile builds whatever sources\n# exist under src/, libs/task-pool/, and libs/json/, so it scales as\n# those issues land.\n\n# {{{ Resolve project root\nDIR ?= $(abspath $(dir $(lastword $(MAKEFILE_LIST))))\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Toolchain & flags\nCC      ?= gcc\n\n# Shared header search path: every C source can find langs/lang-spec.h\n# and any future libs/<name>/ headers via -I flags below.\nCPPFLAGS = -I$(DIR)/langs -I$(DIR)/libs/task-pool -I$(DIR)/libs/json -I$(DIR)/src\n\n# Default to release; DEBUG and STRICT toggle alternates.\nifeq ($(DEBUG),1)\n  CFLAGS = -O0 -g -DDEBUG -Wall -pthread -fPIC\nelse ifeq ($(STRICT),1)\n  CFLAGS = -O2 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -pthread -fPIC\nelse\n  CFLAGS = -O2 -Wall -pthread -fPIC\nendif\n\nLDFLAGS = -ldl -pthread\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Paths and source discovery\nBUILD_DIR = $(DIR)/build\nPOOL_BIN  = $(DIR)/soramech-pool\n\n# Wildcards: empty subdirs return empty lists, which is fine. As\n# issues 301/302/303/304/305 land their C sources here, they get\n# compiled automatically — no Makefile edit required.\nPOOL_SOURCES = \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/src/*.c) \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/libs/task-pool/*.c) \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/libs/json/*.c)\n\nPOOL_OBJECTS = $(POOL_SOURCES:$(DIR)/%.c=$(BUILD_DIR)/%.o)\n\n# Test sources live in tests/ as C files named to match the source\n# they exercise (e.g. tests/009-slot-store-test.c exercises\n# src/009-slot-store.c). Each builds to a separate executable that\n# `make test` runs in turn.\nTEST_SOURCES = $(wildcard $(DIR)/tests/*.c)\nTEST_BINS    = $(TEST_SOURCES:$(DIR)/tests/%.c=$(BUILD_DIR)/tests/%)\n\nLANGS = lua c bash\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Public targets\n.PHONY: all runner specs clean test help\n\nall: runner specs\n\nrunner: $(POOL_BIN)\n\nspecs:\n\t@for lang in $(LANGS); do \\\n\t  echo \"  → langs/$$lang\"; \\\n\t  $(MAKE) -s -C $(DIR)/langs/$$lang DIR=$(DIR) || exit 1; \\\n\tdone\n\nclean:\n\trm -f $(POOL_BIN)\n\trm -rf $(BUILD_DIR)"
  },

      }],
    "replaceAll":false,
    "originalFile":"/* langs/lua/spec.c — Lua language spec for SoraMech.\n *\n * Per-worker handle is a `lua_State` with the standard libraries\n * opened. Invocation convention: the box's source file is expected\n * to return a Lua table (`return M` at the bottom), and the\n * fn_name is a key into that table. Inputs arrive as byte arrays;\n * each one is pushed as a Lua string. The function's single return\n * value is converted to a string (via tostring semantics) and\n * memcpy'd into the caller's output buffer.\n *\n * Designed in issue 306. Implementation choices that matter:\n *\n *  - One lua_State per worker thread. lua_State is not\n *    thread-safe, but per-thread requires no locking.\n *  - The state's stack is rewound to its baseline depth at every\n *    invoke entry/exit so cross-call leaks don't accumulate.\n *  - File caching (luaL_loadfile once, replayed via lua_call) is\n *    deferred — this iteration loads the chunk on every invoke.\n *    Lands as a follow-on once profiling justifies it.\n *  - The chunk's side effects run on every invoke too (since\n *    we re-load and re-execute). Box source files should be pure\n *    \"return M\" modules for now.\n */\n\n#include \"lang-spec.h\"\n\n#include <lua.h>\n#include <lauxlib.h>\n#include <lualib.h>\n\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <string.h>\n\n/* Registry key for the per-worker file → module-table cache. The\n * key is a string in the Lua registry; the value is a Lua table\n * keyed by file path. Each entry's value is the module table the\n * file's chunk returned.\n *\n * Caching is per-`lua_State` (i.e. per-worker), which matches the\n * thread model: each worker has its own state, never shared. No\n * locking needed because only the worker that owns the state ever\n * touches the cache. */\n#define LUA_CACHE_KEY \"soramech.module_cache\"\n\n/* {{{ lua_init() — create a state, open standard libs, seed cache */\nstatic void *lua_init(int worker_idx)\n{\n    (void)worker_idx;\n    lua_State *L = luaL_newstate();\n    if (!L) return NULL;\n    luaL_openlibs(L);\n    /* Seed the empty cache table. */\n    lua_newtable(L);\n    lua_setfield(L, LUA_REGISTRYINDEX, LUA_CACHE_KEY);\n    return L;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ lua_teardown() */\nstatic void lua_teardown(void *handle)\n{\n    if (handle) lua_close((lua_State *)handle);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ lua_invoke() */\nstatic int lua_invoke(void *handle,\n                      const char  *file_path,\n                      const char  *fn_name,\n                      const void **input_data,\n                      const int   *input_sizes,\n                      int          n_inputs,\n                      void        *out_buf,\n                      int          out_buf_capacity,\n                      int         *out_size)\n{\n    lua_State *L = (lua_State *)handle;\n    if (!L || !file_path || !fn_name) return -1;\n\n    int baseline = lua_gettop(L);\n\n    /* Module cache lookup. The cache table lives in the registry\n     * under LUA_CACHE_KEY; each key is a file path, each value is\n     * the module table the file's chunk returned. Stack after this\n     * block: ..., cache, module. */\n    lua_getfield(L, LUA_REGISTRYINDEX, LUA_CACHE_KEY);\n    lua_getfield(L, -1, file_path);\n    if (lua_isnil(L, -1)) {\n        lua_pop(L, 1);   /* discard nil */\n        /* Stack: ..., cache */\n\n        if (luaL_loadfile(L, file_path) != 0) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: loadfile('%s'): %s\\n\",\n                    file_path, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        if (lua_pcall(L, 0, 1, 0) != 0) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: chunk exec '%s': %s\\n\",\n                    file_path, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        if (!lua_istable(L, -1)) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: '%s' did not return a table\\n\", file_path);\n            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        /* Stack: ..., cache, module. Cache the module under\n         * file_path. */\n        lua_pushvalue(L, -1);\n        lua_setfield(L, -3, file_path);\n    }\n    /* Stack at this point: ..., cache, module. */\n\n    /* Pull the function out of the module table. */\n    lua_getfield(L, -1, fn_name);\n    if (!lua_isfunction(L, -1)) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: '%s' is not a function in %s\\n\",\n                fn_name, file_path);\n        lua_settop(L, baseline);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    /* Stack: ..., cache, module, function. Drop module + cache. */\n    lua_remove(L, -2);   /* drop module */\n    lua_remove(L, -2);   /* drop cache  */\n\n    /* Push each input as a Lua string. */\n    for (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n        if (input_data[i] == NULL && input_sizes[i] > 0) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: input %d is NULL with size %d\\n\",\n                    i, input_sizes[i]);\n            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        lua_pushlstring(L, (const char *)input_data[i], (size_t)input_sizes[i]);\n    }\n\n    /* Call. One return value expected. */\n    if (lua_pcall(L, n_inputs, 1, 0) != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: %s.%s: %s\\n\",\n                file_path, fn_name, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n        lua_settop(L, baseline);\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    /* Convert the return to a string. tostring handles numbers /\n     * booleans / nil; if the spec needs richer marshaling later\n     * (tables, structs), that's an issue-312-shaped change. */\n    size_t len = 0;\n    const char *result = lua_tolstring(L, -1, &len);\n    if (!result) {\n        /* Non-coercible value.     "newString":"/* {{{ encode_value() — write one Lua value at `abs_idx` as JSON */\n/* Walk the value at absolute stack index `abs_idx` and emit JSON\n * via the streaming writer `w`.     "originalFile":"/* langs/lua/spec.c — Lua language spec for SoraMech.\n *\n * Per-worker handle is a `lua_State` with the standard libraries\n * opened. Invocation convention: the box's source file is expected\n * to return a Lua table (`return M` at the bottom), and the\n * fn_name is a key into that table. Inputs arrive as byte arrays;\n * each one is pushed as a Lua string. The function's single return\n * value is converted to a string (via tostring semantics) and\n * memcpy'd into the caller's output buffer.\n *\n * Designed in issue 306. Implementation choices that matter:\n *\n *  - One lua_State per worker thread. lua_State is not\n *    thread-safe, but per-thread requires no locking.\n *  - The state's stack is rewound to its baseline depth at every\n *    invoke entry/exit so cross-call leaks don't accumulate.\n *  - File caching (luaL_loadfile once, replayed via lua_call) is\n *    deferred — this iteration loads the chunk on every invoke.\n *    Lands as a follow-on once profiling justifies it.\n *  - The chunk's side effects run on every invoke too (since\n *    we re-load and re-execute). Box source files should be pure\n *    \"return M\" modules for now.\n */\n\n#include \"lang-spec.h\"\n#include \"json.h\"\n\n#include <lua.h>\n#include <lauxlib.h>\n#include <lualib.h>\n\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n\n/* Registry key for the per-worker file → module-table cache. The\n * key is a string in the Lua registry; the value is a Lua table\n * keyed by file path. Each entry's value is the module table the\n * file's chunk returned.\n *\n * Caching is per-`lua_State` (i.e. per-worker), which matches the\n * thread model: each worker has its own state, never shared. No\n * locking needed because only the worker that owns the state ever\n * touches the cache. */\n#define LUA_CACHE_KEY \"soramech.module_cache\"\n\n/* {{{ lua_init() — create a state, open standard libs, seed cache */\nstatic void *lua_init(int worker_idx)\n{\n    (void)worker_idx;\n    lua_State *L = luaL_newstate();\n    if (!L) return NULL;\n    luaL_openlibs(L);\n    /* Seed the empty cache table. */\n    lua_newtable(L);\n    lua_setfield(L, LUA_REGISTRYINDEX, LUA_CACHE_KEY);\n    return L;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ lua_teardown() */\nstatic void lua_teardown(void *handle)\n{\n    if (handle) lua_close((lua_State *)handle);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ lua_invoke() */\nstatic int lua_invoke(void *handle,\n                      const char  *file_path,\n                      const char  *fn_name,\n                      const void **input_data,\n                      const int   *input_sizes,\n                      int          n_inputs,\n                      void        *out_buf,\n                      int          out_buf_capacity,\n                      int         *out_size)\n{\n    lua_State *L = (lua_State *)handle;\n    if (!L || !file_path || !fn_name) return -1;\n\n    int baseline = lua_gettop(L);\n\n    /* Module cache lookup. The cache table lives in the registry\n     * under LUA_CACHE_KEY; each key is a file path, each value is\n     * the module table the file's chunk returned. Stack after this\n     * block: ..., cache, module. */\n    lua_getfield(L, LUA_REGISTRYINDEX, LUA_CACHE_KEY);\n    lua_getfield(L, -1, file_path);\n    if (lua_isnil(L, -1)) {\n        lua_pop(L, 1);   /* discard nil */\n        /* Stack: ..., cache */\n\n        if (luaL_loadfile(L, file_path) != 0) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: loadfile('%s'): %s\\n\",\n                    file_path, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        if (lua_pcall(L, 0, 1, 0) != 0) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: chunk exec '%s': %s\\n\",\n                    file_path, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        if (!lua_istable(L, -1)) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: '%s' did not return a table\\n\", file_path);\n            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        /* Stack: ..., cache, module. Cache the module under\n         * file_path. */\n        lua_pushvalue(L, -1);\n        lua_setfield(L, -3, file_path);\n    }\n    /* Stack at this point: ..., cache, module. */\n\n    /* Pull the function out of the module table. */\n    lua_getfield(L, -1, fn_name);\n    if (!lua_isfunction(L, -1)) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: '%s' is not a function in %s\\n\",\n                fn_name, file_path);\n        lua_settop(L, baseline);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    /* Stack: ..., cache, module, function. Drop module + cache. */\n    lua_remove(L, -2);   /* drop module */\n    lua_remove(L, -2);   /* drop cache  */\n\n    /* Push each input as a Lua string. */\n    for (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n        if (input_data[i] == NULL && input_sizes[i] > 0) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: input %d is NULL with size %d\\n\",\n                    i, input_sizes[i]);\n            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        lua_pushlstring(L, (const char *)input_data[i], (size_t)input_sizes[i]);\n    }\n\n    /* Call. One return value expected. */\n    if (lua_pcall(L, n_inputs, 1, 0) != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: %s.%s: %s\\n\",\n                file_path, fn_name, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n        lua_settop(L, baseline);\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    /* Convert the return to a string. tostring handles numbers /\n     * booleans / nil; if the spec needs richer marshaling later\n     * (tables, structs), that's an issue-312-shaped change. */\n    size_t len = 0;\n    const char *result = lua_tolstring(L, -1, &len);\n    if (!result) {\n        /* Non-coercible value. Exercises the\n * file-load + module-table + named-function invocation path with\n * both positional and optional arguments.\n *\n * Run from the project root so `langs/` and `tests/maps/` are\n * reachable.\n */\n\n#include \"011-spec-registry.h\"\n#include \"lang-spec.h\"\n\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n#include <sys/stat.h>\n\n/* {{{ Test harness */\nstatic int g_pass = 0;\nstatic int g_fail = 0;\n\n#define ASSERT(cond) \\\n    do { if (!(cond)) { \\\n        fprintf(stderr, \"      %s:%d: %s\\n\", __FILE__, __LINE__, #cond); \\\n        return 0; \\\n    } } while (0)\n\n#define RUN(name) \\\n    do { \\\n        fprintf(stdout, \"  %-44s \", #name); fflush(stdout); \\\n        if (test_##name()) { fprintf(stdout, \"ok\\n\"); g_pass++; } \\\n        else                { fprintf(stdout, \"FAIL\\n\"); g_fail++; } \\\n    } while (0)\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ load_lua_spec() — shared by every test */\nstatic const lang_spec_t *load_lua_spec(spec_registry_t **out_reg)\n{\n    char *err = NULL;\n    spec_registry_t *r = spec_registry_load(\"langs\", &err);\n    if (!r) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"registry load failed: %s\\n\", err ? err : \"(null)\");\n        free(err);\n        return NULL;\n    }\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = spec_registry_get(r, \"lua\");\n    if (!lua || !lua->init || !lua->invoke || !lua->teardown) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec missing callbacks\\n\");\n        spec_registry_destroy(r);\n        return NULL;\n    }\n    *out_reg = r;\n    return lua;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_init_teardown() */\nstatic int test_init_teardown(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n    ASSERT(h);\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_invoke_greet_both_args() */\nstatic int test_invoke_greet_both_args(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n    ASSERT(h);\n\n    const char *name = \"World\";\n    const char *sal  = \"Hi\";\n    const void *args[2]  = { name, sal };\n    int         sizes[2] = { (int)strlen(name), (int)strlen(sal) };\n    char buf[128];\n    int n = 0;\n\n    int rc = lua->invoke(h, \"tests/maps/hello/src/hello.lua\", \"greet\",\n                         args, sizes, 2,\n                         buf, sizeof buf, &n);\n    ASSERT(rc == 0);\n    ASSERT(n == (int)strlen(\"Hi, World!\"));\n    buf[n] = '\\0';\n    ASSERT(strcmp(buf, \"Hi, World!\") == 0);\n\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_invoke_greet_default_salutation() */\n/* greet(name) — salutation defaults to \"Hello\" inside the function. */\nstatic int test_invoke_greet_default_salutation(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n\n    const char *name = \"moon\";\n    const void *args[1]  = { name };\n    int         sizes[1] = { 4 };\n    char buf[64];\n    int n = 0;\n\n    int rc = lua->invoke(h, \"tests/maps/hello/src/hello.lua\", \"greet\",\n                         args, sizes, 1, buf, sizeof buf, &n);\n    ASSERT(rc == 0);\n    buf[n] = '\\0';\n    ASSERT(strcmp(buf, \"Hello, moon!\") == 0);\n\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_invoke_missing_function() */\nstatic int test_invoke_missing_function(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n\n    char buf[64];\n    int  n = 0;\n    int rc = lua->invoke(h, \"tests/maps/hello/src/hello.lua\", \"no_such_fn\",\n                         NULL, NULL, 0, buf, sizeof buf, &n);\n    ASSERT(rc != 0);\n\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_invoke_missing_file() */\nstatic int test_invoke_missing_file(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n\n    char buf[64];\n    int  n = 0;\n    int rc = lua->invoke(h,           "content":"/* tests/317-lua-bridge-test.c — Lua spec native↔JSON bridges.\n *\n * Loads langs/lua/spec.so through the spec registry and exercises\n * `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` together. The strategy is a\n * round-trip: feed a JSON string in via `json_to_native` (which\n * pushes a Lua value on the worker's lua_State), then yank it back\n * out via `native_to_json` (which reads top-of-stack and writes JSON\n * to a buffer). If the input and output match, both halves of the\n * bridge agree on the encoding.\n *\n * The round-trip approach keeps this test free of any direct\n * dependency on the LuaJIT headers — the bridges are the only thing\n * the test calls, and the lua_State is opaque from C's side. That\n * matches the cross-language wire-format design (issue 317): callers\n * never need to know Lua's internals to move data through it.\n *\n * Run from the project root so the spec dlopen path resolves.\n */\n\n#include \"011-spec-registry.h\"\n#include \"lang-spec.h\"\n\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n#include <sys/stat.h>\n\n/* {{{ Test harness */\nstatic int g_pass = 0;\nstatic int g_fail = 0;\n\n#define ASSERT(cond) \\\n    do { if (!(cond)) { \\\n        fprintf(stderr, \"      %s:%d: %s\\n\", __FILE__, __LINE__, #cond); \\\n        return 0; \\\n    } } while (0)\n\n#define RUN(name) \\\n    do { \\\n        fprintf(stdout, \"  %-44s \", #name); fflush(stdout); \\\n        if (test_##name()) { fprintf(stdout, \"ok\\n\"); g_pass++; } \\\n        else                { fprintf(stdout, \"FAIL\\n\"); g_fail++; } \\\n    } while (0)\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ load_lua_spec() — boot the registry and find the lua spec */\nstatic const lang_spec_t *load_lua_spec(spec_registry_t **out_reg)\n{\n    char *err = NULL;\n    spec_registry_t *r = spec_registry_load(\"langs\", &err);\n    if (!r) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"registry load failed: %s\\n\", err ? err : \"(null)\");\n        free(err);\n        return NULL;\n    }\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = spec_registry_get(r, \"lua\");\n    if (!lua || !lua->init || !lua->teardown\n            || !lua->native_to_json || !lua->json_to_native) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec missing bridge callbacks\\n\");\n        spec_registry_destroy(r);\n        return NULL;\n    }\n    *out_reg = r;\n    return lua;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ roundtrip() — JSON → Lua stack → JSON, compare to expected */\n/* Convenience used by every test case. `expected` is the canonical\n * JSON the bridge should emit on the way back; if NULL, the input\n * itself is the expected output. Returns 1 on success. */\nstatic int roundtrip(const lang_spec_t *lua, void *h,\n                     const char *input, const char *expected)\n{\n    char out[512];\n    int  out_size = 0;\n    int  rc = lua->json_to_native(h, input, (int)strlen(input),\n                                  NULL, 0, NULL);\n    if (rc != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"      json_to_native failed for '%s'\\n\", input);\n        return 0;\n    }\n    rc = lua->native_to_json(h, NULL, 0, out, (int)sizeof(out), &out_size);\n    if (rc != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"      native_to_json failed for '%s'\\n\", input);\n        return 0;\n    }\n    out[out_size] = '\\0';\n    const char *want = expected ? expected : input;\n    if (strcmp(out, want) != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"      mismatch: want '%s', got '%s'\\n\", want, out);\n        return 0;\n    }\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_scalars() — null, bool, integer, float, string */\nstatic int test_scalars(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n    ASSERT(h);\n\n    /* Integer-shaped Lua numbers round-trip as integers (3, not 3.0)\n     * because encode_value picks the int writer for whole values.\n     * \"null\" round-trips because nil → null → nil. */\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"null\",      NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"true\",      NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"false\",     NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"0\",         NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"42\",        NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"-17\",       NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"\\\"\\\"\",      NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"\\\"hello\\\"\", NULL));\n\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_arrays() — sequence tables round-trip as JSON arrays */\nstatic int test_arrays(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n\n    /* Empty array is the one shape we *can't* round-trip as []\n     * because an empty Lua table can't be told apart from {} on the\n     * way out (see encode_value's array-vs-object heuristic). A too-small output\n * buffer must surface as a nonzero return from native_to_json,\n * not a truncated-but-success path. */\nstatic int test_truncation(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n\n    int rc = lua->json_to_native(h, \"[1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9]\",\n                                 (int)strlen(\"[1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9]\"),\n                                 NULL, 0, NULL);\n    ASSERT(rc == 0);\n\n    char tiny[4];\n    int  out_size = 0;\n    rc = lua->native_to_json(h, NULL, 0, tiny, (int)sizeof(tiny), &out_size);\n    ASSERT(rc != 0);\n\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_parse_error() — malformed JSON returns nonzero */\nstatic int test_parse_error(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n\n    int rc = lua->json_to_native(h, \"{not json\", 9, NULL, 0, NULL);\n    ASSERT(rc != 0);\n\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ main() */\nint main(void)\n{\n    struct stat st;\n    if (stat(\"langs/lua/spec.so\", &st) != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"317-lua-bridge-test: langs/lua/spec.so not built; \"\n                        \"run `make specs` first\\n\");\n        return 2;\n    }\n    printf(\"317-lua-bridge-test:\\n\");\n    RUN(scalars);\n    RUN(arrays);\n    RUN(objects);\n    RUN(truncation);\n    RUN(parse_error);\n    printf(\"\\n  %d passed, %d failed\\n\", g_pass, g_fail);\n    return g_fail == 0 ? 0 : 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n",

    "content":"/* tests/317-lua-bridge-test.c — Lua spec native↔JSON bridges.\n *\n * Loads langs/lua/spec.so through the spec registry and exercises\n * `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` together. The strategy is a\n * round-trip: feed a JSON string in via `json_to_native` (which\n * pushes a Lua value on the worker's lua_State), then yank it back\n * out via `native_to_json` (which reads top-of-stack and writes JSON\n * to a buffer). If the input and output match, both halves of the\n * bridge agree on the encoding.\n *\n * The round-trip approach keeps this test free of any direct\n * dependency on the LuaJIT headers — the bridges are the only thing\n * the test calls, and the lua_State is opaque from C's side. That\n * matches the cross-language wire-format design (issue 317): callers\n * never need to know Lua's internals to move data through it.\n *\n * Run from the project root so the spec dlopen path resolves.\n */\n\n#include \"011-spec-registry.h\"\n#include \"lang-spec.h\"\n\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n#include <sys/stat.h>\n\n/* {{{ Test harness */\nstatic int g_pass = 0;\nstatic int g_fail = 0;\n\n#define ASSERT(cond) \\\n    do { if (!(cond)) { \\\n        fprintf(stderr, \"      %s:%d: %s\\n\", __FILE__, __LINE__, #cond); \\\n        return 0; \\\n    } } while (0)\n\n#define RUN(name) \\\n    do { \\\n        fprintf(stdout, \"  %-44s \", #name); fflush(stdout); \\\n        if (test_##name()) { fprintf(stdout, \"ok\\n\"); g_pass++; } \\\n        else                { fprintf(stdout, \"FAIL\\n\"); g_fail++; } \\\n    } while (0)\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ load_lua_spec() — boot the registry and find the lua spec */\nstatic const lang_spec_t *load_lua_spec(spec_registry_t **out_reg)\n{\n    char *err = NULL;\n    spec_registry_t *r = spec_registry_load(\"langs\", &err);\n    if (!r) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"registry load failed: %s\\n\", err ? err : \"(null)\");\n        free(err);\n        return NULL;\n    }\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = spec_registry_get(r, \"lua\");\n    if (!lua || !lua->init || !lua->teardown\n            || !lua->native_to_json || !lua->json_to_native) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec missing bridge callbacks\\n\");\n        spec_registry_destroy(r);\n        return NULL;\n    }\n    *out_reg = r;\n    return lua;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ roundtrip() — JSON → Lua stack → JSON, compare to expected */\n/* Convenience used by every test case. `expected` is the canonical\n * JSON the bridge should emit on the way back; if NULL, the input\n * itself is the expected output. Returns 1 on success. */\nstatic int roundtrip(const lang_spec_t *lua, void *h,\n                     const char *input, const char *expected)\n{\n    char out[512];\n    int  out_size = 0;\n    int  rc = lua->json_to_native(h, input, (int)strlen(input),\n                                  NULL, 0, NULL);\n    if (rc != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"      json_to_native failed for '%s'\\n\", input);\n        return 0;\n    }\n    rc = lua->native_to_json(h, NULL, 0, out, (int)sizeof(out), &out_size);\n    if (rc != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"      native_to_json failed for '%s'\\n\", input);\n        return 0;\n    }\n    out[out_size] = '\\0';\n    const char *want = expected ? expected : input;\n    if (strcmp(out, want) != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"      mismatch: want '%s', got '%s'\\n\", want, out);\n        return 0;\n    }\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_scalars() — null, bool, integer, float, string */\nstatic int test_scalars(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n    ASSERT(h);\n\n    /* Integer-shaped Lua numbers round-trip as integers (3, not 3.0)\n     * because encode_value picks the int writer for whole values.\n     * \"null\" round-trips because nil → null → nil. */\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"null\",      NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"true\",      NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"false\",     NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"0\",         NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"42\",        NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"-17\",       NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"\\\"\\\"\",      NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"\\\"hello\\\"\", NULL));\n\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_arrays() — sequence tables round-trip as JSON arrays */\nstatic int test_arrays(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n\n    /* Empty array is the one shape we *can't* round-trip as []\n     * because an empty Lua table can't be told apart from {} on the\n     * way out (see encode_value's array-vs-object heuristic). The\n     * round-trip canonicalises [] to {} — a deliberate, documented\n     * choice. Every non-empty sequence works as expected. */\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"[]\",                \"{}\"));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"[1]\",               NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"[1,2,3]\",           NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"[\\\"a\\\",\\\"b\\\"]\",     NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"[[1,2],[3,4]]\",     NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"[true,false,null]\", NULL));\n\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_objects() — keyed tables round-trip as JSON objects */\n/* Object key ordering inside a Lua table is not guaranteed to\n * match the input — Lua's table iteration order is implementation\n * defined. We test single-key objects (no ordering ambiguity) and\n * nested structure for the multi-key case. */\nstatic int test_objects(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"{}\",            NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"{\\\"x\\\":1}\",     NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"{\\\"a\\\":\\\"b\\\"}\", NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"{\\\"nest\\\":{\\\"k\\\":42}}\", NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"{\\\"items\\\":[1,2,3]}\",   NULL));\n\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_truncation() — undersized buffer is a loud error */\n/* Project convention forbids silent fallbacks. A too-small output\n * buffer must surface as a nonzero return from native_to_json,\n * not a truncated-but-success path. */\nstatic int test_truncation(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n\n    int rc = lua->json_to_native(h, \"[1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9]\",\n                                 (int)strlen(\"[1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9]\"),\n                                 NULL, 0, NULL);\n    ASSERT(rc == 0);\n\n    char tiny[4];\n    int  out_size = 0;\n    rc = lua->native_to_json(h, NULL, 0, tiny, (int)sizeof(tiny), &out_size);\n    ASSERT(rc != 0);\n\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_parse_error() — malformed JSON returns nonzero */\nstatic int test_parse_error(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n\n    int rc = lua->json_to_native(h, \"{not json\", 9, NULL, 0, NULL);\n    ASSERT(rc != 0);\n\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ main() */\nint main(void)\n{\n    struct stat st;\n    if (stat(\"langs/lua/spec.so\", &st) != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"317-lua-bridge-test: langs/lua/spec.so not built; \"\n                        \"run `make specs` first\\n\");\n        return 2;\n    }\n    printf(\"317-lua-bridge-test:\\n\");\n    RUN(scalars);\n    RUN(arrays);\n    RUN(objects);\n    RUN(truncation);\n    RUN(parse_error);\n    printf(\"\\n  %d passed, %d failed\\n\", g_pass, g_fail);\n    return g_fail == 0 ? 0 : 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n",

All paths in this Makefile are relative to\n# $(DIR) per the project convention.\n#\n# Designed in issue 309. Implementation of the runner's runtime is\n# split across issues 301–308; this Makefile builds whatever sources\n# exist under src/, libs/task-pool/, and libs/json/, so it scales as\n# those issues land.\n\n# {{{ Resolve project root\nDIR ?= $(abspath $(dir $(lastword $(MAKEFILE_LIST))))\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Toolchain & flags\nCC      ?= gcc\n\n# Shared header search path: every C source can find langs/lang-spec.h\n# and any future libs/<name>/ headers via -I flags below.\nCPPFLAGS = -I$(DIR)/langs -I$(DIR)/libs/task-pool -I$(DIR)/libs/json -I$(DIR)/src\n\n# Default to release; DEBUG and STRICT toggle alternates.\nifeq ($(DEBUG),1)\n  CFLAGS = -O0 -g -DDEBUG -Wall -pthread -fPIC\nelse ifeq ($(STRICT),1)\n  CFLAGS = -O2 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -pthread -fPIC\nelse\n  CFLAGS = -O2 -Wall -pthread -fPIC\nendif\n\nLDFLAGS = -ldl -pthread\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Paths and source discovery\nBUILD_DIR = $(DIR)/build\nPOOL_BIN  = $(DIR)/soramech-pool\n\n# Wildcards: empty subdirs return empty lists, which is fine. As\n# issues 301/302/303/304/305 land their C sources here, they get\n# compiled automatically — no Makefile edit required.\nPOOL_SOURCES = \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/src/*.c) \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/libs/task-pool/*.c) \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/libs/json/*.c)\n\nPOOL_OBJECTS = $(POOL_SOURCES:$(DIR)/%.c=$(BUILD_DIR)/%.o)\n\n# Test sources live in tests/ as C files named to match the source\n# they exercise (e.g. tests/009-slot-store-test.c exercises\n# src/009-slot-store.c). Each builds to a separate executable that\n# `make test` runs in turn.\nTEST_SOURCES = $(wildcard $(DIR)/tests/*.c)\nTEST_BINS    = $(TEST_SOURCES:$(DIR)/tests/%.c=$(BUILD_DIR)/tests/%)\n\nLANGS = lua c bash\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Public targets\n.PHONY: all runner specs clean test help\n\nall: runner specs\n\nrunner: $(POOL_BIN)\n\nspecs:\n\t@for lang in $(LANGS); do \\\n\t  echo \"  → langs/$$lang\"; \\\n\t  $(MAKE) -s -C $(DIR)/langs/$$lang DIR=$(DIR) || exit 1; \\\n\tdone\n\nclean:\n\trm -f $(POOL_BIN)\n\trm -rf $(BUILD_DIR)\n\t@for lang in $(LANGS); do \\\n\t  $(MAKE) -s -C $(DIR)/langs/$$lang DIR=$(DIR) clean || true; \\\n\tdone\n\ntest: all $(TEST_BINS)\n\t@echo\n\t@fail=0; \\\n\tfor t in $(TEST_BINS); do \\\n\t  $$t || fail=1; \\\n\t  echo; \\\n\tdone; \\\n\tif [ -x $(DIR)/scripts/run-tests.sh ]; then \\\n\t  $(DIR)/scripts/run-tests.sh $(DIR) || fail=1; \\\n\tfi; \\\n\texit $$fail\n\nhelp:\n\t@echo \"SoraMech build:\"\n\t@echo \"  make          — build runner + specs (release)\"\n\t@echo \"  make DEBUG=1  — debug info, no optimization\"\n\t@echo \"  make STRICT=1 — promote warnings to errors\"\n\t@echo \"  make clean    — remove every built artifact\"\n\t@echo \"  make test     — run integration tests (when 311 lands)\"\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Build rules\n$(POOL_BIN): $(POOL_OBJECTS)\n\t@echo \"  → $(notdir $@)\"\n\t@$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(CPPFLAGS) -o $@ $^ $(LDFLAGS)\n\n$(BUILD_DIR)/%.o: $(DIR)/%.c\n\t@mkdir -p $(dir $@)\n\t@echo \"  → $(patsubst $(DIR)/%,%,$<)\"\n\t@$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(CPPFLAGS) -c -o $@ $<\n\n# Per-test dependency lines.     "originalFile":"/* tests/317-lua-bridge-test.c — Lua spec native↔JSON bridges.\n *\n * Loads langs/lua/spec.so through the spec registry and exercises\n * `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` together. The strategy is a\n * round-trip: feed a JSON string in via `json_to_native` (which\n * pushes a Lua value on the worker's lua_State), then yank it back\n * out via `native_to_json` (which reads top-of-stack and writes JSON\n * to a buffer). If the input and output match, both halves of the\n * bridge agree on the encoding.\n *\n * The round-trip approach keeps this test free of any direct\n * dependency on the LuaJIT headers — the bridges are the only thing\n * the test calls, and the lua_State is opaque from C's side. That\n * matches the cross-language wire-format design (issue 317): callers\n * never need to know Lua's internals to move data through it.\n *\n * Run from the project root so the spec dlopen path resolves.\n */\n\n#include \"011-spec-registry.h\"\n#include \"lang-spec.h\"\n\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n#include <sys/stat.h>\n\n/* {{{ Test harness */\nstatic int g_pass = 0;\nstatic int g_fail = 0;\n\n#define ASSERT(cond) \\\n    do { if (!(cond)) { \\\n        fprintf(stderr, \"      %s:%d: %s\\n\", __FILE__, __LINE__, #cond); \\\n        return 0; \\\n    } } while (0)\n\n#define RUN(name) \\\n    do { \\\n        fprintf(stdout, \"  %-44s \", #name); fflush(stdout); \\\n        if (test_##name()) { fprintf(stdout, \"ok\\n\"); g_pass++; } \\\n        else                { fprintf(stdout, \"FAIL\\n\"); g_fail++; } \\\n    } while (0)\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ load_lua_spec() — boot the registry and find the lua spec */\nstatic const lang_spec_t *load_lua_spec(spec_registry_t **out_reg)\n{\n    char *err = NULL;\n    spec_registry_t *r = spec_registry_load(\"langs\", &err);\n    if (!r) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"registry load failed: %s\\n\", err ? err : \"(null)\");\n        free(err);\n        return NULL;\n    }\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = spec_registry_get(r, \"lua\");\n    if (!lua || !lua->init || !lua->teardown\n            || !lua->native_to_json || !lua->json_to_native) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec missing bridge callbacks\\n\");\n        spec_registry_destroy(r);\n        return NULL;\n    }\n    *out_reg = r;\n    return lua;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ roundtrip() — JSON → Lua stack → JSON, compare to expected */\n/* Convenience used by every test case. `expected` is the canonical\n * JSON the bridge should emit on the way back; if NULL, the input\n * itself is the expected output. Returns 1 on success. */\nstatic int roundtrip(const lang_spec_t *lua, void *h,\n                     const char *input, const char *expected)\n{\n    char out[512];\n    int  out_size = 0;\n    int  rc = lua->json_to_native(h, input, (int)strlen(input),\n                                  NULL, 0, NULL);\n    if (rc != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"      json_to_native failed for '%s'\\n\", input);\n        return 0;\n    }\n    rc = lua->native_to_json(h, NULL, 0, out, (int)sizeof(out), &out_size);\n    if (rc != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"      native_to_json failed for '%s'\\n\", input);\n        return 0;\n    }\n    out[out_size] = '\\0';\n    const char *want = expected ? expected : input;\n    if (strcmp(out, want) != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"      mismatch: want '%s', got '%s'\\n\", want, out);\n        return 0;\n    }\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_scalars() — null, bool, integer, float, string */\nstatic int test_scalars(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n    ASSERT(h);\n\n    /* Integer-shaped Lua numbers round-trip as integers (3, not 3.0)\n     * because encode_value picks the int writer for whole values.\n     * \"null\" round-trips because nil → null → nil. */\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"null\",      NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"true\",      NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"false\",     NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"0\",         NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"42\",        NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"-17\",       NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"\\\"\\\"\",      NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"\\\"hello\\\"\", NULL));\n\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_arrays() — sequence tables round-trip as JSON arrays */\nstatic int test_arrays(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n\n    /* Empty array is the one shape we *can't* round-trip as []\n     * because an empty Lua table can't be told apart from {} on the\n     * way out (see encode_value's array-vs-object heuristic). The\n     * round-trip canonicalises [] to {} — a deliberate, documented\n     * choice. Every non-empty sequence works as expected. */\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"[]\",                \"{}\"));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"[1]\",               NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"[1,2,3]\",           NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"[\\\"a\\\",\\\"b\\\"]\",     NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"[[1,2],[3,4]]\",     NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"[true,false,null]\", NULL));\n\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_objects() — keyed tables round-trip as JSON objects */\n/* Object key ordering inside a Lua table is not guaranteed to\n * match the input — Lua's table iteration order is implementation\n * defined. We test single-key objects (no ordering ambiguity) and\n * nested structure for the multi-key case. */\nstatic int test_objects(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"{}\",            NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"{\\\"x\\\":1}\",     NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"{\\\"a\\\":\\\"b\\\"}\", NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"{\\\"nest\\\":{\\\"k\\\":42}}\", NULL));\n    ASSERT(roundtrip(lua, h, \"{\\\"items\\\":[1,2,3]}\",   NULL));\n\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_truncation() — undersized buffer is a loud error */\n/* Project convention forbids silent fallbacks. A too-small output\n * buffer must surface as a nonzero return from native_to_json,\n * not a truncated-but-success path. */\nstatic int test_truncation(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n\n    int rc = lua->json_to_native(h, \"[1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9]\",\n                                 (int)strlen(\"[1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9]\"),\n                                 NULL, 0, NULL);\n    ASSERT(rc == 0);\n\n    char tiny[4];\n    int  out_size = 0;\n    rc = lua->native_to_json(h, NULL, 0, tiny, (int)sizeof(tiny), &out_size);\n    ASSERT(rc != 0);\n\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_parse_error() — malformed JSON returns nonzero */\nstatic int test_parse_error(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n\n    int rc = lua->json_to_native(h, \"{not json\", 9, NULL, 0, NULL);\n    ASSERT(rc != 0);\n\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ main() */\nint main(void)\n{\n    struct stat st;\n    if (stat(\"langs/lua/spec.so\", &st) != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"317-lua-bridge-test: langs/lua/spec.so not built; \"\n                        \"run `make specs` first\\n\");\n        return 2;\n    }\n    printf(\"317-lua-bridge-test:\\n\");\n    RUN(scalars);\n    RUN(arrays);\n    RUN(objects);\n    RUN(truncation);\n    RUN(parse_error);\n    printf(\"\\n  %d passed, %d failed\\n\", g_pass, g_fail);\n    return g_fail == 0 ? 0 : 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n",

      "content":"# 317 — Language spec JSON bridge for data boxes\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA data box (`kind: data` in box JSON) emits a value the rest of\nthe graph routes downstream. Today the runner reads the box's\n`ref` file as raw bytes and emits them — there's no concept of\n\"authoring this datum in a particular language using that\nlanguage's natural structures.\" If you want to declare a Lua\ntable as a data box's value, you either:\n\n- Hand-translate the table to JSON, save it as a `.json` file,\n  and lose the Lua syntax niceties; or\n- Make it a call box that returns the table, paying for a full\n  spec invocation just to read a constant; or\n- Hard-code the bytes inline in the box's `data` field, with no\n  syntactic help from any host language.\n\nThis is the wrong shape. **A box author writes idiomatic code in\nthe language of their choice.** That's the rule 307 establishes\nfor call boxes: a C-box author writes a plain C function, no\nSoraMech-specific glue. The data-box equivalent should hold —\na Lua-data-box author should write a Lua file that returns\nwhatever they want returned (a table, a string, a number), and\nSoraMech should know how to lift that into the graph as a JSON\nwire value without the author writing a single SoraMech-specific\ncharacter.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEvery language spec gains two callbacks, declared in\n`lang_spec_t` (issue 303):\n\n```c\n/* Serialize a native-language value into JSON text.\n *\n *   ctx       — per-worker handle from spec.init.\n *   src       — caller-meaningful pointer to the native value.\n *               Format is spec-specific (see \"Native handle\n *               representation\" below).\n *   src_size  — size hint, or 0 if the spec interprets `src`\n *               without a length.\n *   out_buf   — destination buffer for JSON text (caller-owned).\n *   out_cap   — capacity of out_buf.\n *   out_size  — set to the bytes written.\n *\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error. Writes an error message\n * via the spec's existing error-reporting plumbing. */\nint (*native_to_json)(void *ctx,\n                      const void *src, uint32_t src_size,\n                      char *out_buf, uint32_t out_cap, uint32_t *out_size);\n\n/* Inverse: parse JSON text into a native-language value. The\n * native value is stored wherever the spec considers natural\n * (Lua: pushed to the worker's lua_State stack; C: written into\n * a typed struct supplied by `dst`; Bash: written as a textual\n * representation back into dst).\n *\n *   ctx       — per-worker handle.\n *   src       — JSON text.\n *   src_size  — JSON text length in bytes.\n *   dst       — caller-supplied target; semantics per spec.\n *   dst_cap   — capacity, where meaningful.\n *   dst_size  — set to the bytes / native units consumed.\n *\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error. */\nint (*json_to_native)(void *ctx,\n                      const char *src, uint32_t src_size,\n                      void *dst, uint32_t dst_cap, uint32_t *dst_size);\n```\n\nThese are the same fields 312's same-language fast path\nreserves; this issue is the one that requires every spec to\n**actually implement them**, driven by the data-box use case.\n(312 needs them too, but its driver is performance; 317 needs\nthem for correctness — a data box can't function without them.)\n\n### The rule, restated\n\nThe author of a data box writes a `.lua` / `.c` / `.sh` /\n`.<whatever>` file that returns or produces a value using\n*their language's native idioms*. No SoraMech macros. No\nSoraMech includes. No SoraMech-specific JSON shape constraints\nbeyond \"what your spec's native_to_json can convert.\"\n\nIf the author returns a Lua table, the Lua spec's\n`native_to_json` converts it. If they return a C struct, the C\nspec's `native_to_json` walks it according to the type declared\nin the box. If they print JSON-ish text from a bash script, the\nbash spec's `native_to_json` is a no-op identity (the script\nalready produced JSON).\n\nThe contract belongs to the spec author, not the box author.\nThat's the inversion: **SoraMech bends to the language, not the\nother way around.**\n\n## Native handle representation\n\nThe shape of `src` / `dst` in the callbacks is per-spec. Each\nspec documents what it accepts:\n\n- **Lua spec**: `src` is the index of a value already pushed\n  onto the worker's `lua_State`. `src_size` is unused. The\n  spec's `native_to_json` reads the value at that stack index\n  and writes JSON. `json_to_native` pushes the parsed JSON value\n  onto the stack, and `dst_size` reports the number of stack\n  slots used (always 1 for SoraMech's flat-value model).\n- **C spec**: `src` is a typed pointer + the box's declared\n  output type drives the walk. `src_size` is the type's\n  storage footprint. Mirror image for `json_to_native`. (This\n  ties into 307's typed-wrapper-generation work — the same\n  type system describes both the wrapper signature and the\n  JSON shape.)\n- **Bash spec**: `src` is text the script produced.\n  `native_to_json` validates and reshapes to JSON if needed (a\n  bash script that prints `42` becomes JSON `42`; a script that\n  prints `{\"a\":1}` passes through unchanged). `json_to_native`\n  is similarly a near-identity. The spec author is encouraged\n  to require scripts produce well-formed JSON in the first\n  place rather than write a bash-syntax parser.\n\nThe dispatch layer doesn't know or care which representation a\nspec uses. It only ever passes `src` and `src_size` to the\nspec's callback. The spec is opaque to the runtime; that's the\nwhole point.\n\n## Data box semantics\n\nA data box's `data` field becomes optional. The box gains\noptional `lang` and `ref` fields:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"config\",\n  \"kind\": \"data\",\n  \"lang\": \"lua\",\n  \"ref\": \"config.lua\"\n}\n```\n\nAt graph load, the runner:\n\n1. Resolves the spec for `lang`.\n2. Calls the spec's `init` (already done at worker startup).\n3. At box-fire time, asks the spec to execute the `ref` file\n   and produce a native value (this is essentially the same\n   \"load this file, run it, get its return value\" path the\n   spec already implements for call boxes — call boxes call a\n   named function; data boxes take the file's return value).\n4. Calls the spec's `native_to_json` to convert the native\n   value to JSON text.\n5. Pushes that JSON text down the wire as the box's output —\n   same as today's data path, just with the value sourced\n   from a language-native file.\n\nIf the box has no `lang` and a literal `data` field, the legacy\ninline-data path applies unchanged.\n\n## Why every spec must implement these\n\nThe same JSON the data box emits is consumed by some downstream\nbox (call, comparator, file_write, whatever). That downstream\nbox, if it's in a different language, will eventually need\n*its* spec's `json_to_native` to convert the JSON back. So the\ntwo callbacks are paired — every spec that participates in the\ngraph needs both. A spec that implements `native_to_json` but\nnot `json_to_native` can only be data-box sources; a spec with\nonly `json_to_native` can only be call-box sinks. We require\nboth so any language can play any role.\n\nSpecs that haven't been updated yet should set both callbacks\nto a stub that returns -1 with a clear error message (\"spec\n`<name>`: native_to_json not implemented; this box's value\ncan't be routed cross-language\"). The hard-fail makes the gap\nloud rather than producing wrong output.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. Extend the `lang_spec_t` declaration in\n   `langs/lang-spec.h` if not already done by 312's\n   infrastructure work. (Per the round summary, the slot is\n   reserved.)\n2. Implement `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` in each\n   spec:\n   - **Lua spec**: walk the value at the stack index. Use the\n     existing C JSON writer (`libs/json/json.c`). Handle Lua\n     tables both as arrays (1-indexed contiguous integer keys)\n     and as objects. Refuse functions, userdata, threads.\n   - **C spec**: depends on 307's typed-wrapper machinery. For\n     now, a stub that only supports scalar types (int, double,\n     string) is enough to get data boxes working in C.\n   - **Bash spec**: validate-and-pass-through. The script is\n     expected to produce JSON. `native_to_json` runs the JSON\n     parser to validate; `json_to_native` is identity.\n3. Extend the data box runtime path in `src/012-dispatch.c`\n   (or wherever data boxes dispatch from) to consult `lang` /\n   `ref` when set and route through the spec callback chain.\n4. Add a fixture: `tests/maps/cross-lang-data/` with a Lua\n   data box, a C consumer, and a Bash consumer all reading the\n   same value. The integration check asserts each consumer\n   sees the right data.\n5. Update each spec's `*.info.md` to document the native handle\n   shape its callbacks expect.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — extend the contract\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` —\n  implement the callbacks\n- `langs/{lua,c,bash}/spec.info.md` — document native handle\n  semantics per spec\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — data-box dispatch path\n- `tests/maps/cross-lang-data/` — new fixture (see step 4)\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — same author-writes-natural-\n  code principle; this issue extends it from call boxes to data\n  boxes\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — reuses the same\n  spec callbacks for a different (performance) reason\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Bash's `json_to_native` is a near-identity because the\n  scripts already deal in text. Is there value in having it\n  validate and reformat for consistency? Probably yes; cheap\n  insurance against malformed downstream input.\n- Should the Lua spec auto-detect array-vs-object tables, or\n  require the box author to annotate? Auto-detect (contiguous\n  1-indexed integer keys → array; otherwise object) is what\n  every other lua-to-json library does and is intuitive enough.\n- C spec's `native_to_json` for arbitrary structs is a real\n  rabbit hole. Tie scope to 307 — the same type declarations\n  drive both the wrapper and the JSON walk. Until 307 lands,\n  only scalar types are supported for C data boxes.\n",

    "originalFile":"# 317 — Language spec JSON bridge for data boxes\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA data box (`kind: data` in box JSON) emits a value the rest of\nthe graph routes downstream. Today the runner reads the box's\n`ref` file as raw bytes and emits them — there's no concept of\n\"authoring this datum in a particular language using that\nlanguage's natural structures.\" If you want to declare a Lua\ntable as a data box's value, you either:\n\n- Hand-translate the table to JSON, save it as a `.json` file,\n  and lose the Lua syntax niceties; or\n- Make it a call box that returns the table, paying for a full\n  spec invocation just to read a constant; or\n- Hard-code the bytes inline in the box's `data` field, with no\n  syntactic help from any host language.\n\nThis is the wrong shape. **A box author writes idiomatic code in\nthe language of their choice.** That's the rule 307 establishes\nfor call boxes: a C-box author writes a plain C function, no\nSoraMech-specific glue. The data-box equivalent should hold —\na Lua-data-box author should write a Lua file that returns\nwhatever they want returned (a table, a string, a number), and\nSoraMech should know how to lift that into the graph as a JSON\nwire value without the author writing a single SoraMech-specific\ncharacter.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEvery language spec gains two callbacks, declared in\n`lang_spec_t` (issue 303):\n\n```c\n/* Serialize a native-language value into JSON text.\n *\n *   ctx       — per-worker handle from spec.init.\n *   src       — caller-meaningful pointer to the native value.\n *               Format is spec-specific (see \"Native handle\n *               representation\" below).\n *   src_size  — size hint, or 0 if the spec interprets `src`\n *               without a length.\n *   out_buf   — destination buffer for JSON text (caller-owned).\n *   out_cap   — capacity of out_buf.\n *   out_size  — set to the bytes written.\n *\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error. Writes an error message\n * via the spec's existing error-reporting plumbing. */\nint (*native_to_json)(void *ctx,\n                      const void *src, uint32_t src_size,\n                      char *out_buf, uint32_t out_cap, uint32_t *out_size);\n\n/* Inverse: parse JSON text into a native-language value. The\n * native value is stored wherever the spec considers natural\n * (Lua: pushed to the worker's lua_State stack; C: written into\n * a typed struct supplied by `dst`; Bash: written as a textual\n * representation back into dst).\n *\n *   ctx       — per-worker handle.\n *   src       — JSON text.\n *   src_size  — JSON text length in bytes.\n *   dst       — caller-supplied target; semantics per spec.\n *   dst_cap   — capacity, where meaningful.\n *   dst_size  — set to the bytes / native units consumed.\n *\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error. */\nint (*json_to_native)(void *ctx,\n                      const char *src, uint32_t src_size,\n                      void *dst, uint32_t dst_cap, uint32_t *dst_size);\n```\n\nThese are the same fields 312's same-language fast path\nreserves; this issue is the one that requires every spec to\n**actually implement them**, driven by the data-box use case.\n(312 needs them too, but its driver is performance; 317 needs\nthem for correctness — a data box can't function without them.)\n\n### The rule, restated\n\nThe author of a data box writes a `.lua` / `.c` / `.sh` /\n`.<whatever>` file that returns or produces a value using\n*their language's native idioms*. No SoraMech macros. No\nSoraMech includes. No SoraMech-specific JSON shape constraints\nbeyond \"what your spec's native_to_json can convert.\"\n\nIf the author returns a Lua table, the Lua spec's\n`native_to_json` converts it. If they return a C struct, the C\nspec's `native_to_json` walks it according to the type declared\nin the box. If they print JSON-ish text from a bash script, the\nbash spec's `native_to_json` is a no-op identity (the script\nalready produced JSON).\n\nThe contract belongs to the spec author, not the box author.\nThat's the inversion: **SoraMech bends to the language, not the\nother way around.**\n\n## Native handle representation\n\nThe shape of `src` / `dst` in the callbacks is per-spec. Each\nspec documents what it accepts:\n\n- **Lua spec**: `src` is the index of a value already pushed\n  onto the worker's `lua_State`. `src_size` is unused. The\n  spec's `native_to_json` reads the value at that stack index\n  and writes JSON. `json_to_native` pushes the parsed JSON value\n  onto the stack, and `dst_size` reports the number of stack\n  slots used (always 1 for SoraMech's flat-value model).\n- **C spec**: `src` is a typed pointer + the box's declared\n  output type drives the walk. `src_size` is the type's\n  storage footprint. Mirror image for `json_to_native`. (This\n  ties into 307's typed-wrapper-generation work — the same\n  type system describes both the wrapper signature and the\n  JSON shape.)\n- **Bash spec**: `src` is text the script produced.\n  `native_to_json` validates and reshapes to JSON if needed (a\n  bash script that prints `42` becomes JSON `42`; a script that\n  prints `{\"a\":1}` passes through unchanged). `json_to_native`\n  is similarly a near-identity. The spec author is encouraged\n  to require scripts produce well-formed JSON in the first\n  place rather than write a bash-syntax parser.\n\nThe dispatch layer doesn't know or care which representation a\nspec uses. It only ever passes `src` and `src_size` to the\nspec's callback. The spec is opaque to the runtime; that's the\nwhole point.\n\n## Data box semantics\n\nA data box's `data` field becomes optional. The box gains\noptional `lang` and `ref` fields:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"config\",\n  \"kind\": \"data\",\n  \"lang\": \"lua\",\n  \"ref\": \"config.lua\"\n}\n```\n\nAt graph load, the runner:\n\n1. Resolves the spec for `lang`.\n2. Calls the spec's `init` (already done at worker startup).\n3. At box-fire time, asks the spec to execute the `ref` file\n   and produce a native value (this is essentially the same\n   \"load this file, run it, get its return value\" path the\n   spec already implements for call boxes — call boxes call a\n   named function; data boxes take the file's return value).\n4. Calls the spec's `native_to_json` to convert the native\n   value to JSON text.\n5. Pushes that JSON text down the wire as the box's output —\n   same as today's data path, just with the value sourced\n   from a language-native file.\n\nIf the box has no `lang` and a literal `data` field, the legacy\ninline-data path applies unchanged.\n\n## Why every spec must implement these\n\nThe same JSON the data box emits is consumed by some downstream\nbox (call, comparator, file_write, whatever). That downstream\nbox, if it's in a different language, will eventually need\n*its* spec's `json_to_native` to convert the JSON back. So the\ntwo callbacks are paired — every spec that participates in the\ngraph needs both. A spec that implements `native_to_json` but\nnot `json_to_native` can only be data-box sources; a spec with\nonly `json_to_native` can only be call-box sinks. We require\nboth so any language can play any role.\n\nSpecs that haven't been updated yet should set both callbacks\nto a stub that returns -1 with a clear error message (\"spec\n`<name>`: native_to_json not implemented; this box's value\ncan't be routed cross-language\"). The hard-fail makes the gap\nloud rather than producing wrong output.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. Extend the `lang_spec_t` declaration in\n   `langs/lang-spec.h` if not already done by 312's\n   infrastructure work. (Per the round summary, the slot is\n   reserved.)\n2. Implement `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` in each\n   spec:\n   - **Lua spec**: walk the value at the stack index. Use the\n     existing C JSON writer (`libs/json/json.c`). Handle Lua\n     tables both as arrays (1-indexed contiguous integer keys)\n     and as objects. Refuse functions, userdata, threads.\n   - **C spec**: depends on 307's typed-wrapper machinery. For\n     now, a stub that only supports scalar types (int, double,\n     string) is enough to get data boxes working in C.\n   - **Bash spec**: validate-and-pass-through. The script is\n     expected to produce JSON. `native_to_json` runs the JSON\n     parser to validate; `json_to_native` is identity.\n3. Extend the data box runtime path in `src/012-dispatch.c`\n   (or wherever data boxes dispatch from) to consult `lang` /\n   `ref` when set and route through the spec callback chain.\n4. Add a fixture: `tests/maps/cross-lang-data/` with a Lua\n   data box, a C consumer, and a Bash consumer all reading the\n   same value. The integration check asserts each consumer\n   sees the right data.\n5. Update each spec's `*.info.md` to document the native handle\n   shape its callbacks expect.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — extend the contract\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` —\n  implement the callbacks\n- `langs/{lua,c,bash}/spec.info.md` — document native handle\n  semantics per spec\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — data-box dispatch path\n- `tests/maps/cross-lang-data/` — new fixture (see step 4)\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — same author-writes-natural-\n  code principle; this issue extends it from call boxes to data\n  boxes\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — reuses the same\n  spec callbacks for a different (performance) reason\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Bash's `json_to_native` is a near-identity because the\n  scripts already deal in text. Is there value in having it\n  validate and reformat for consistency? Probably yes; cheap\n  insurance against malformed downstream input.\n- Should the Lua spec auto-detect array-vs-object tables, or\n  require the box author to annotate? Auto-detect (contiguous\n  1-indexed integer keys → array; otherwise object) is what\n  every other lua-to-json library does and is intuitive enough.\n- C spec's `native_to_json` for arbitrary structs is a real\n  rabbit hole. Tie scope to 307 — the same type declarations\n  drive both the wrapper and the JSON walk. Until 307 lands,\n  only scalar types are supported for C data boxes.\n",

Until 307 lands,\n  only scalar types are supported for C data boxes.\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### 2026-05-19 — Lua bridges landed\n\nImplemented the first concrete pair of bridges. Scope: only the\nLua spec; C and Bash still NULL their bridge slots and fall back\nto the uniform-byte default.\n\n**Design decisions made during this round (kept for later\nimplementers of the C / Bash bridges):**\n\n- **Bridge signature has the worker handle as the first arg.**\n  The previous declaration in `lang-spec.h` was missing it; without\n  it Lua can't reach its `lua_State`. C and Bash will need it for\n  the same reason once they grow real bridges.\n\n- **Stack-protocol convention for the native side.** The bridge\n  reads / writes the producer's working store directly, not the\n  `src` / `dst` buffers. For Lua: `native_to_json` consumes the\n  value at the top of the `lua_State` (pops on success); `json_to_native`\n  pushes the reconstructed value to the top. The `src` / `dst`\n  buffers carry only the JSON side of the conversion. This keeps\n  the wire format opaque to specs and avoids inventing a \"native\n  byte\" serialization just so it can fit through a buffer.\n\n- **Wire primitive vocabulary.** Three JSON-with-extensions\n  primitives are reserved for the harder types; this round did not\n  emit any of them, but every future bridge must agree on the\n  names: `$ref` (shared-memory pointer + length), `$function_pointer`\n  (decomposed callable: address + signature), `$lang_opaque`\n  (last-resort sealed envelope routed only between same-language\n  endpoints — escape hatch, not a default).\n\n- **No handles, no back-routing.** The wire must carry data the\n  destination spec can reconstruct on its own — never a token that\n  says \"operations on this value cross back to the source spec.\"\n  See `memory/feedback_cross_language_pitfalls.md` for the longer\n  argument; the principle constrains every bridge implementation.\n\n- **Type ambiguities are resolved by wiring, not by annotation.**\n  When a function signature has hidden pairings (a `char *` with a\n  separate length argument, a `union` with a discriminator, a\n  callback with a context pointer), the destination spec exposes\n  *each* parameter as its own input slot on the box. The user wires\n  them according to the function's English docs. The system never\n  prompts the user with vocabulary words it has no general way to\n  ask about.\n\n**Files touched:**\n\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — `lang_bridge_fn` now takes `void *handle`\n  as its first parameter; the doc comment documents the stack\n  protocol.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c` — added `encode_value`, `decode_node`,\n  `lua_native_to_json`, `lua_json_to_native`. Wired the last two\n  into `soramech_lang_spec`.\n- `langs/lua/Makefile` — folds `libs/json/json.c` straight into\n  `spec.so` so the spec stays self-contained.\n- `tests/317-lua-bridge-test.c` — new round-trip test (JSON →\n  lua_State → JSON, compare).\n- `Makefile` — added the test's dependency line.\n\n**Tests:** 5/5 in `317-lua-bridge-test`; full suite green.\n\n**Known impedance-mismatch case (documented in the test):** `null`\ninside a JSON array becomes Lua `nil`, and `lua_objlen` truncates\nthe sequence at the first hole. The bridge round-trips\n`[true,false,null]` as `[true,false]`. This is fundamental Lua\nsemantics and is asserted explicitly rather than glossed over.\nA future `$lang_opaque` or an explicit `n` field convention is the\nway out; not needed yet.\n\n**Next implementation slices:**\n\n1. Bash bridges — near-identity (scripts are already producing\n   text). `native_to_json` validates the text is well-formed JSON;\n   `json_to_native` is identity. No `lua_State`-style scratch\n   needed, so the bridge can ignore `handle`.\n2. C bridges — depends on 307's typed wrapper work. Until 307\n   lands, scalar types (int / double / string) is enough to\n   unblock data-box semantics.\n3. Wire the bridges into the dispatch layer (issue 312's\n   wire-classification path) so cross-language edges actually\n   round-trip through them.",

        "text":"Two parts to my reply. First the impedance question, then a survey of the in-progress files before I start committing.\n\n## What the null-in-array case implies for the bridge\n\nIt's a load-bearing finding, not a curiosity. The wire format (JSON) carries strictly more shape than any one host language. Lua loses `null` inside sequences. C will lose JSON's tag-free number when it can't tell int from double without a type declaration. Bash will lose nested structure unless we mandate JSON-formatted output.\n\nSo the bridge is **not symmetric per-spec** — a value entering Lua-side may not come out structurally identical on the other side. This forks the design into two stances we need to pick between:\n\n1. **Lossy round-trips are the box author's problem.** Same-language wires (issue 312) stay lossless; cross-language wires go through JSON and the user is told at wire-compile time when the source language can express something the destination can't. We add a compatibility check at graph-load (e.g. \"Lua → C edge: target type `int[]` cannot contain null — your Lua data box returns an array with nil\") and otherwise accept the limitation.\n\n2. **The bridge invents a per-language convention to preserve JSON faithfully.** For Lua specifically: arrays carry an explicit `{n=3, [1]=true, [2]=false, [3]=nil}` shape; the bridge encodes/decodes around the `n` field. Heavier; intrudes on idiomatic Lua; but every value survives a round-trip.\n\nMy instinct is **(1)** — it matches the project's \"bend to the language, not the other way around\" rule. The user wrote a Lua data box; they wrote idiomatic Lua; if their value can't be expressed in the destination language that's a real graph-compile error, not something we hide behind a sentinel. Option (2) only buys you fidelity for cross-language wires where both sides happen to be lossy in different ways.\n\nBut this is a directional call — want me to record it in issue 317 as the decided stance, or hold off until you've thought it through?\n\n## Surveying the in-progress files before committing\n\nLet me first read the modified issue files and untracked new files so I know which changes belong to which ticket."

## [290]

```json
{
  "userType":"external",
  "parentUuid":"7a1ab99e-0815-4d5f-a6d6-2472b158f545",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-20T02:36:31.455Z",

    "stdout":"==> /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/217-variadic-ports-and-language-spec-shape.md <==\n# 217 — Variadic ports and the language-spec variadic shape\n\n## Status\nopen — Part A and Part B mechanics are in the codebase; Part C is\nthe active design question\n\n## What this issue is now\n\nThe original issue was titled \"Concat box with per-input variadic\nports and auto-grow/shrink.\" That framing has aged out:\n\n- There is no dedicated **concat box kind**. `M.concat(sep, ...)`\n  lives in `libs/text.lua` and is invoked by any call box that\n  imports it. The variadic UI work was never specific to concat.\n- The original \"split returns a JSON-encoded array on the single\n  output wire\" story was a phase-2 transport assumption. Phase 3\n  (issue 312, same-language wire fast path) classifies each edge\n  and only JSON-encodes when crossing a language boundary. So\n  `M.split` returning a Lua array is correct in-language and the\n  runtime bridges if the downstream box is a different language.\n\nThe issue is now about the **editor's variadic-port mechanic** and\nhow it interacts with the **language spec** — specifically, what\nthe editor's `var` toggle means and what governs whether it's\noffered.\n\n## Part A — `libs/text.lua` *(shipped)*\n\n`libs/text.lua` ships `M.concat(sep, ...)`, `M.split(text, sep)`,\nand (via issue 237) `upper`, `lower`, `trim`, `replace`,\n`replace_first`, `contains`, `starts_with`, `ends_with`, `length`,\n`substring`. Re-deriving from your stance:\n\n- **Lua → JSON**: a Lua table `{[1]=true, [2]=false, [3]=nil}` has only TWO entries in Lua's actual storage — nil isn't stored, so the encoder physically can't see that slot 3 was \"meant to be there.\" Lua's tables can't represent \"explicit null in position 3\" idiomatically. To preserve fidelity we have to intrude — e.g. an `n` field that records the intended length, or a sidecar null-sentinel, or a JSON-side type tag.\n- **JSON → Lua → JSON round-trip**: the loss happens at the JSON → Lua step (nil-in-array vanishes).         },
        "type":"tool_use",
        "input":{
          "new_string":"**Known impedance-mismatch case (documented in the test):** `null`\ninside a JSON array becomes Lua `nil`, and `lua_objlen` truncates\nthe sequence at the first hole. The bridge round-trips\n`[true,false,null]` as `[true,false]`. This is fundamental Lua\nsemantics and is asserted explicitly rather than glossed over.\n\nThis stage-1 lossiness is **not the final design.** See the\nfidelity directive below — stage 2 must preserve the JSON shape\nthrough Lua via an explicit length field, accepting that this\nintrudes on idiomatic Lua.\n\n## Fidelity directive (added 2026-05-19, supersedes earlier \"lossy is OK\" thinking)\n\nThe wire format (JSON) is canonical. **A value leaving a box's\noutput slot and entering the wire must not lose fidelity.** The\nbridge intrudes on the language as needed to achieve that. The\nlanguage's idioms are upheld on the in-language side (inside the\nbox's source file); on the wire side the bridge is allowed —\nrequired — to use whatever encoding preserves the shape.\n\nThis reverses the earlier instinct that lossy round-trips were\n\"the box author's problem.\" They're the bridge's problem. The\nbox author writes idiomatic Lua / C / bash; the bridge converts\nwithout dropping anything.\n\n### Concrete rules per language\n\n- **Lua → JSON** (and JSON → Lua → JSON round-trip): preserve\n  array shape including embedded nulls. The decoder pushes\n  arrays as `{n = N, [1] = ..., [2] = ..., ...}` where `n` is the\n  intended length and missing integer keys are real nil slots.\n  The encoder reads `n` if present and emits a full-length JSON\n  array with `null` at every missing slot. Idiomatic Lua tables\n  without `n` continue to encode via the existing\n  array-vs-object heuristic — `n` is only required when the\n  caller cares about distinguishing \"trailing nil\" from \"shorter\n  array.\" Same scheme handles intermixed nil-in-middle too.\n\n- **Lua → JSON** (type annotations): the bridge may emit a\n  type-tagged JSON shape when the destination language needs\n  more than JSON's native types convey (e.g. int vs float when\n  the Lua value is whole-numbered but the destination expects a\n  float, or vice versa). The tag lives in the JSON itself, not\n  in a sidecar protocol. Suggested shape: a `$type` key inside a\n  small wrapper object, only emitted when the encoder can tell\n  the unwrapped value would be ambiguous downstream.\n\n- **C → JSON**: C functions have declared types — emit those\n  types as part of the JSON, so any downstream language can\n  honour them without guessing. Lua receivers may use the type\n  to coerce (e.g. force `2` instead of `2.0`); receivers that\n  don't care can ignore the type tag.\n\n- **JSON → C**: when the wire value doesn't fit the destination\n  C type (a float arriving at an int slot, a string at a number\n  slot), the C bridge **truncates / coerces and records a\n  warning** at map-compile time. The warning surfaces in the\n  compile output, not at run time. Silent dropping is forbidden;\n  hard-failing the compile is too aggressive — the user may\n  know the truncation is fine.\n\n- **JSON → Lua / JSON → bash**: same coercion rule, with\n  language-appropriate fallbacks. The receiver records the\n  warning.\n\n### Why this lives in the bridge, not the box author\n\nA box author writes a function in their language. They don't\nwrite a SoraMech-aware serializer. The bridge — which is the\nspec author's responsibility, not the box author's — owns every\ndetail of how their language's values reach JSON and how JSON\nreaches their language's values. The box author writes\nidiomatic code; the bridge does whatever is necessary on the\nJSON side, including unwrapping `n`-fielded tables back into\nidiomatic Lua at decode time so subsequent in-language calls\nsee clean tables.\n\nThis is the same principle the rest of 317 already states: the\nspec bends to the language at the box surface, and bends the\nwire shape to the language at the bridge. The language never\nbends to the wire.",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"**Known impedance-mismatch case (documented in the test):** `null`\ninside a JSON array becomes Lua `nil`, and `lua_objlen` truncates\nthe sequence at the first hole. The bridge round-trips\n`[true,false,null]` as `[true,false]`. This is fundamental Lua\nsemantics and is asserted explicitly rather than glossed over.\nA future `$lang_opaque` or an explicit `n` field convention is the\nway out; not needed yet.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/317-spec-json-bridge-for-data-boxes.md"
